articles.title: Trump's war on reality: when AI becomes a substitute for victory
articles.body:
Trump's war on reality: when AI becomes a substitute for victory
TEHRAN – In yet another delusional outburst from the decaying American empire, Donald Trump has once again proven that Washington's leadership has lost all touch with reality. His August 31 declaration that "Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!" represents not strategic analysis, but the desperate hallucinations of a regime accustomed to imposing its will through deception.
Nations do not cease to exist because a bankrupt politician declares them so on social media. Iran's ancient civilization has weathered far greater storms than the current Zio-American pressure campaign and will certainly outlast the current crop of Western leaders whose grip on reality grows more tenuous by the day.
More concerning is Trump's brazen use of artificial intelligence as an instrument of psychological warfare. The fabricated video purporting to show Kharg Island's destruction, later admitted to be AI-generated by Vice President JD Vance, represents a new low in American propaganda. When Washington presents imaginary destruction as accomplished fact, it reveals its fundamental weakness: the inability to achieve strategic objectives through legitimate means. The Zionist-inspired American regime has long understood the power of spectacle, from Hollywood's vilification of Iran to the systematic erasure of Palestinian identity. But war is less forgiving than electoral theater. Missiles do not disappear because a bankrupt real estate mogul declares the enemy finished. Sovereign nations do not surrender because Washington announces their defeat through artificial images.
The contradiction in American policy toward Iran is glaring. If Iran is already "dead," why does Washington continue to warn Tehran about future consequences? Why does the administration still describe Iranian attacks as a serious threat to American forces and commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf? The answer is simple: the battlefield reality contradicts the propaganda. Iran has not only survived Washington's maximum pressure campaign but has demonstrated remarkable resilience. Despite facing the most comprehensive economic warfare in modern history, Iran continues to advance its scientific capabilities, maintain regional influence, and defend its sovereignty. Iran's military capabilities remain formidable, as evidenced by the embarrassing failures of American and Israeli operations against Iranian assets. The Islamic Republic's air defense systems, naval presence in the strategic Persian Gulf, and missile capabilities continue to pose a genuine deterrent to Zionist ambitions in the region.
One cannot separate Washington's hostility toward Iran from the corrosive influence of the Zionist lobby on American foreign policy. The relentless push for confrontation serves Tel Aviv's interests far more than America's. Why should American soldiers sacrifice their lives for Israeli security? Why should American taxpayers fund endless conflicts that only benefit the apartheid regime in occupied Palestine? The Iranian people have repeatedly demonstrated their capacity to resist foreign domination. From the 1979 Islamic Revolution to the present, Iran has consistently rejected Western attempts to impose its will. The American war of words against Iran is fundamentally a war against national sovereignty and the right to chart one's own destiny free from imperial interference.
Perhaps most disturbing is Washington's callous exploitation of human suffering. Reported casualty figures from American sources have shifted dramatically from tens of thousands to more than 100,000 alleged deaths with little evidence to support these claims. If accurate, these figures represent a humanitarian catastrophe demanding independent verification. If inaccurate, their use as political slogans reduces human tragedy to mere ammunition in Washington's propaganda war. The Islamic Republic has repeatedly called for international investigations into American and Israeli war crimes, including the systematic assassination of Iranian scientists, cyberattacks on civilian infrastructure, and economic warfare that constitutes collective punishment under international humanitarian law.
Washington's reckless rhetoric also threatens the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Any serious confrontation in the Persian Gulf would have devastating consequences for regional security and the global economy. These realities cannot be managed through memes, AI-generated videos, or declarations that an entire nation is "dead." The Islamic Republic has consistently demonstrated its commitment to regional stability, unlike the American regime that has left a trail of destruction from Afghanistan to Libya to Yemen.
When political leaders become more invested in declaring victory than establishing facts, credibility becomes collateral damage. The United States' strategic asset should be its credibility, yet every false image or exaggerated claim weakens this foundation. Propaganda can shape perception, but perception cannot substitute for strategy. AI can manufacture the image of a destroyed island. Social media can manufacture the appearance of triumph. None of it can manufacture victory. Military power can destroy infrastructure, but it cannot, by itself, manufacture political outcomes. This is a lesson America learned in Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq, and will inevitably learn in its confrontation with Iran.
While Washington indulges in fantasies of Iranian collapse, the Islamic Republic continues to demonstrate remarkable resilience. Iran has transformed challenges into opportunities for self-reliance and technological advancement, from nuclear technology to biotechnology, from aerospace to nanotechnology. Iran's political system, grounded in Islamic values and republican institutions, has proven its legitimacy through successive elections and popular participation. The American claim that Iran is a "failed state" ignores the reality of a functioning government that provides services to its citizens, maintains security across its vast territory, and continues to exert influence from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean.
The broader issue extends far beyond Iran. The American empire is in terminal decline, unable to accept that the unipolar moment has passed. Washington's desperate attempts to maintain global hegemony through sanctions and military threats reflect not strength but weakness. China, Russia, and the emerging multipolar order represent a future that respects national sovereignty and cultural diversity. Iran will continue strengthening its ties with these powers, reducing its vulnerability to American pressure. The so-called "America First" policy reveals itself as "America Alone," isolated from the global consensus that rejects unilateralism.
Trump may dominate the news cycle with a post. He may make an artificial image trend across social media. None of that changes the battlefield reality.
Iran will continue its path of dignity, resistance, and development. The Islamic Republic will survive American propaganda, Zionist ambitions, and imperial pressures. Iranian civilization has endured for millennia; it will not collapse because a bankrupt American politician declares it "dead" on social media. The American empire, meanwhile, continues its inevitable decline, hoisted by its own petard of deception and moral bankruptcy. History will judge which civilization truly failed.

articles.title: Faith in fakes: How anti-Russian hysteria is driving the EU’s drone hoax
articles.body:
Faith in fakes: How anti-Russian hysteria is driving the EU’s drone hoax
Is it a bird? Is it a plane? Is it a well-timed ploy to ramp up defense spending? Germany's evidence-free claim that a drone found lying between Ukrainian cargo planes on the canopy of Leipzig/Halle airport is part of a pattern.
Last year's late-autumn drone sighting hysteria that swept across Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands and Belgium, was used by the bloc to amplify and entrench an anti-Russia stance that has seen it throw hundreds of billions it cannot afford into weapons and a war its chosen side cannot win.
Tens of millions of Euro has since been spent on the back of a 'scare' that has been shown to have been irrational, exuberant and driven by vested interests.
The most bizarre national security scare in recent European history began at Copenhagen’s Kastrup Airport on September 2 last year. According to Denmark’s Frihedsbrevet news site, an airport employee told her supervisors that she saw two drones approach the area “stealthily,” adding that “they are big. They are not toys.”
The airport was temporarily shut down, and within hours, reports of a similar drone incursion came in from Oslo, Norway.
“I can only say that this is in my eyes a serious attack on Danish critical infrastructure,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at the time. “I cannot in any way deny that it is Russia.” Her Norwegian counterpart, Gahr Store, came to a similar conclusion. “Russia has violated Norwegian airspace on three occasions this spring and summer,” he claimed. “We cannot determine whether this was done intentionally or due to navigation errors. Regardless of the cause, this is not acceptable.”
“It is clear we are witnessing a pattern of persistent contestation at our borders,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. “Our critical infrastructure is at risk. And Europe will respond to this threat with strength and determination.”
Open-source investigators insisted that the sightings were a hoax from the outset. Sleuths on the Metabunk forums concluded that the ‘drone’ seen at Kastrup Airport in the above footage was actually a small single-engine plane. FlightRadar24 data showed one such plane – a Socata TB-20 Trinidad – passing over the airport’s main runway twice at the time of the sighting.
Where were drones spotted?
Nevertheless, panic spread across northern Europe as drones were supposedly spotted at the following airports, military bases, and infrastructure sites in the following days and weeks:
- September 23: Aalborg Airport, Denmark
- September 24: Aalborg Airport, Billund Airport, Sonderborg, Esbjerg and Skrydstrup airports, Denmark
- September 25: Billund Airport, Denmark; Thyssenkrupp factory, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany; University Medical Center, Kiel, Germany; Bundeswehr base, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Germany
September 26: Karup Air Base, Skrydstrup Air Base, Jutland Dragoon Regiment base, Denmark
- September 27: Orland Main Air Station, Norway
- September 28: Bronnoysund Airport, Norway; Borris Camp, Denmark
- October 2: Munich Airport, Germany; Elsenborn-Butgenbach Air Base, Belgium
- October 3: Munich Airport, Germany
- October 31: Berlin-Brandenburg Airport, Germany
- November 2: Bremen Airport, Germany; Kleine Brogel Air Base, Belgium
- November 6: Gothenburg Airport, Sweden; Brussels Airport, Antwerp Port, Belgium
- November 9: Liege Airport, Doel Nuclear Power Plant, Belgium
- November 22: Volkel Air Base, Netherlands
- December 1: In the Irish Sea off Dublin, during Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s arrival by plane
Police across northern Europe received thousands of additional drone reports from civilians. In Denmark alone, nearly 6,000 reports of suspected drones were filed.
Did the drones even exist?
Not only is there no proof that Russia was connected with these sightings, there is no evidence that any drones were present at all. No wreckage has been recovered, no perpetrators have been identified, and no footage of the drones exists, except for the video from Copenhagen that apparently shows a light aircraft.
Despite being certain that Denmark was under “hybrid attack,” Mette Frederiksen acknowledged in late September that there could be an “alternate explanation” for the sightings. Six months later, six government sources told Denmark’s TV2 that they don’t “have any technical evidence to support that Denmark was subjected to a hybrid attack with drones.” Frihedsbrevet’s sources came to a similar conclusion, with the airport employee who reported the initial sighting admitting that she could have been mistaken.
Airport management still insist that drones were present in the area on September 22, but police have not acknowledged any drones, only “reports” of drones.
Danish troops reportedly opened fire on a drone over Borris Camp on September 28. According to an investigation by TV2, the only aircraft operating in the area at the time was a turboprop passenger plane. The Danish military, if TV2’s reporting is correct, nearly shot down a civilian aircraft over a false alarm.
After interviewing witnesses and reviewing surveillance footage, Norwegian police closed their investigation on November 6, stating that they were “unable to confirm or deny whether drones were actually observed on the night of September 23.”
German police have not been able to confirm any drone activity; Dutch officials have identified no threat, with internal documents stating that there was “no indication of sabotage or attacks on vital objects.” Dutch and Belgian authorities have found no credible basis for panic, with Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken issuing a half-apology last month for attempting to pass off a video of a police helicopter as evidence of nefarious aerial activity.
Did they just lie?
Out of every country involved, Denmark’s leaders were most insistent that Russia was behind the spate of sightings. Frederiksen, Defense Minister Troels Lund Poulsen, and Justice Minister Peter Hummelgaard all described the incidents as “attacks,” despite nothing being attacked and no attackers being present.
“I consider it a new reality that Denmark and Europe are under more violent and frequent hybrid attacks,” Frederiksen said in a televised address on September 25. “And even though the authorities cannot conclude who is behind the hybrid attacks…there is primarily one country that poses a threat to Europe's security – and that is Russia.”
The flood of tips and reports from the public can be written off either as mass hysteria, or – more charitably – as a natural reaction from Europeans primed by their politicians and media to believe that Russia is planning an all-out war on the continent. As for why Frederiksen would stoke this fear, however, some clues can be found in her actions.
At the time, Denmark was just over a year into an historic rearmament program. After a €5.4 billion military budget hike in 2024, Frederiksen announced last February that defense spending would be increased from 2.4% to 3% of GDP by 2030 (since increased to 3.5%). By late 2025, Denmark had purchased hundreds of armored combat vehicles, signed contracts for new air defense systems, increased annual conscription numbers, and, for the first time in its history, introduced compulsory military service for women.
Denmark, she said last February, needs to undergo a “massive rearmament,” because “We don’t know what [Russian President Vladimir Putin] is planning, but we know that he and Russia are in the process of rearming.”
Frederiksen referenced this rearmament again in her September address, declaring that “the events of recent days only emphasize how important it is.”
Denmark held the EU’s rotating presidency at the time, and Frederiksen added that the alleged drone threat would be made front and center when EU leaders met in Copenhagen the following week, and that she would push for “the establishment of an actual drone wall.”
The EU’s drone wall
Frederiksen kept her word. Published on October 16, the European Commission’s ‘Defense Readiness Roadmap’ stated that a ‘European Drone Defense Initiative’ – the so-called “drone wall” comprising sensors and interceptors – would be operational along the bloc’s eastern borders with Russia and Belarus by 2027.
🚨🇪🇺 “We need to act now”Ursula von der Leyen now wants to build a “Drone Wall” on the Eastern Flank of Europe to protect from the alleged Russian Aggression. pic.twitter.com/UAGH93fKRc
— Concerned Citizen (@BGatesIsaPyscho) October 1, 2025
Drones continued to dominate the agenda at a European Council summit in Brussels in December. “The European Council strongly condemns all recent hybrid attacks against the European Union and its Member States,” read a statement released after the meeting. “In the light of Russia’s and Belarus’ intensified hybrid campaign, it calls for accelerated efforts to strengthen resilience, protect critical infrastructure, and…decisively ramp up Europe’s defense readiness by 2030.”
None of this is to suggest that Denmark orchestrated the drone panic to justify its remilitarization, or to sell the EU’s “drone wall.” Both initiatives were already underway at the time. Instead, it illustrates how Danish and EU officials saw an opportunity not to let a crisis go to waste, and kept the drone threat alive even as their own police forces, to put it mildly, struggled to substantiate it.
Belgium's very own drone crisis
Frederiksen wasn’t the only national leader who saw an opportunity amid the panic. Remember Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken? After police hotlines were flooded with more than 550 reports of drones between September and December, Francken bypassed the standard bidding process to authorize the purchase of €50 million worth of drone detection and jamming systems.
An investigation by Belgium’s VRT broadcaster has since found that none of the reports of drones were credible, and Francken has been hammered by the opposition for sharing an image of a ‘drone’ over Brussels Airport that turned out to be a police helicopter. VRT found that the defense ministry ignored warnings from Belgium’s Inspectorate of Finance and purchased detection antennas at an inflated price, and Francken is now the subject of an inquiry by the Brussels Public Prosecutor's Office.
The debacle is reminiscent of the Agusta-Dassault affair. During the 1980s, defense contractors Agusta and Dassault paid the equivalent of €4 million in bribes to secure no-bid contracts for AW109 transport helicopters and electronic warfare equipment. Once exposed, the scandal led to the criminal conviction of Belgian Defense Minister Guy Coeme and Foreign Minister and NATO Secretary General Willy Claes.
So did Russian drones spook the EU?
Nearly eight months after the first ‘drones’ were spotted over Copenhagen, the crisis is still being milked across Europe. In early May, long after the threat had been debunked in Denmark, Norway, Belgium, and the Netherlands, the Dutch defense ministry announced that it would acquire approximately 900 “electro-optical aiming devices” for use against UAVs, “without prior announcement due to the urgency of a crisis situation.”
Questioned by the Belgian parliament in April, Francken insisted that there is “no other plausible explanation” for the reports other than Russian drones, and that the only way to prove or disprove this is to invest in drone defense technology. “As long as you don’t have the means to detect and neutralize drones, it stands to reason that you cannot immediately produce physical evidence,” he told lawmakers.
The Dutch and Belgians aren’t letting a lack of evidence stop them from pursuing the defense deals that they wanted from this crisis, and the EU is unlikely to step in and pump the brakes.
The EU's censorious and paranoid media industry is the perfect environment for fake news to fester, as long as it suits the bloc. Remember, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's claims of “GPS jamming” hitting her plane on a trip to Bulgaria last September, and how, despite it being roundly debunked within days, it has been allowed to fester to serve her political agenda.
Anti-Russian hysteria is the animating political force in the EU, and the bloc’s leaders clearly aren’t going to let police and media investigations, or common sense, put a stop to the show.

articles.title: Putin on Kiev’s ‘terrorism,’ British ‘legitimate targets’ and a ‘military secret’ (KEY REMARKS)
articles.body:
Putin on Kiev’s ‘terrorism,’ British ‘legitimate targets’ and a ‘military secret’ (KEY REMARKS)
Russian President Vladimir Putin has outlined Russia’s accelerating battlefield gains in Ukraine, denounced Kiev’s increasingly desperate threats to civilian aviation as a bid for “state terrorism,” and warned that British military facilities on Ukrainian soil would be “legitimate targets.”
Speaking to reporters in Bishkek, Putin also addressed Moscow’s strikes on ships carrying weapons to Ukraine, contacts with US intelligence and Trump’s envoys, relations with Germany, and what he described as the West’s “sharks of imperialism.”
Here are the key takeaways:
’The enemy will crumble’
Putin said Ukrainian forces are steadily losing ground, while cautioning against predicting exactly when a decisive turning point could come because “war is cruel and difficult to predict.”
Russian troops are not merely advancing but “increasing the pace of the offensive,” he said, giving a detailed rundown of developments across the front. Putin said Russian forces are approaching Slavyansk, Kramatorsk and Druzhkovka, while claiming that roughly 5,000 Ukrainian troops have been physically encircled near the Krasnooskolskoye Reservoir. He also reported advances in Zaporozhye Region and toward Sumy.
“I have no doubt that the enemy will ‘crumble.’ The question of timing is always very complicated.”
The Russian president also rejected proposals merely to freeze the conflict along the current front line.
“We don’t want to freeze it. We want to end the war and achieve a lasting, absolute peace – both in Ukraine and in Europe.”
’No negotiations with terrorists’
Asked about Vladimir Zelensky’s threat to civilian airlines using Russian airspace, Putin said the remarks amounted to “a bid for state terrorism,” contrasting them with Kiev’s simultaneous calls for “negotiations and personal meetings.”
“You don’t negotiate with terrorists,” Putin said, warning that if attacks on civilian aircraft were actually carried out, Moscow would find a way to respond.
Asked whether Ukrainian political and military leaders could become targets, Putin said Moscow has so far refrained from such strikes because it may ultimately need people on the Ukrainian side with whom to negotiate.
“This is a bid for terrorism; it is not yet a transition to terrorism. If it comes to that, we will see how to respond. We will find the tools.”
’They hit ours – they’ll get an answer’
Putin said the Russian military has been ordered to prepare “massive strikes” against Ukrainian energy facilities in response to attacks on Russian civilian and fuel infrastructure. Ukrainian drones again attempted overnight to penetrate the air defenses of Moscow and St. Petersburg and strike three Russian oil refineries, but the attacks were repelled, according to the president.
“They hit ours – they’ll get an answer. That’s roughly how things stand.”
Putin also said a recent decree allowing temporary state management of poorly protected critical infrastructure was intended to force private companies and state agencies to cooperate more closely on defense against drone attacks, rejecting suggestions that it amounted to nationalization.
’Kiev opened Pandora’s box’
Putin stressed that Russia had not been attacking Ukrainian shipping at random, but had targeted only vessels that were bringing weapons or ammunition into Ukraine, arguing that secondary explosions following the attacks confirmed the nature of their cargoes.
“We did carry out precision strikes on certain vessels, but they were genuinely selective.”
The president said Moscow expanded its maritime response only after Zelensky launched his much-touted 40-day campaign against the Russian economy and logistics. According to Putin, Kiev failed to inflict any “critical damage” but hit around 100 vessels and killed several sailors, including foreign nationals.
“You yourselves opened Pandora’s box – now take what comes.”
Putin recalled that the original Black Sea grain initiative had been promoted as essential to averting hunger in developing countries, particularly in Africa. Yet, according to him, only around 0.2% of Ukrainian grain exported under the arrangement reached developing markets, while most went to comparatively wealthy European countries.
CIA contacts and Trump’s ‘welcome guests’
Putin dismissed the idea that contacts between Russian and American intelligence chiefs were unusual, noting that such channels remained open even during the Cold War. He singled out Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, describing the Trump confidants as sincere interlocutors who have the US president’s trust.
“Mr. Kushner and Witkoff are always welcome guests here, and we work with them with pleasure.”
Moscow is open to additional participants in Ukraine talks if they can make a concrete contribution, Putin added, while warning against allowing diplomacy to revolve in a “meaningless mode.”
British targets and a ‘military secret’
Putin confirmed that any British military facilities established on Ukrainian territory would be considered legitimate targets by Russian forces.
“Any military facilities in Ukraine are our legitimate targets – British ones, any others.”
Asked whether British military-industrial facilities inside the UK itself could become targets if British weapons were used to strike Russia, Putin declined to reveal where Moscow’s red lines lie.
“That’s a secret. A military secret.”
Germany just needs to ‘press the button’
Putin also rejected German accusations surrounding a drone incident in Leipzig, arguing that Berlin is invoking the threat of an “aggressive Russia” to distract from domestic political and economic problems.
He recalled earlier accusations that Moscow had sabotaged its own Nord Stream pipelines, calling the allegation absurd given Russia’s interest in selling gas to Europe.
Russia remains capable of supplying Germany with gas, he said.
“They only need to press the button.”
German leaders, however, lack the political will to do so because of US sanctions, Putin said, describing Berlin’s broader Russia policy as contrary to the interests of the German people.
Western ‘sharks of imperialism’
Putin was also asked to explain a recent analogy involving orcas, polar bears and Russia’s confrontation with the West.
He joked that comparing the collective West to an orca would be unfair to the animal, describing killer whales as intelligent creatures. Instead, he revived an old Soviet expression: “the sharks of imperialism.”
“If someone tries to drag us down the food chain and gobble us up, they may get hit in the teeth. Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks.”

articles.title: Agenstvo: CIA director traveled to Moscow to urge peace talks. Putin planned to meet him but changed his mind.
articles.body:
Agenstvo: CIA director traveled to Moscow to urge peace talks. Putin planned to meet him but changed his mind.
Vladimir Putin had planned to meet with CIA Director John Ratcliffe during his August 25 visit to Moscow but called it off after learning the purpose of the trip, a source close to the Kremlin told the independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo.
According to the source, Ratcliffe urged Russian leadership to reach a deal to end the war with Ukraine as soon as possible, arguing that Russia’s military and economic situation is deteriorating and that the Kremlin would be better off striking a deal now rather than waiting to weaken further.
Ratcliffe met with Sergey Naryshkin, head of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), and Alexander Bortnikov, head of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to Western media. The substance of one of those conversations reached Putin, prompting the Kremlin to call off his personal meeting with Ratcliffe — a meeting Putin had initially cleared his schedule to hold.
The New York Times previously reported that Ratcliffe shared with Bortnikov his “bleak assessment” of Russia’s position in the war with Ukraine and called for peace talks to begin.
The Agentstvo source said the CIA director’s message sounded as though “Volodymyr Zelensky is already standing on Poklonnaya Hill, looking at the Kremlin through binoculars.” “Everyone understands that’s not the case. It seems Ratcliffe got the wrong address,” he added.
It remains unclear whether the CIA director’s position on the Russia–Ukraine war reflected the view of the White House as a whole.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow marked the first trip by the head of the American intelligence agency to Russia since the start of the full-scale war. The visit was unannounced and conducted in secrecy.
The Kremlin announced that Putin did not meet with Ratcliffe, though the American official spoke with representatives of Russia’s intelligence agencies.
Western media have offered several theories about the purpose of the CIA director’s visit, from urging the start of peace talks and warning against an attack on NATO countries to calling for reduced cooperation with Iran.
According to the American news outlet Axios, Ratcliffe also proposed a meeting of the presidents of the United States, Russia, and Ukraine. The Kremlin stated that such a meeting would only be possible to “finalize agreements.”
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: ‘Gifts are on the way’: Iran says it will no longer exercise restraint with US allies after strikes
articles.body:
Iran launched retaliatory strikes on US bases in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain, overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday, following the US's renewal of strikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran on Tuesday.
Sirens sounded in Kuwait as the country's air defenses confronted attacks by hostile drones, "following the sinful Iranian aggression," Kuwait's army said in a post on X/Twitter on Wednesday morning.
"The sounds of explosions, if heard, are the result of air defense systems intercepting the hostile attacks."
Meanwhile, the Bahraini Interior Ministry announced "an alert of potential threat" in the country, with local sources telling Iranian state media IRIB that at least four consecutive explosions were heard.
Iran strikes Iraq
In a statement the IRGC claimed to have carried out a combined missile and drone attack on US bases in Erbil, Iraq.
The attack "destroyed a maintenance center and technical equipment warehouses belonging to the US military and destroying the US spy balloon guidance system at the base," the IRGC statement claimed.
"The Ground Force fighters also set the base’s fuel depots on fire and killed several of the US Forces," it added. "A large number of American troops were sent to hell."
IRIB also reported that explosions were heard near the US consulate in Erbil, Iraq. Local media also reported an impact.
Neither the US nor Iraq have confirmed such attacks.
Jordanian army intercepted 10 of 13 Iranian ballistic missiles
Sirens sounded in Jordan as air defenses intercepted 10 of the 13 Iranian missiles that entered the country's airspace, the Jordanian Armed Forces confirmed in a statement on Wednesday. The three impacts were in remoted areas, away from population centers, the statement added.
There were no American casualties from Iranian attacks on US military bases in Jordan, two US officials told Reuters.
Iran targeted a US Marine base in Jordan with ballistic missiles, the IRGC spokesperson announced on Tuesday evening, claiming that "a large number of US forces were killed" at the Camp Titin base.
The IRGC "carried out a heavy ballistic missile attack on the US Marine base in Jordan known as Camp Titin, located on the shores of the Gulf of Aqaba, killing a large number of US forces and destroying several important facilities and attack helicopters."
An El Al flight from Tel Aviv to Bangkok was forced to turn around mid air due to Iranian fire towards Jordan, N12 News reported. The plane is now continuing on its way to Thailand.
In a later statement the IRGC spokesperson said that combatants from the IRGC "carried out a heavy ballistic missile attack on the hangars housing RQ-4 and MQ-9 long-range unmanned aircraft at the US air base in Jordan known as Prince Hassan."
"Several drones were destroyed, and several pilots and flight technical crew members were killed," the IRGC claimed, contrary to American reports. "Several of their technical infrastructure facilities were also set on fire."
Iranian military spokesperson threatens Bahrain, Kuwait
Shortly after the US strikes began, Iranian military spokesperson Ebrahim Zolfaghari stated that Iran “will no longer exercise restraint regarding Bahrain and Kuwait” in a post on X/Twitter.
“Gifts are on the way,” Zolfaghari warned.
Saudi-owned news outlet Al Arabiya, citing an Iranian military official, reported that Iran had begun launching missiles and drones towards US-linked targets.
Iranian semi-official news outlet Tasnim shared an additional statement from Zolfaghari in which he reportedly said Iran will "deliver crushing and devastating blows to the despicable and malevolent American enemy."
Iran "launched a massive strike using kamikaze drones a few hours ago, targeting radar facilities and concentrations of American terrorist forces at the Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain," the IRGC spokesperson claimed on Wednesday morning.
"Combatants of the IRGC have delivered a crushing and sweeping response to the enemy's hostile actions," the statement added."
There has not been any confirmation from Bahrain or the US of the attack.
Trump warns there'll be 'little left of Islamic Republic of Iran' should it respond
CENTCOM and US President Donald Trump confirmed the strikes, noting that they are being carried out in retaliation for Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the recent attack on US troops stationed in the region.
"The United States is, as we speak, striking Iranian Targets near the Strait of Hormuz," he wrote. "The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait, which currently has no mines (They have been completely removed or detonated!), and the Iranians shooting eight missiles, all successfully knocked down, at our Military Base in Jordan."
Trump threatened Iran that, should it respond to the "very justified attack," it will be hit "again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!"
Iranian state media reported that several explosions were heard in the eastern area of the city of Bandar Abbas and across southern Iran.

articles.title: Iran launches retaliatory strikes after latests US airstrikes
articles.body:
Tasnim and Fars news agencies have reported that the Iranian armed forces fired missiles and drones towards aggressor US bases in the region.
The IRGC public relations office said in a sttaement issued on Tuesday night that the "regret-inducing response" to the aggression by the US military had begun.
The IRGC also said that the US aggression latest of which happened on Tuesday night would strengthen the lock on the Hormuz Strait.
There were reports of missiles being fired from Karaj next to Tehran, Kermanshah and Aligoudarz in Lorestan Province in the west of Iran.
There were also reports of civilian casualties in Hormuzgan province as a resut of the US aggression.
Mehr News Agency also reported later that sound of air defense were heard in the east of the capital Tehran on Tuesday midnight.
Meanwhile, Barak Ravid, American news website "Axios" reporter said in a post on social media that the US base in Jordan came under attack by Iranian ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says 12 killed, dozens injured in Russia's overnight airstrikes
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
At least 12 people were killed and dozens injured in overnight Russian strikes across Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday.
 
In a statement on Telegram, Zelenskyy said this figure included seven people killed in an attack on a railway depot in Kyiv.
 
Also, four people were killed and 13 injured in the city of Boryspil, where a five-story residential building was damaged, and about 50 residents were evacuated, he added.
 
Zelenskyy also said there were strikes on industrial facilities in the area.
 
In Odesa and the surrounding region, strikes damaged energy and export infrastructure, leaving thousands of households without electricity, Zelenskyy noted.
 
He also said a border crossing with Romania was damaged.
 
Zelenskyy added that strikes also affected the Kherson, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy, and Dnipropetrovsk regions. Among those killed was an Indian citizen, he said.
 
The Ukrainian president attributed the scale of the casualties to insufficient air-defense capabilities and called on partners to increase deliveries of air-defense systems, including through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative and bilateral arrangements.
 
Zelenskyy said rescue and recovery operations were continuing in Kyiv and the surrounding region, where nearly 350 emergency workers had been deployed.
 
Separately, the Russian Defense Ministry said its armed forces carried out a large-scale overnight strike using long-range precision weapons and attack drones on Ukraine's military targets, including the production site of Flamingo missiles.
 
According to the ministry, the strikes hit military-industrial and fuel-and-energy facilities in Kyiv and the Kyiv region involved in the production of missile and drone systems and their components, as well as facilities supplying fuel to Ukrainian forces, including the Borispol oil refinery.
 
The ministry also said it struck Ukraine's facilities used to store military-related cargo and fuel in Odesa and the Odesa region, including the ports of Odesa and Chornomorsk.
 
It claimed that units of Russia's Vostok group of forces had captured Chervona Krynytsia and Novopavlivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
 
It also said Ukraine responded with air attacks, while Russian air defenses destroyed 13 aerial bombs and 1,050 drones.
 
In Russia's Samara region, authorities reported damage to civilian facilities as Russian forces worked to repel a Ukrainian drone attack.
 
Regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said there were no deaths according to preliminary information and that emergency and Defense Ministry units were operating at the affected sites.
 
Damage was also reported in the port area of Ust-Luga in the Leningrad region following a drone attack.
 
Regional Governor Alexander Drozdenko said a fire broke out and emergency services were working at the scene and that the information on the extent of the damage was still being clarified.
 
Separately, Russian authorities and media reported a wave of messages alleging that explosive devices had been placed at schools, kindergartens, hospitals, and other social facilities in the Leningrad region.
 
The reports prompted checks at affected facilities. Regional authorities described the messages as an attempt to disrupt the start of the school year, although the origin of the messages and the authenticity of the threats had not been established.
 
In Moscow, visitors were evacuated from the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts and tours were canceled for several hours, according to reports. The museum was temporarily closed, and reports said another museum in the city was also closed, citing technical reasons.
 
Independent verification of claims by both sides is challenging due to the ongoing conflict.

articles.title: Ukraine spent three years learning to catch Russian drones—so Russia made them fly faster
articles.body:
Russia is sending jet-powered drones against Ukrainian cities in growing numbers—no longer only the Iranian Shahed-238 it fields as the Geran-3, but the newer, faster Geran-4 and Geran-5. The fear everyone voices is their speed, but speed breaks the cheap layer, not the missiles.
Ukraine's expensive air-defense missiles already routinely shoot down cruise missiles, and to them, a fast drone is just one more target. The strain falls on the cheap layer instead—the interceptor drones Ukraine built to down thousands of Shaheds a month for a few thousand dollars each, a fraction of a missile's price.
Those were designed to catch slow drones, and against jet speed, they struggle. If that layer breaks, the cost of defending Ukraine's skies climbs—and the Defense Ministry has already started paying to keep it from breaking.
The shift is not marginal, and it continues to accelerate. Russia had sent more than 2,500 jet-powered Shaheds against Ukraine by 30 August, against roughly 1,500 in July, informal presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov wrote—the drones, he noted, were launched practically straight from the factory. Russia fired roughly 1,400 jet-powered drones since the start of 2026 to June, and air defenses recorded about 180 in all of 2025, Colonel Oleksandr Zaruba of Ukraine's State Research Institute said.
A record month, and the weapon built to beat it
Ukrainian interceptor drones destroyed more than 33,000 Russian drones of all types in March 2026—roughly double the February total and a record for the cheapest layer of Ukraine's air defense, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.
Russia sent Shaheds—cheap, propeller-driven, long-range, lumbering in at about 185 kilometers per hour (115 mph)—in mass raids meant to swamp Ukraine's defenses. Ukraine adapted, with mobile fire teams, electronic warfare, and layered engagement, then added interceptor drones that destroy incoming drones for a fraction of a surface-to-air missile's cost.
As Ukraine got better at catching propeller drones, Russia reached for speed—jet-powered versions that fly more than three times faster than the Shaheds Ukraine spent three years learning to intercept.
By August, Ukraine's military intelligence said Russia had stopped building the Geran-3 and shifted to the newer jets, producing roughly 3,000 of them a month.
Conventional air defense already handles this
The worry centers on velocity: a jet drone flies several times faster than a propeller-driven or electric one, reducing the time defenders have to detect, identify, and hit it. But the fear aims at the wrong place, said Oleksii Kolesnyk, director of the Ukrainian firm Reactive Drones.
"A jet-powered UAV is, in many ways, similar to a cruise missile. For conventional air defense, jet-powered drones are simply another aerial target," he told Euromaidan Press.
Ukraine's surface-to-air systems routinely intercept cruise missiles. A fast drone is standard work for them—though Zelenskyy said in late August that the jets are the hardest to intercept, and that combat aircraft now mainly protect against them.
The strain lands on the interceptor drones
An interceptor drone, unlike a ground-launched missile, has to chase its target down and ram it, which worked against slow Shaheds. Against something near cruise-missile speed, the geometry breaks.
The problem exists almost only for interceptor drones, Kolesnyk said—they were never designed for these speeds. At jet velocities, guidance, target tracking, and the final homing onto the target all hit technical ceilings, and faster interceptors alone will not fix it.
"New technical solutions will be needed," he said.
Interceptor drones are why Ukraine can answer mass raids without firing a missile worth hundreds of thousands of dollars at each incoming drone. Break that math, and the affordability of Ukraine's whole air defense shifts.
The Defense Ministry's answer
Through the defense-tech accelerator Brave1, Ukraine backed 12 technologies under the EU4UA Defence Tech grant program, offering up to €150,000 each for high-speed interceptors capable of reaching 450 kilometers per hour (about 280 mph) or more.
Ukraine is testing four new drone interceptors as Russia floods its skies with faster Gerans
That push has since produced candidates. By late August, Ukraine had four interceptor systems built to run down the jets, all already in field testing, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said, and the Alexa Spatium had entered service. Ukraine now wants to bring them up to standard and build them in the thousands.
Not a revolution, but an evolution with a long history
Colonel Oleksandr Saienko, a former Ukrainian brigade commander, rejected the idea that any of this is new.
"This is better described as an evolution of unmanned systems rather than a completely new stage of warfare," he said.
Trending Now
Jet drones long predate this war. "The first jet-powered UAVs appeared back in the 1970s," he said, pointing to Soviet reconnaissance drones beginning with the Tu-143 and continuing with the Tu-141 and Tu-243—platforms Ukraine itself later flew in the Donbas war and the full-scale invasion. What has changed is scale, and the problem the drones now solve: arriving before the defender can react.
Ukrainian intelligence: Russia’s new jet-powered Geran-4 attack drone runs on Chinese turbojets
Saienko's warning points past the engine.
"The decisive advantage will not belong to whoever simply has a jet engine. It will belong to whoever integrates these platforms into an effective reconnaissance-strike system, protects them against electronic warfare, manufactures them at scale, and keeps costs manageable," he said.
His frame is the kill chain—detect, identify, decide, engage—and every gain in speed compresses that cycle. "If a target is flying at 500 to 700 kilometers per hour, even a delay of several dozen seconds may make interception impossible," he said, adding: "Radars must see sooner, command systems must classify automatically, and operators get less time—until automation becomes a requirement."
Why hasn't every drone gone jet-powered
Speed solves one problem and creates several. "They are simply another category of strike UAV," Kolesnyk said.
Compact turbojets are expensive and hard to source for smaller drones. Bigger airframes have to be reinforced to take the loads and vibration, which adds weight and cost. Fuel burn climbs far above that of the electric or piston drones built for endurance, and higher speed leaves less room for navigation errors.
So, jet drones fill a niche rather than taking over the whole strike fleet. "They are most effective at ranges of roughly 200 to 600 kilometers," Kolesnyk said—fast strikes on high-value or time-sensitive targets, where getting there quickly matters more than flying cheaply or far.
Russia unleashes its Geran-5 air defense killer on Ukraine, equipped with British Raspberry Pi microcomputer tracker
Ukraine didn't drop first-person-view (FPV) drones when fiber-optic ones arrived, and jam-resistant drones didn't replace the rest. Each capability added a layer rather than erasing the previous one. Saienko expects the same. "The emergence of jet aviation did not eliminate piston-engine aircraft. The same principle applies," he said. Cheap propeller drones are ideal for mass attacks, while jet platforms handle speed.
The next fight is over reaction time
Jet drones force defenders to decide faster, and that is the harder demand. A slow propeller drone is a wasteful target for an expensive missile. A cruise missile demands an instant answer. A jet drone sits in between—and an operator has to sort which weapon meets which target in seconds, while holding scarce interceptors back for the worst threats. Every misjudgment costs something.
"The challenge is no longer only interception—it is detecting, identifying, and assigning the target quickly enough," Saienko said.
Both experts reach the same conclusion from opposite ends: Kolesnyk through the technical limits of the interceptor drone, Saienko through the entire defensive network. Both land on automation—AI-driven target recognition, distributed sensors, and fast data sharing to shrink the gap between spotting a target and hitting it. The winner won't necessarily fly the fastest aircraft. It will process information faster than its opponent.
Over four days at the end of August, Russia fired about 800 jet drones at Ukraine, Ukraine's president said—a type most of Ukraine's cheap interceptors still cannot catch. And the problem won't stay Ukraine's alone. Drones from the same broad Shahed family have already strayed into NATO airspace and turned up in other wars. The interception race Ukraine is running now is one everyone will eventually run.

articles.title: Live: Deadly Russian air attack hits energy and rail infrastructure in Kyiv
articles.body:
'Safe days in Russian skies are over,' warns Zelensky
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday warned airlines, insurance firms and passengers that Russian airspace would be "completely unsafe" and filled with Ukrainian drones for the duration of the war. His address came after a night of relentless Russian bombardment in Ukraine, which killed at least a dozen people. Read our liveblog to see how all the day's events unfolded.
Russian attacks damage infrastructure in Ukraine's Odesa, official says
Russian attacks damaged infrastructure and residential buildings in the Ukrainian Black Sea port of Odesa on Wednesday, Serhiy Lysak, the head of the city's military administration, said on Telegram without providing details.
Putin alleges Germany planted evidence in order to frame Russia for Leipzig drone attack
Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Germany on Tuesday of planting evidence in order to blame Moscow for a drone attack last month at Leipzig airport.
Putin, speaking to reporters, did not say what he was basing the accusation on.
He said that by levelling accusations against Russia, the German government was trying to resolve domestic problems caused by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's falling approval ratings.
Putin says Russia has advanced in Donetsk region, surrounded some Ukrainian troops
President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that Russian troops had captured 270 square km of Ukraine’s Donetsk region in August and a large group of Ukrainian troops were surrounded.
Reuters could not independently verify his statement.
Russia continues to advance towards the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Putin said, adding that Moscow's forces were preparing to launch massive strikes against energy infrastructure in Ukraine.
Putin says Russia is open to concrete talks on Ukraine
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that Moscow was open to "concrete" talks on settling the Ukraine conflict if new momentum could be injected.
Speaking to reporters after a summit in Kyrgyzstan, Putin also restated his confidence that Russian forces would prevail in Ukraine and Kyiv's forces would "crumble".
He said that the main challenge for Russia was drones, but said that Moscow was dealing with it.
German sanctions over drone incident will have 'consequences': Russian ambassador
Measures against Russia announced by the German government over an alleged attempted "hybrid attack" at a strategic airport last month will have "consequences", the Russian ambassador to Germany said Tuesday.
In a statement published to the embassy's Telegram channel, Sergey Nechayev called Berlin's claim that Moscow was behind the drone incident "unsubstantiated, absurd, and contrary to common sense", adding that the sanctions were "an unprecedented escalation of Russian-German relations and will not be without consequences".
Macron backs new sanctions on Russia over Germany drone incident
French President Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday called for fresh sanctions on Russia over an incident involving an explosive-laden drone at a German airport in August, which Berlin has blamed on Moscow.
"France is fully in solidarity with Germany and supports the adoption of new European sanctions against Russia," Macron wrote on X.
Zelensky warns 'safe days in Russian skies are over'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday warned airlines, insurance firms and passengers that Russian airspace would be "completely unsafe" and filled with Ukrainian drones for the duration of the war.
"Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia's key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe," he said on X. "There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he added, warning "the safe days in Russia's skies are over."
Kremlin says Putin, Xi and Trump may hold a trilateral meeting
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Tuesday that Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping may hold a trilateral meeting at the next summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
At least 12 killed and over a dozen injured in Russian strikes on Kyiv
Germany blames Russia for last month's attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives.
The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on the evening of Aug. 4 and the device was defused.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that the attempted attack fits into a known pattern of “Russian hybrid operations.” He said the German government “comes to the conclusion that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig on Aug. 4.”
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that the Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed effective Sept. 18 and the contract under which the Russian House, a cultural center in Berlin, is operated will be rescinded.
Ukraine hopes for bolstered support as EU defence ministers meet in Dublin
EU defence ministers are grappling with bolstering Ukraine's air defences, as worries grow over Russia's campaign to destabilise Kyiv's European backers. This comes as Moscow is taking advantage of Kyiv running low on US-built air defence missiles to intensify its attacks on the country.
EU ministers are also expected to discuss Russia's hybrid war against Ukraine's European allies. FRANCE 24's Angela Diffley tells us more.
One person killed in drone attack on Russia's Belgorod, authorities say
One person was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, local authorities said on Tuesday.
Russian hybrid attacks will not 'scare' EU off supporting Ukraine: Kallas
The EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas vowed Tuesday that Russia would not succeed in scaring the 27-nation bloc off supporting Ukraine, as worries grow over a hybrid campaign by Moscow to destabilise Kyiv's European backers.
"Russia is hitting Europe with a wave of increasingly kinetic hybrid attacks," Kallas told journalists after a meeting of European Union defence ministers in Ireland. "Russia wants to scare us away from supporting Ukraine. They will not succeed."
Russia hit thermal power plant in Ukraine's south, Naftogaz says
A Russian drone and missile attack on Monday damaged the thermal power plant in Ukraine's southern Odesa region, state energy company Naftogaz said on Tuesday.
Russia targets Kyiv and its region for sixth consecutive night of attacks
At least nine people have been killed and 14 injured in Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight. Moscow targeted Kyiv and the wider region in the attack, hitting a railway depot in the Kyiv. Russia's defence ministry said it had also struck infrastructure in the Southern Odesa region.
Russia has intensified strikes on the beleaguered Ukrainian cities in recent weeks disrupting the daily lives of millions of people and triggering up to a dozen air-raid alerts a day.
Four people killed by Ukrainian drones in Russian-controlled Luhansk region, Moscow says
Four people were killed and three more wounded by a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian-controlled part of Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine, the region's Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said.
Brussels floats fresh plans to increase sanctions against Russia
Beyond ramping up intelligence sharing and police cooperation, the EU is trying to raise the cost of the war for the Kremlin by bolstering support for Ukraine and hitting Moscow with sanctions.
Brussels has floated fresh plans to add 1,600 more firms and individuals to its already long list of Russians sanctioned over the war.
Meanwhile discussion has resurfaced on whether the bloc should tap some 200 billion euros ($235 billion) of frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
A proposal to use the funds failed last year after opposition from Belgium, where the bulk of the assets are held, and the EU came up with a 90 billion euro loan for Kyiv off its own back. But there is already a sense that the money might not last the two years it was intended for and the EU may need to find a way sooner or later to use the immobilised Russian funds.
"As each day passes, the cost of the war is rising," the top diplomats of the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden wrote in a letter last week.
Russia fired more than 2,800 drones at Ukraine in August as battlefield tactics evolve
Over the course of the month of August, Russia launched more than 2,800 jet-propelled drones at Ukraine, a type of drone that is harder to shoot down.
That has come with a massive uptick in the number of drones used, considerind those now found on the front line are quite a new model: Ukrainian authorities say they are pressed into service almost immediately after leaving the factory.
FRANCE 24's Oliver Farry looks at those new drones, and how Russia is using them to try and change the course of the war.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

articles.title: Russia is secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles capable of targeting US aircraft carriers - report
articles.body:
- i24NEWS
- Middle East
- Iran & Eastern States
- Russia is secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles - report
Russia is secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles - report
The FT report indicates that the support continued throughout the US war with Iran, as Tehran intends to develop a new class of weapon capable of threatening US aircraft carriers
Russia has been secretly supporting Iranian missile development since 2023, according to a report in the Financial Times on Tuesday.
The goal of the program, codenamed C430L, was to help Iran develop missiles capable of taking out US Navy aircraft carriers in the Middle East.
In particular, they aimed to develop a ramjet propulsion system that would allow Iranian missiles to fly at several times the speed of sound.
Fast, low-flying missiles would give Western air defences less time to react increasing the impact of such an attack.
The transfer of advanced missile technology would have required approval from the highest political echelons in Russia, amid speculation that this was a technology exchange. Iran supports Russian drone development, and Russia supports Iranian missile development, in addition to the already existing intelligence cooperation between the two.
Leaks seen by the Financial Times showed that preparations for the deal were underway before the deal was signed in November 2023, only a month after October 7.
"Russia is trying to broaden the Ukraine war and draw the US into different theatres," said Nicole Grajewski, a professor at Sciences Po University in Paris.
The investigation also showed that the support continued throughout the war with Iran in February, and provided significant assistance to Iran during its attacks on the Gulf states.
Iran has long sought to develop a ramjet propulsion system, as far back as 2019, when then supreme leader Ali Khamenei was seen inspecting development sites. Iranian media also reported the testing of ramjet prototypes in August 2023.

articles.title: EU Frets over Kyiv’s Defences, ‘Hybrid’ Threat From Moscow
articles.body:
EU defense and foreign ministers gathering in Ireland from Tuesday will grapple with bolstering Ukraine’s air defenses amid growing worries over Russia’s campaign to destabilize Kyiv’s European backers.
Moscow has taken advantage of Ukraine running low on US-built air defense missiles to pummel the country, while Kyiv has hit back against Russian infrastructure with its own long-range strikes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The Russian attacks on the Ukrainians are getting harsher and harsher,” an EU official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Defense ministers -- who meet Tuesday before foreign ministers hold talks Wednesday -- are expected to speak with Ukraine’s new acting defense minister Yevgeniy Khmara.
But there appears little they can do to massively increase the supply of desperately needed air interceptors to Ukraine -- beyond pressuring European countries that still have stockpiles and urging the likes of Japan and South Korea to share more.
While the Kremlin escalates its air campaign against Ukraine, there have been growing worries that Moscow is also looking to deflect from its battlefield troubles by ramping up operations in Europe.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said his country has increasingly “found itself in the crosshairs of hybrid attackers” after an explosive-laden drone was found in August at Leipzig airport, a crucial military transport hub.
Berlin hasn’t yet officially blamed Russia over the incident -- but the clear suggestion is that the finger of blame is pointing at Moscow.
6 Wounded, Including a Child, in Russian Strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Region
Fuelling the concerns over Russia’s intentions, CIA chief John Ratcliffe paid a surprise visit to Moscow last week, with US media reporting he warned Russia against attacking any NATO country.
EU officials insist they don’t see Moscow preparing for a military attack any time soon, but they are bracing for more incidents in the grey zone beneath open conflict.
“What we see is these hybrid and then not-so-hybrid attacks continuing and our assumption is that those will go on,” the EU official said.
While Merz said that those behind the incidents in Germany will “pay for them”, Europe has struggled to counter the low-level campaign of sabotage and interference it blames on Moscow.
- Sanctions, assets, reforms -
Beyond ramping up intelligence sharing and police cooperation, the EU sees bolstering support for Ukraine and hitting Moscow with sanctions as ways to raise the costs for the Kremlin.
Brussels has floated fresh plans to add 1,600 more firms and individuals to its already long list of Russians sanctioned over the war.
Meanwhile, discussion has resurfaced on whether the bloc should tap some 200 billion euros ($235 billion) of frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine.
A proposal to use the funds failed last year after opposition from Belgium, where the bulk of the assets are held, and the EU offered a 90-billion-euro loan to Kyiv off its own back.
But there is already a sense that the money might not last the two years it was intended for, and the EU may need to find a way, sooner or later, to use the immobilized Russian funds.
“As each day passes, the cost of the war is rising as Russia’s relentless attacks continue unabated,” the top diplomats of the Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden wrote in a letter last week.
New British foreign minister Ed Miliband and Ukraine’s Andriy Sybiga will join their EU counterparts for a long-scheduled meeting in Ireland, where the bloc holds its rotating presidency.
But while crises rage around the globe from Ukraine to Iran, the EU ministers will also open a debate on reforming how the bloc runs its diplomacy as it seeks impact in an increasingly hostile world.
While some advocate overhauling the EU’s diplomatic service under foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, others say now is not the time for institutional reshuffling and that the 27 nations need to focus on better coordinating their positions.

articles.title: Russian drone struck a Ukrainian fire truck on its way to a house fire—four rescuers injured
articles.body:
A Russian drone hit a fire truck driving to a call in the village of Kushuhum outside Zaporizhzhia on 1 September, injuring four rescuers, the head of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ivan Fedorov, reported. The crew was on its way to a house fire that Russian shelling had started. The strike came hours after a countrywide Russian air assault overnight.
A drone hit the crew before they reached the fire
Fedorov said a Russian drone struck the State Emergency Service vehicle in Kushuhum as it drove to put out a fire. The truck took damage, and the crew was hurt. He said the men were under the supervision of medics.
The Main Directorate of the State Emergency Service in Zaporizhzhia Oblast confirmed the attack, and added that all four injured firefighters had been taken to hospital with injuries of differing severity. The directorate specified what the crew had been sent to: a fire in a detached house in the suburb, started by Russian shelling.
Over the past 24 hours, Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia city and district killed two people and injured eight, Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out strikes on 57 settlements across the region.
The night before: a countrywide strike
Overnight into 1 September, Russia attacked with ballistic and cruise missiles, anti-radar missiles, Banderol munitions, and 218 Shahed-type strike drones, about a third of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force reported. By preliminary data, air defenses downed or suppressed 199 targets. Odesa and Kyiv oblasts were the main directions of the strike.
Russia killed 12 people across Ukraine, among them a citizen of India, and injured dozens, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Russia killed four people and injured 13 and damaged a five-story residential building, and 50 people were evacuated. Nearly 350 rescuers worked in Kyiv and the surrounding oblast alone.
Russia’s 6-day attack on Kyiv that started two days after CIA head’s visit to Moscow, culminates with massive ballistic missile strike on eve of school year
In Kyiv, a ballistic strike on Ukrzaliznytsia railway facilities killed seven people, six of them railway workers, and one more employee remains hospitalized. The capital's overall toll for the night stood at eight killed.
In Odesa Oblast, Russian drones, guided bombs, and missiles injured seven civilian men, four of whom went to hospital, and struck the Orlivka ferry crossing on the border with Romania again, the regional prosecutor's office found.
Ukraine has documented Russia striking the people who respond
As of May, Ukraine has documented 11,000 Russian first-person-view drone attacks on civilians, among them repeat strikes on the same spot once medics and firefighters arrive. Ukraine's UN envoy has built part of the case for expelling Russia from the Security Council on that practice.
Rescue workers in Zaporizhzhia have been caught that way before. After a strike on a Poltava Oblast gas site, Russia hit the crews who came to the fire. Firefighters in Chernihiv Oblast went to hospital mid-rescue. In Kryvyi Rih in August, a second Russian attack reached rescue workers thirty minutes after a drone strike on a shopping center, and a repeat strike killed a 20-year-old volunteer paramedic in Kyiv the same month.

articles.title: ‘Russia Always Calculates Its Strikes to Destroy Lives’: Zelensky Says After Deadly Overnight Attack
articles.body:
At least 12 people were killed and dozens injured in a Russian overnight missile and drone attack across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
According to him, nearly 350 rescuers were involved in Kyiv and the Kyiv region alone, noting that Russia used a significant number of ballistic missiles and attack drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In Boryspil, Kyiv region, a residential five-story building was damaged and 50 people were evacuated. Four people were killed and 13 injured in the city, Zelensky reported on X.
In Kyiv, a strike on a railway depot killed seven people.
“Russia always calculates its strikes precisely so as to destroy lives as much as possible,” Zelensky said.
He said Russia’s ability to cause mass casualties depended on whether Ukraine had sufficient air defense capabilities.
Odesa and the surrounding region was also targeted by guided aerial bombs and drones from the evening onward. Thousands of households were left without electricity, while Russian strikes also damaged a border crossing with Romania and export infrastructure, Zelensky said.
Russian attacks also targeted Kherson, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy, and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
Zelensky said the victims included an Indian citizen and offered condolences to those who lost relatives and loved ones.
Zelensky calls for more air defense
President Zelensky thanked partners choosing to help Ukraine obtain anti-ballistic defense systems through the PURL initiative and bilateral deliveries. However, “It is very important that these deliveries increase in the autumn,” he added.
India-Russia: A Changing Equation
Zelensky argued that further military assistance would directly affect the number of casualties caused by Russian attacks.
“The number of victims of Russian terror directly depends on every new aid package,” he said.

articles.title: Why Russia’s jet-powered ‘Geran’ drones are so hard to shoot down, and what Kyiv’s falling interception rate means for the future of the war
articles.body:
Why Russia’s jet-powered ‘Geran’ drones are so hard to shoot down, and what Kyiv’s falling interception rate means for the future of the war
Russian forces have changed how they strike Kyiv, launching nearly continuous waves of drone attacks throughout the day rather than only at night, as they did before. The Russian army is also increasingly using jet-powered Geran drones — Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed — which fly much faster than older, propeller-driven models and are harder to shoot down.
The city has settled into an uneasy new rhythm as a result, The New York Times reported. Shopping centers and stores close several times a day because of air-raid alerts, and a growing number of residents are spending their nights in shelters. Locals believe Russia is trying to “spread chaos.” “They want people to flee Kyiv. They want to interrupt our regular life,” one resident told the newspaper.
“Right now, Russia’s tactic is to wear down Ukraine and Ukrainians — first and foremost, our people,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said on Monday that Russian forces had launched more than 1,500 drones over the previous four days, about 800 of them — more than half — jet-powered.
By comparison, Russia fired just 300 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in all of June and about 1,500 of them in July, according to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president on technology.
Along with the numbers, Russia has changed the pattern of the attacks themselves, the BBC reported: the drones come in smaller batches than before, but more often. Russia now sends over three or four jet-powered drones, sometimes as many as 10, roughly every half hour, the BBC said.
On August 27 alone, Kyiv recorded 13 air-raid alerts lasting a combined 15 hours — a record since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Jet-powered drones are harder to shoot down because of their speed. In the winter of 2026, Ukraine was shooting down 95–98% of propeller-driven Shaheds. On August 27, Ukrainian forces shot down 88% of all drones, conventional and jet-powered alike; on August 31, just 79%.
An unnamed Ukrainian government official told The Wall Street Journal that Ukraine already has drones capable of shooting down the newest Geran models, but only a few hundred of them — far short of the thousands it needs.
Ukraine is working to develop countermeasures against jet-powered drones, and sources in the country’s defense industry told the BBC they expect Ukraine to have a counter within the next month.
As Russian strikes on Kyiv intensify, Ruslan Horbenko, a lawmaker from Zelensky’s Servant of the People party, said Kyiv and the Kyiv region could be officially designated front-line areas. The designation brings benefits including war-risk insurance, exemption from mobilization, and wage guarantees for utility workers. A government resolution to that effect has already been drafted, he said.
The war in photographs: Kyiv
Overnight, Russian forces again struck Kyiv and the surrounding region with ballistic missiles and drones, killing 12 people and injuring more than 20 across the region, according to authorities. Six of the dead were employees of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway; they were killed in a strike on a rail depot in Kyiv.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
