articles.title: Which American weapon — and how — caused the Lamerd massacre on the first day of the attack on Iran?
articles.body:
Which American weapon — and how — caused the Lamerd massacre on the first day of the attack on Iran?
TEHRAN — The apparent first combat use of a new US precision missile during the war against Iran has raised fresh concerns over the potential impact of advanced American weapons on civilian populations, with an investigation by Airwars finding evidence that the munition scattered lethal fragments across an area far wider than its publicly advertised fragmentation radius.
An Airwars analysis of three apparent Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) attacks in the southern Iranian city of Lamerd on February 28, the first day of the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, found that one strike produced visible damage extending at least 170 meters from the estimated point of detonation. Civilians were reportedly killed at distances of up to more than 50 meters from the explosion.
According to the investigation, the attacks killed at least 21 civilians, including at least seven children and two women, while as many as 170 others were injured.
The findings are particularly significant because the PrSM is designed not simply to destroy a target through a conventional blast, but to detonate shortly before reaching the ground and disperse tens of thousands of metal pellets in a 360-degree pattern.
The weapon's fragmentation mechanism means that people, buildings and vehicles within its lethal or damaging range can be struck by high-velocity projectiles even if they are not located directly at the point of impact.
Airwars said the distinctive pattern left by the munition was visible across streets, buildings and vehicles in Lamerd. Rather than the large crater normally associated with many conventional missile strikes, the aftermath showed thousands of small impact marks consistent with the dispersal of fragmentation pellets.
A weapon designed for long-range precision
The PrSM is manufactured by Lockheed Martin and is launched from the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, or HIMARS. The company says the missile can strike targets at ranges of up to 500 kilometers, making it a significantly longer-range weapon than earlier systems employing similar fragmentation technology.
Each missile is reportedly capable of carrying approximately 180,000 pellets, although key technical details, including the exact size of its warhead and the distance its fragments can travel, have not been publicly disclosed.
The missile appears to be an evolution of the Alternate Warhead version of the US Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System. That weapon also disperses large numbers of pellets but has a reported range of about 70 kilometers, less than one-sixth that of the PrSM.
The apparent use of the PrSM in Iran therefore represents more than the deployment of another battlefield weapon. It demonstrates the extension of a fragmentation-based strike capability to considerably greater distances, while raising questions about how such a weapon can be employed safely in or near populated areas.
Airwars said neither the US Department of War nor Lockheed Martin has publicly specified the PrSM's fragmentation or lethal radius. By contrast, promotional material produced by Lockheed Martin appears to indicate a maximum fragmentation radius of roughly 50 meters. The damage documented in Lamerd was therefore more extensive than the radius suggested by the promotional material analyzed by Airwars.
Michael Meier, a former Special Assistant to the US Army Judge Advocate General for the Law of Armed Conflict, warned that the weapon's use in densely populated locations could create an inherent risk to civilians.
 
 “You would be hard pressed to find a reason to use the PrSM in a densely populated area,” Meier said, adding that if the lethality radius were around 100 meters, civilian casualties would be inevitable.
Three strikes in less than a minute
Airwars reconstructed the sequence of events using CCTV footage, images published by Iranian media and testimonies collected by journalists who visited the affected locations.
The investigation identified three separate strikes over a distance of roughly 550 meters in the Shahrak Isar and Tal-e Khandagh residential neighborhoods and at the Shahid Naimi sports hall. The strikes reportedly occurred within approximately 31 seconds.
The first strike hit Shahrak Isar at approximately 17:37:46. Airwars identified damage extending almost 80 meters from the estimated impact point. Masoumeh Monfared and her son, Abedin Gharibdoos, were reportedly killed outside their home, around 40 meters from the estimated epicenter.
Ten seconds later, another missile reportedly struck the Tal-e Khandagh neighborhood. Two-year-old Avina Barzegar was killed while playing in the yard of her home. A memorial marker identifies the location, which Airwars estimated to be approximately 50 meters from the missile's estimated point of detonation. The investigation identified observable pellet damage extending at least that far.
The third strike hit the Shahid Naimi sports hall at approximately 17:38:17. At least seven civilians were reportedly killed, most of them children.
Among the victims was 12-year-old Ilya Khatami, who was reportedly struck while attempting to flee after playing football. Another boy, Abdul Mosavar Rahmani, and football coach Mahmoud Najafi were also killed. Two teenage girls, Helma Ahmadizadeh and Elham Zaeri, were reportedly killed inside the sports center while practicing volleyball.
The investigation also identified damage at a learning center approximately 170 meters from the sports hall strike. Airwars described this as the furthest documented damage associated with the three attacks, although it cautioned that the actual radius could have been greater because of limitations in the available imagery.
Dispute over responsibility
The US military has denied responsibility for the Lamerd strikes. US Central Command argued that CCTV footage was consistent with the dimensions and silhouette of an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile.
However, damage analysis cited by Airwars from The New York Times challenged that assessment. Experts consulted in that analysis reportedly concluded that the pattern of destruction was inconsistent with a Hoveyzeh missile and instead identified the weapons as PrSMs, making the Lamerd attacks the missile's likely first known combat use.
The distinction is important because the physical evidence left at the sites corresponds to the PrSM's known operating concept. The missile reportedly detonates 15 to 20 meters above the ground, distributing fragments over a broad area rather than producing a single large crater.
Airwars also found no reports indicating that militants were killed or military infrastructure was struck at the three locations. An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps compound is located north of the sports hall, but the investigation found no evidence that it was the target of the attacks.
Meier stressed that the legality of a strike depends on assessing the military target, the anticipated effects of the weapon and whether expected civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the anticipated military advantage.
He also questioned the apparent military rationale of the strike, noting that the IRGC compound remained standing and therefore asking whether it could have been considered a sufficiently high-value target to justify the potential effects of the weapon.
A weapon likely to shape future conflicts
The controversy surrounding the PrSM comes as the United States moves to substantially expand production of the weapon.
In July, the US Department of War announced an $8.4 billion contract with Lockheed Martin to accelerate PrSM production. Britain subsequently announced a deal to acquire the missiles as well.
The scale of investment suggests that the missile is expected to become an increasingly important component of US and allied long-range strike capabilities.
Yet the Lamerd strikes have placed a critical question at the center of the debate: whether a weapon capable of dispersing enormous numbers of lethal fragments across a wide area can be reliably employed in environments where civilian populations and military targets exist in close proximity.
For Iran, the findings add to concerns over the civilian consequences of the US-Israeli military campaign. Beyond the immediate casualties, they raise broader questions about the growing use of long-range precision weapons whose effects can extend considerably beyond their intended points of impact.
The central concern is therefore not simply the range or accuracy of the PrSM, but the consequences of deploying a highly destructive fragmentation weapon in populated areas. As the United States and its allies invest heavily in expanding such capabilities, the experience in Lamerd could become an important case in assessing whether claims of precision and deep-strike capability adequately account for the risks borne by civilians on the ground.

articles.title: Despite Ukrainian strikes, Russian online marketplaces Ozon and Wildberries are still selling supplies for Russia’s military. Here’s what we found.
articles.body:
Despite Ukrainian strikes, Russian online marketplaces Ozon and Wildberries are still selling supplies for Russia’s military. Here’s what we found.
In early August, amid a wave of strikes on Wildberries warehouses, we looked into what goods are being ordered for the Russian army on Russian online marketplaces. It turned out that almost anything is available there, including body bags for the dead. At that time, Ukraine had not yet struck Ozon’s facilities, which fueled conspiracy theories. In the second half of August, however, Ukraine’s armed forces began hitting that company’s warehouses as well. Meduza decided to check whether the marketplaces are still selling goods that end up going to the front. Here’s what we found.
What exactly we checked
A month ago, Meduza reviewed posts in 71 Telegram channels and six VKontakte communities that raise donations for Russian soldiers. The channels’ authors often specify exactly what they’re raising money for, and sometimes post direct links to items for sale.
Those posts contained 3,709 direct links to Wildberries. Volunteers supplying the Russian army ordered both “civilian” items, such as food or clothing, and gear clearly intended for military use at the front, including body armor and drone components.
Volunteers used Ozon almost as actively: the posts contained 3,609 links and 1,025 different product listings, including similar drone components. Volodymyr Zelensky has officially cited that role in supplying drone components as the reason for the strikes on Wildberries warehouses.
Yet no targeted strikes hit Ozon facilities before August 22. By September 1, however, the strikes had become systematic.
The first target was a logistics center in Chapaevsk, in Samara region. The next day, drones hit a center in Orenburg, forcing the evacuation of more than 300 employees. On August 24, Ozon reported strikes on four more facilities: in Enem (Krasnodar Krai), Makhachkala, Adygeysk, and Nevinnomyssk (Stavropol region). Overnight on August 27, drones again struck the Orenburg facility, along with a warehouse in Ufa. Overnight on August 29, Ukrainian drones struck an Ozon logistics site in Rostov region. The following day, a strike on Belgorod damaged an Ozon sorting center and delivery hub.
After the initial strikes on the marketplace’s facilities, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry announced that now it was “Ozon’s turn,” calling the strikes themselves “long-range sanctions.” The ministry called the strikes part of a campaign against “storage centers for dual-use goods,” meant to disrupt supplies to the Russian army while also damaging the Russian economy.
What’s still for sale on Ozon: drone drop systems, exoskeletons, and body armor
After Ukraine began striking Ozon, we rechecked every link to the marketplace that had appeared in the channels and communities of pro-Russian volunteers. We found 604 of the 1,025 items still available for purchase.
Another 313 listings remain on the marketplace, though Ozon marks them as temporarily out of stock. For 29 items, delivery is unavailable to any of the 25 Russian cities we checked. Seventy-nine listings have been removed entirely.
Among the 1,000 items, we separately identified 51 whose Ozon descriptions explicitly mention military or tactical use. Of those, 29 remain for sale, 13 are out of stock, two are unavailable for delivery, and six have been removed.
Ozon still sells the Exorise “Muravei” (“Ant”) assault exoskeleton for about 54,000 rubles. Also still available is an FPV video receiver for 7,500 rubles, a device that receives a real-time video feed from a drone; through it, the operator sees the picture from the onboard camera and can fly the drone “first-person.” The seller’s listing states outright that the device is well suited for use in the “SVO.”
Also still available is a cargo drop system for drones for about 5,000 rubles (Z-volunteers have ordered it along with other drone accessories). These devices let users attach a small payload to a drone and release it at a chosen point; at the front, they can be used both to deliver supplies and to drop munitions. In reviews on Ozon, buyers note: “Works great, the little bombs are falling.”
Also still on the marketplace is a magazine for the Makarov pistol. The listing describes it as “combat” and “standard-issue.” It costs about 2,200 rubles and appeared on one of the lists of items needed by Russian soldiers.
Other listings are directly tied to weapons and gear as well.
For example, a handguard for the AK-12, AK-15, and TR-3 carbine is for sale; it covers the front part of the weapon, helps with grip, and allows attachments like grips, flashlights, and other accessories. A carrier for the 6B45 combined-arms body armor, which volunteers bought for naval infantry, is also available. This is the base of the body armor into which protective plates and anti-fragmentation panels are inserted. The empty carrier alone does not stop bullets. One buyer left this review on the product page: “We’ll test it in the SVO, I’ll follow up.”
Another item still available is an “anti-drone” blanket. According to the seller, it helps soldiers become less visible to drones. Volunteers have noted that they receive many requests for these blankets from service members.
On the blanket’s page, one buyer wrote: “Ordered for the fighters in the SVO… I hope they save someone’s lives.” Another reviewer said the blankets “were sent as humanitarian aid to the SVO zone,” and another user said her husband loved the blanket and that “it’s badly needed in the SVO right now.”
What was removed? (Almost nothing)
There’s no sign that Ozon has fully removed so-called dual-use goods (meaning items that can be used for both civilian and military purposes). Nor does Ozon publicly disclose who removed each listing, the seller or the marketplace itself, so the reasons could vary widely, up to and including the possibility that an item burned in one of the attacked warehouses.
By the end of August, only 79 of the 1,025 previously identified items ordered for Russian soldiers had disappeared from the marketplace entirely, about 8% of the sample. Most of the vanished items were entirely “civilian”: specific brands of coffee, sugar, and buckwheat, shovels, underwear, toilet paper, tires, and even an electric wheelchair.
However, 22 of the vanished items were more clearly tied to use in the war. Among other things, the following specific listings disappeared: muzzle attachments for assault rifles (designed for firing at drones); the “MRAK” drop system and batteries for drones (volunteers wrote that they were needed so drones could fly “farther, longer, and actively destroy the enemy”); ceramic plates for body armor; and a digital radio with encryption (bought for Russian assault troops).
The listing for a perimeter alarm device also disappeared. Volunteers ordered 10 of these devices for a special unit engaged in “counter-sabotage operations” in the Belgorod direction. According to the fundraiser’s organizers, the alarm system was meant to warn soldiers of an approaching enemy.
Even so, equivalents (including exact ones) of most of the vanished items are still available on Ozon from other sellers. So it’s clear the marketplace did not deliberately remove these listings.
Moreover, some sellers of “military” goods on Ozon already announced sales during the warehouse strikes. One explained that they were cutting prices because they’d rather “sell [the goods] for next to nothing than have them go up in smoke.”
Volunteers also keep using the marketplaces
We checked posts in the same channels and communities through August 24 and found 34 new fundraisers. Thirty of them contained links to Ozon, for a total of 197 listings.
One recent fundraiser asked for two packs of 50 tourniquets each for a medical evacuation team. For mobile fire teams that, according to volunteers, protect front-line roads from drones, organizers are asking for 10 tablets. The screens are meant to display thermal-imaging footage, letting the crew see a fuller picture and track aerial targets longer.
Another channel was raising money for two 3D printers (33,000 rubles each) and a filament dryer. The equipment was intended for the workshop of the “SVO Museum,” which prints parts for the front, including for units that work with drones.
Drone components themselves also keep showing up in recent fundraisers. For example, for a group of soldiers with the call sign “Lis” (“Fox”), organizers asked for a Walksnail Avatar HD video kit, which transmits a live feed from the drone’s camera to the operator; a video receiver to pick up that signal; a three-axis gimbal to stabilize and rotate the camera; and an ELRS receiver through which the drone gets its control commands.
The marketplace is also still used to buy food and clothing for soldiers. Throughout August 2026, one channel repeatedly updated its shopping list of food for assault units near Kupyansk (the same town Russia’s Defense Ministry long ago officially declared “captured”). The cart included coffee, tea, nuts, and packs of Snickers bars. Another fundraiser asked for single-serving packets of ketchup, mustard, mayonnaise, jam, condensed milk, honey, and caramel.
On Wildberries, the picture is about the same. ‘Military’ goods remain for sale.
By the end of August, of the 1,616 Wildberries listings linked to in volunteer fundraisers, 785, almost half, remained for sale. Another 621 pages could still be opened, but the item was marked as sold out. Of the 210 links that wouldn’t open, 194 still had their name and other technical data in Wildberries’ system, while only 16 listings had disappeared completely.
As with Ozon, there’s no way to determine from public data whether the seller or the marketplace itself removed a given item.
But there’s no sign that Wildberries has fully removed its “military” assortment either. For example, a Yamal-601 satellite internet kit remains for sale for about 275,000 rubles. The seller describes it outright as “suitable for the SVO.” In reviews, buyers write: “The soldiers are happy,” “Thanks from the guys in the SVO zone,” and “Used in the SVO.”
You can also order an exoskeleton for about 55,000 rubles (here’s the volunteer fundraiser for it), body armor with plates for almost 30,000 (fundraiser), an “anti-drone” blanket for 16,700 (fundraiser), a drone battery for 26,700 (fundraiser), and a night-vision device for about 6,000 rubles (fundraiser).
At the same time, pages for a 60-round magazine for the AK-74, active shooting earmuffs, and a few other items won’t open. But this looks like ordinary turnover in the product lineup. A significant portion of “military” goods on Wildberries are still sold quite openly, with sellers stating as much directly in the product descriptions.
Drone strikes are costing marketplaces market value. Still, they’ve probably made a good profit during the war.
The warehouse strikes hit Ozon’s stock price directly. A single share of the marketplace cost 2,979 rubles on the eve of the first strike, August 21. In the first trading session after the series of strikes, the price fell to 2,112.5 rubles, and by midday on August 28 it stood at about 2,207 rubles, 26% lower than before the strikes. According to data from the Moscow Exchange, Ozon’s market capitalization fell by roughly 26% over that period, from 645 billion to 475 billion rubles. This is not a direct loss for the company but a shift in how investors value it. Ozon has not yet disclosed the cost of the damaged facilities and goods.
The largest stake in Ozon, 34.95%, belongs to entities linked to investor Alexander Chachava. The Anti-Corruption Foundation claims that the money used to buy it came through a loan of 51.23 billion rubles from a company tied to Gennady Timchenko, a billionaire very close to Putin. Investigators believe the stake may have been purchased in the interests of Putin’s inner circle.
Wildberries has no shares on any exchange (it’s a private company), so its value can’t be tracked the same way. According to a recent ranking by the Russian business magazine Forbes Russia, Tatyana Kim’s fortune fell from $7.1 billion to $5 billion over the past year. But those $2.1 billion can’t be counted as losses from the strikes: the valuation was recorded on July 18, when the strikes had only just begun. The potential damage to Wildberries itself and to the sellers who stored goods there was estimated at up to 878 billion rubles as of mid-August, though the company never confirmed that figure.
It’s nearly impossible to estimate how much the marketplaces have earned during the war. Volunteer fundraisers with direct links to products are a tiny fraction of the overall flow of orders for “military” goods.
Some sense of the scale can be gleaned indirectly from calculations by Verstka, an independent Russian news outlet that gained access to Ozon’s internal analytics data. The outlet’s journalists found 33 categories of goods that could be used at the front. In just one year, marketplace users ordered more than 2 million units of these goods, worth a combined 25 billion rubles.
Representatives of Ozon and Wildberries did not respond to Meduza’s requests for comment by the time this article was published.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Iran is ‘little war’ compared to US spending on Ukraine – Trump
articles.body:
Iran is ‘little war’ compared to US spending on Ukraine – Trump
The Iran war is “relatively little” for the US compared with the vast amount of weaponry Washington gave Ukraine under Joe Biden, President Donald Trump has said. He claimed his predecessor handed Kiev $300 billion worth of arms for free.
Trump made the remarks while taking questions from reporters at an Oval Office event on Monday as fighting in the Middle East flared up again after weeks of relative calm. US forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, prompting Tehran to retaliate with missile attacks on US forces in Jordan and the UAE.
Asked whether the prolonged operation against Iran was draining US military resources needed elsewhere, Trump shrugged off the concern. “This is a relatively little war for us. This is not a big war,” he said, adding that the US has “so much ammunition and munitions” stationed around the world that it could draw on additional supplies if needed.
“You know where the money went was Ukraine,” Trump continued, arguing that Washington has used “very little” weaponry against Iran by comparison.
He then contrasted US expenditures on Iran with Washington’s support for Ukraine under his predecessor.
“Joe Biden gave Ukraine over $300 billion worth of stuff free,” Trump said, adding that under his administration Ukraine “has to pay for it” through European NATO members. The $300 billion figure is widely disputed. A May report by the Special Inspector General for Operation Atlantic Resolve put total US appropriations for Ukraine and the broader response to the conflict at about $195 billion since February 2022, of which $67.8 billion was committed in defense articles and services to Kiev.
Trump’s description of the Iran conflict as a “little war” comes as it enters its seventh month despite his repeated declarations of victory. He proclaimed “total and complete victory” in early April and has since repeatedly said Washington had won or was close to ending the conflict.
The war has consumed billions of dollars’ worth of US weaponry, with War Secretary Pete Hegseth putting the overall cost at $37.5 billion by July. Washington fired more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles in the first four weeks alone – despite producing only a few hundred annually – along with more than 1,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors.
The strain has also hit US weapons inventories in Europe, where supplies of Patriot interceptors and other key munitions have fallen to “beyond critical” levels as weapons are diverted to the Middle East, media reported last week, citing US and NATO officials.
Washington has meanwhile stepped up economic pressure on Tehran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned on Sunday that the US could unleash “financial violence” against Iran, threatening to impose new secondary sanctions every week to punish Tehran and those doing business with it.

articles.title: Russia’s 6-day attack on Kyiv that started two days after CIA head’s visit to Moscow, culminates with massive ballistic missile strike on eve of school year
articles.body:
On 1 September — the day Ukraine marks Knowledge Day, when schoolchildren and students are meant to begin the new academic year — Russia launched a massive attack on Kyiv and its region with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. Moscow used different types of its fast, deadly weapons, including ship-launched Kalibr, and hypersonic Zircon missiles, and jet-powered drones to target the Ukrainian capital.
This attack was the culmination of a 6-day assault on the capital and region that began on 27 August. It started two days after CIA Director John Ratcliffe arrived in Moscow on 25 August. US President Donald Trump announced that the visit was linked with US-initiated peace efforts to end the war against Ukraine. Throughout this 5-day period, air raid sirens sounded every hour in the capital and region, paralyzing life in Kyiv, according to Sky News.
As early as the day after the 5-day attack began, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky stated that Russia had destroyed about 90% of the food logistics infrastructure of retail chains, according to UkrInform.
Russia injures three children and continues the attack
As a result of the "ballistic" attack on Kyiv and the region, hits from enemy missiles and strike drones were recorded at 28 locations, and debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations, according to the Air Force of Ukraine.
In addition, some enemy missiles did not reach their targets, and the locations of those missiles are being clarified.
"Unfortunately, as a result of the Russian attack, there are dead and injured. The attack continues, with more than ten Russian drones in the airspace," the military reported.
According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, civilian infrastructure was damaged in 5 of Kyiv's 10 districts — Holosiivskyi, Darnytskyi, Dniprovskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, and Solomianskyi.
"As a result of the attack, unfortunately, 8 people died. Another 7 people were injured, including 3 children," the Kyiv authorities said.
Railway workers are still receiving treatment and remain hospitalized
Russia struck a railway facility, a critical link in the country's logistics chain, as its airways have been closed since 2022.
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, head of the board of Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways), stated that Russia carried out a targeted ballistic attack on Kyiv's railway infrastructure. Russia killed six railway workers.
According to him, another employee was injured and is in the hospital, where they are receiving the necessary care.
He added that dozens of employees managed to take shelter and survive the attack. They are now being helped to recover from what they experienced.
Pertsovskyi noted that the strike caused "extensive destruction," including the complete destruction of one workshop, and that efforts to extinguish fires at the facility were still ongoing.
He said that, due to the attack's consequences, movement was temporarily restricted on two railway sections, but it was later restored.
Earlier, a source close to the Russian president told The Economist that Vladimir Putin most likely regarded Ratcliffe's visit as a sign of American weakness. He already interpreted former CIA Head Bill Burns' meeting with Russian authorities in 2021 the same way, where he warned about the consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine. Three months after the meeting, Russia launched the full-scale invasion.

articles.title: German politician wants to send Taurus missiles to Ukraine after Russian drone attack in Leipzig airport
articles.body:
Wolfgang Kubicki, chair of Germany’s pro-business liberal Free Democratic Party (FDP), proposed that Berlin summon Russia’s ambassador and use the prospect of Taurus missiles for Ukraine as leverage against further hybrid attacks during an appearance on German broadcaster ntv.
Kubicki’s proposal does not change German policy. The FDP has no seats in the Bundestag, Germany’s federal parliament, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz has ruled out supplying the missiles. However, it recasts military aid to Ukraine as a potential cost Moscow would face for hybrid attacks inside Germany. Berlin has since formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig/Halle operation that prompted his remarks.
Kubicki said “a reasonable person” would tell the ambassador that Germany had so far withheld Taurus missiles. If the hybrid threat continued, Berlin should do everything possible to ensure Ukraine received the weapons it needed to defend itself against Russia, he added.
Taurus, the weapon Kubicki spoke about, is a German-Swedish cruise missile launched from military aircraft, with a range exceeding 500 kilometers. Ukraine has sought it for years to strike military targets far behind Russian lines.
Germany refused to supply Taurus missiles in 2025 while funding hundreds of Ukrainian-made long-range systems. Merz again ruled out a transfer in March, arguing that Ukrainian weapons were more effective.
Leipzig sharpens Germany’s hybrid-war debate
Germany formally blamed Russia on 1 September for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport and said it would close the Russian consulate in Bonn and terminate the agreement under which the Russian House cultural center operates in Berlin, DW reported. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt cited evidence from German and allied intelligence services, as well as investigations across Europe. Russia has denied involvement.
The operation that prompted Kubicki’s warning involved an explosives-laden drone that struck the wing of a Ukrainian Antonov An-124 heavy cargo aircraft on the evening of 4 August but failed to detonate, Die Zeit reported. The airport handles civilian freight and NATO logistics, while Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines uses it as a base.
Investigators later found evidence that three drones were involved and discovered about 50 grams of suspected military explosive near the runways.

articles.title: Indian among 12 killed in Russian strikes on Kiev region after Modi-Putin talks
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tueday said an Indian national was among those killed in the latest overnight Russian attacks, adding a new dimension to the strikes just a day after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek.
Russia launched a large aerial attack in and around Ukraine’s capital overnight into Tuesday morning, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than a dozen others, including three children, local authorities said.
Zelenskyy said the death underscored the human cost of Russia's war in Ukraine and called for the violence to end. Modi, during his meeting with Putin on Monday, had said there was no solution to the Ukraine conflict on the battlefield and that the war must end "for humanity's sake", according to a readout of the meeting.
Ukraine’s air force said that Russia began the attack at 6 pm on Monday (1500 GMT), using ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, as well as 218 drones and decoys. About a third of the drones were reportedly jet-powered.
The main targets were the Kiev and Odessa regions, the air force said in a statement on Telegram.
The overnight strikes marked the sixth consecutive day of Russian attacks on Kiev, following a stretch of air raid alerts that began last week.
The latest attack struck civilian infrastructure and residential buildings in several districts of Kiev, with eight people killed in the city itself and three others in the surrounding region.
The death toll
The Russian strikes killed seven people in the Darnytskyy district of the capital, authorities said. One person was seriously wounded and hospitalised, the emergency service said. At another site in the district, an explosion wounded two people, including a child.
An eighth person was killed in the Holosiivskyy district, when a nonresidential building was hit and caught fire, the emergency service said in a statement. In the Solomianskyy district, a drone strike hit a residential building, causing damage. Emergency workers rescued a man and freed a woman trapped beneath the rubble.
The other three people who died were in areas of the Kiev region outside the city, and 12 were wounded. In Boryspil, three cars caught fire.
Emergency crews evacuated 48 people and rescued two from under the rubble. Eight people were injured, including two children. Also in Boryspil, a truck caught fire at an infrastructure facility, damaging the building. Two people were killed and three others injured, the emergency service said. A service station in Boryspil was also damaged, killing one person.
The Odessa region came under a major Russian attack overnight, damaging civilian infrastructure and wounding one person, regional head Oleh Kiper said.
Two residential buildings were damaged, while a fire broke out at a sewing factory. Russian forces also struck the Orlivka international ferry crossing on the border with Romania, he said.
Ukrainian forces said they destroyed or suppressed 199 aerial targets, including five ballistic missiles and 187 drones. Missile and drone strikes were recorded at 28 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at another 10 sites, it said.
Russia says attack targeted military-industrial and fuel and energy facilities
Russia's defence ministry, meanwhile, said its forces had carried out a "massive strike" using long-range weapons and attack drones.
It said the attack targeted military-industrial and fuel and energy facilities in Kiev and the surrounding region.
The ministry also said it had struck infrastructure in the southern Odessa region and the ports of Odessa and Chornomorsk.
Both sides have escalated long-range strikes in recent months, targeting infrastructure such as warehouses, businesses, and oil and port facilities, as well as ships, increasing civilian casualties.
Ukraine faces a shortage of interceptor missiles, particularly US-made Patriot systems used against ballistic threats.

articles.title: Two decades after Beslan, Russia faces terrorism of a different kind
articles.body:
Two decades after Beslan, Russia faces terrorism of a different kind
On September 1, 2004, during celebrations marking the first day of the school year, a group of Islamist terrorists occupied Beslan’s School No. 1 in the Caucasus region of Russia, and captured over 1,100 hostages, including students, their families, and teachers.
After three days of tense negotiations, during which 26 women and children were released, Russian special forces had to storm the building in an emergency operation after explosions were heard inside the school, which had been rigged to detonate by the militants. The Beslan terrorist attack claimed the lives of 334 people, including 186 children, 17 teachers and school staff, ten FSB officers, and two rescue workers.
Russia spent decades fighting the Islamist threat from the 1990s to late 2010s and refining its prevention mechanisms. Indeed, President Vladimir Putin was the first to call his US counterpart on September 11, 2001.
But a new danger has arisen with the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, posed not by suicide bombers but by drones and missiles – sent from the West, striking at night, in a systematic campaign of terror launched by Ukraine that targets Russian civilians.
Since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, Ukrainian attacks have killed more than 8,000 civilians and injured almost 20,000 more, according to Rodion Miroshnik, who leads the Russian Foreign Ministry mission tracking Ukrainian war crimes. At least 266 civilians, including seven children, were killed in Ukrainian attacks in the first 90 days of 2026, and 1,459 others were injured, according to Miroshnik’s estimates.
RT looks back at the deadliest Ukrainian strikes on civilians, which Russia has condemned as terrorist attacks aimed at compensating for the setbacks the Ukrainian military has suffered on the front line, where Russian forces have been on the offensive for months.
Tragedy on New Year’s Eve
On December 30, 2023, Ukrainian forces bombarded the Russian city of Belgorod, located around 40 km from the border, using multiple-launch rocket systems. The shelling targeted a popular city mall that traditionally held festive events on New Year’s Eve. The strike claimed the lives of 14 people, including two children, and left 108 people, among them 15 children, injured.
Crocus City Hall
The 2024 massacre, second only to the Beslan attack in its tragic scale, saw four armed men opening fire on concertgoers in a music venue that was filling with around 3,000 people ahead of a show by the rock band Picnic.
They set the hall on fire and murdered 151 people and injured 609 others. The Russian Investigative Committee concluded that, although the attack was carried out by a regional offshoot of Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS), it was organized on behalf of Ukraine.
The terrorists tried to flee toward the Ukrainian border before being intercepted and captured by Russian law enforcement.
Dark holiday season
On January 1, 2026, a cafe and hotel in Khorly, a Black Sea village in Kherson Region, were struck by three Ukrainian drones, including one carrying an incendiary mixture, during New Year’s celebrations. The strike killed 29 people and left more than 50 injured. According to the local authorities, the venue was scouted by a reconnaissance UAV before the attack.
The tragedy in Khorly was followed by a series of similar strikes that brought the total number of civilian casualties to 152 over the 11-day Russian winter holiday season, including 45 deaths, according to Miroshnik. Three minors were among those killed, the diplomat said at the time.
Horror at hospital
On March 12, 2026, Ukrainian forces struck a medical facility in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR). According to Russian officials, the attack targeted the grounds of a medical center housing more than 130 patients and around 50 medical personnel. Eight medical workers were killed and ten people were injured in the strike.
Starobelsk ‘We will never forget’
On May 22, three waves of Ukrainian kamikaze drones struck the main academic building and dormitory of the Starobelsk Professional College in the Lugansk People’s Republic in a nighttime attack. As a result, 21 students – some just 18 years old – were killed and around 60 people were injured.
President Vladimir Putin called it a deliberate ”terrorist act,” while the nation’s newly appointed human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, accused Ukrainian forces of carrying out a “targeted strike that killed 21 children.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week that Moscow will “never forget and will seek justice for [Ukrainian leader Vladimir] Zelensky’s bloody terror attack in Starobelsk.”
‘Monstrous crime’
On June 17, 2026, a Ukrainian drone struck a bus carrying a Belarusian youth soccer team in Bryansk Region, Russia. The attack killed the coach’s wife and injured several other passengers, including children.
Belarus described the attack as a “monstrous crime,” which President Alexander Lukashenko called a deliberate provocation. Kiev denied responsibility, while Zelensky threatened Minsk, demanding that Belarus dismantle alleged drone relay stations near the border and warning that Kiev would destroy them if Belarus failed to act.
Deadly drone raid
On August 10, 2026, the Ukrainian military launched a massive long-range drone strike on Nizhnekamsk in the Republic of Tatarstan, Russia, more than 2,000 km away from Ukraine’s border with Russia. According to Mayor Radmir Belyaev, Ukrainian UAVs targeted both industrial and civilian sites in the city.
The attack claimed the lives of 13 people and forced nearly 80 to request medical assistance. Nearly 30 people were hospitalized. Russia’s Investigative Committee said one of the civilians killed was a minor. The agency has designated the Ukrainian attack as an act of terrorism, stressing that the targeted locations “had nothing to do with military activities.”

articles.title: CENTCOM begins wave of strikes on Iran in retaliation for targeting of US troops in region
articles.body:
US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that it completed a wave of strikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran early on Wednesday.
According to CENTCOM, the strikes were carried out in retaliation for Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the recent attack on US troops stationed in the region.
"US forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," CENTCOM said in a post on X/Twitter.
"The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."
Iranian state media reported that several explosions were heard in the cities of Bandar Abbas, Ahvaz, and Sirik.
Following the strikes, electrical power to several parts of the Hormozgan province was lost, Iranian state media IRIB reported. Power has been restored to Qeshm county in Hormozgan, the area's governor announced on Wednesday morning.
IRIB claimed that a US airstrike on Sirik hit a wedding, killing four and injuring 63. The US did not immediately respond to the allegations.
Air defenses were also reportedly activated in eastern Tehran, Iran's semi-official Tasnim News Agency said.
The US military attacked two Iranian government tankers during Tuesday's strikes on Iran, US officials told Axios.
This is the first time that the US has struck an Iranian tanker under a new "tanker for tanker" policy rather than to stop a ship violating the naval blockade. The policy, which Axios said was approved by US President Donald Trump, aims to deter Iranian attacks on tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump confirms strikes, says they are 'very justified'
US President Donald Trump later confirmed the strikes in a post to Truth Social, echoing CENTCOM's reasoning for the strikes.
"The United States is, as we speak, striking Iranian Targets near the Strait of Hormuz," he wrote. "The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait, which currently has no mines (They have been completely removed or detonated!), and the Iranians shooting eight missiles, all successfully knocked down, at our Military Base in Jordan."
Trump threatened Iran that, should it respond to the "very justified attack," it will be hit "again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!"
Iran will respond to the US' newest wave of strikes with an attack "several times larger," Tasnim reported on Tuesday night, citing a senior Iranian military source.
In a statement shared by Tasnim, the General Staff of Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters stated that it would "deliver crushing and devastating blows to the despicable and malevolent American enemy."
"The more the terrorist US military persists in its malign activities in the region, the heavier the losses it will be forced to bear."
"We have repeatedly declared, and are resolved, that under no circumstances will we yield on the rights of the heroic Iranian nation, and we will impose a heavy cost on the American enemy," it stated.
Iran's foreign ministry responds to US strikes
"The United States’ catalogue of atrocities against the nation of Iran is now complete: a residential home in Kuhestak, #Sirik, was brutally attacked tonight while families were celebrating a wedding," Esmaeil Baghaei, spokesperson for Iran's foreign ministry said in a post on X.
"More than 50 innocent men, women and children were martyred or wounded."
"This cruelty cannot be separated from the chain of atrocities that preceded it in #Minab, #Lamerd, Qeshm and elsewhere nor from the strikes on military targets that were dressed in deceptive justifications," Baghaei added.
"More dangerous than the bomb itself is the normalization of bombing; and more dangerous than silence is the conversion of silence into legitimacy."
"Iran will respond to these savage crimes with firmness," Baghaei said. "Turning a blind eye to injustice does not contain it; it only emboldens the perpetrators."
US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak Island
On Sunday, the US launched its first strikes against Iran in weeks, targeting two launchers on Larak Island after IRGC forces were identified as preparing the launchers to fire towards the Strait of Hormuz.
In response, Iran launched a number of missiles towards US troops and military assets stationed in Jordan.
Trump on Monday confirmed that all but one of the missiles were intercepted by US air defense systems and that nothing of importance was hit during the attack, during a Monday phone call with Fox News’s Trey Yingst.
Trump vowed that the US would “hit [Iran] hard’ in retaliation for their attempt to target US troops.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: 12 killed in overnight strikes across Ukraine, including Indian citizen
articles.body:
Twelve people were killed as a result of Russian strikes on Ukraine on the night of September 1, including a foreign national, reported President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"In total, 12 people were killed, among them a citizen of India, and dozens more were injured as a result of the attack. My condolences to everyone who lost family and loved ones," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram.
He noted that response operations following the Russian attack have been ongoing since overnight in many cities and communities. Specifically, nearly 350 firefighters are deployed in Kyiv and the region alone.
"A significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were involved in the strike. Unfortunately, there is destruction of residential and civilian infrastructure. In Boryspil, an ordinary five-story building was damaged. Fifty people were evacuated. The necessary services are on site. Enterprises were also hit. In total, there are four dead and 13 injured in the city. My condolences," the President stated.
Additionally, strikes using guided aerial bombs and drones on Odesa and the region continued since evening. Thousands of families were left without power, and efforts are underway to restore it promptly. The Russians also demonstratively damaged a checkpoint on the border with Romania, as well as export infrastructure.
In Kyiv, seven people were killed in a strike on a railway depot.
Kherson, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy, and Dnipropetrovsk regions were also under shelling.
"Russia always calculates its strikes specifically to destroy life to the maximum extent, and it succeeds only when air defense assets are insufficient. I am grateful to everyone helping Ukraine receive anti-ballistic defense within the PURL framework and bilateral deliveries, and it is crucial that these arrivals increase in the autumn. The number of victims of Russian terror directly depends on every new aid package," the President emphasized.
According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, as a result of the massive strike on Kyiv and Kyiv region, eight people were killed and seven injured in the capital, while four people were killed and 14 injured in Kyiv region. In Kyiv’s Darnytsky district, seven employees of JSC Ukrzaliznytsia were killed as a result of the strike.

articles.title: UN counted 183 Ukrainian children killed or wounded in July, the highest since 2022
articles.body:
July 2026 was the worst month for Ukrainian children since April 2022 by the number killed and injured, the Ukrainian military's strategic communications directorate reported. It cited UNICEF data, Ukraine's state register of children affected by the war, and figures from the UN monitoring mission. The directorate published the count on 1 September—the day the school year begins.
July broke a four-year record
The directorate reported that 17 children died in July 2026 and 166 were injured. That is half again more than in June. The UN monitoring mission has not recorded a higher number of Ukrainian children hurt by Russian aggression since April 2022, the first spring of the full-scale invasion, when at least 62 children were killed and 149 injured.
As of 1 September, Russia had killed 739 Ukrainian children and injured 2,840 since the full-scale invasion began, according to the directorate, while the UN's own verified count for the same period is higher, at 820 children killed and 3,126 injured. Russia has illegally deported or displaced a further 20,610—abducted, in the directorate's words. Europol has previously traced 45 deported children all the way to the military units that moved them and handed the evidence to Kyiv.
In March 2023, the International Criminal Court in The Hague issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin over the unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children from occupied territory.
437 killed, over 2,600 injured: Ukraine’s deadliest month for civilians since 2022, UN says
Empty classrooms are one part of it
Many schools did not open on 1 September because Russia keeps Ukrainian cities under constant fire, the directorate said. It argued that Russia's "genocidal practices" reach beyond education and culture.
In the occupied territories, Russia works on the children it already controls. It sent 582,000 children in 2,000 schools a first lesson on the unity of the peoples of Russia, with no Ukrainian language taught.
What these months look like on the ground
The monthly figure is built from strikes like the one near Kryvyi Rih, where rescuers pulled two children alive from the rubble of a village house and three others did not survive. In June, a Russian strike injured three children on a beach in Zaporizhzhia.
Russia’s 6-day attack on Kyiv that started two days after CIA head’s visit to Moscow, culminates with massive ballistic missile strike on eve of school year
In August, Russian ballistic and hypersonic missiles damaged a children's hospital in Kyiv. The capital and other cities have been under repeated attack for days at a stretch.

articles.title: Charges filed in absentia against Russian general and colonel over attacks on Okhmatdyt and Reuters journalists
articles.body:
Charges filed in absentia against Russian general and colonel over attacks on Okhmatdyt and Reuters journalists
According to Ukrinform, the SSU reported this.
“According to the case file, one of the suspects is Russian Major General Mykola Varpakhovych, commander of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division of the Russian Armed Forces. The investigation established that on July 8, 2024, the officer issued a combat order to carry out a missile strike on the “Okhmatdyt” National Children’s Specialized Hospital in Kyiv,” the statement reads.
The SSU noted that at that time, long-range aviation units under Varpakhovich’s command carried out a precision strike on the medical facility using an “Kh-101” air-to-ground cruise missile, which was launched from a Russian Tu-95MS missile-carrying bomber.
“At the time of the attack, there were over 600 patients in the hospital. Two people were killed, including a doctor, and dozens more were injured. The missile completely destroyed the toxicology wing and damaged four other buildings where surgical operations were being performed and children with cancer were being treated,” the SSU reported.
Another suspect is Russian Colonel Alexander Lutovinov, commander of the missile brigade of the 49th Combined Arms Army of the Russian Federation’s Southern Military District.
According to the investigation, he organized a missile strike on the “Sapphire” hotel complex in Kramatorsk on August 24, 2024. As a result of this attack, a security advisor for the international news agency Reuters was killed, and five of his colleagues sustained injuries of varying severity.
According to the investigation, the decision to carry out the strike was made by Colonel General Alexei Kim, deputy chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, whom the SSU has already notified of the charges against him in absentia.
“In accordance with his criminal order, Lutovinov directly ordered his subordinates to launch an ‘Iskander-M’ ballistic missile from the Rostov region,” the SSU emphasized.
Investigators from the SSU’s Main Investigative Directorate have charged Varpakhovych and Lutovinov in absentia under Part 2 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (war crimes resulting in loss of life).
Comprehensive measures are underway to bring them to justice.
As previously reported, on July 8, 2024, Russia carried out a terrorist attack on the Okhmatdyt National Children’s Specialized Hospital. The strike killed two people and injured 35, including nine children.
The hospital’s toxicology wing was destroyed, and the surgical and new wings, as well as the Ministry of Health’s pediatric cardiology center, were damaged.
Five buildings of the medical facility were damaged, including the toxicology wing, the Soviet-era surgical wing, and the new treatment and diagnostic wing, as well as a transformer substation.
On the night of August 24, 2024, Russian forces launched a missile strike on a hotel in Kramatorsk where Reuters journalists were staying. Reuters security adviser Ryan Evans, a former British military officer, was killed.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia kills 12 Ukrainians and foreign national in overnight attack
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Russia kills 12 Ukrainians and foreign national in overnight attack
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reported that 12 people, including a foreign national, were killed in the Russian attack on Ukraine on the night of 31 August-1 September.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote: "Overall, 12 people were killed, among them an Indian citizen, and dozens more were injured in the attack. My condolences to everyone who has lost family and loved ones."
Details: Zelenskyy noted that efforts to deal with the aftermath of the Russian attack have been ongoing since the night in many cities and districts, with almost 350 rescue workers deployed in the city of Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast alone.
A significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack. Residential and civilian infrastructure was damaged.
An ordinary five-storey residential building was damaged in the city of Boryspil, Kyiv Oblast. Fifty people have been evacuated. Emergency services are working at the scene. Businesses were also struck. Overall, four people were killed and 13 injured in the city.
Russian forces attacked Odesa and the surrounding region with guided aerial bombs and drones from the evening onwards. Thousands of households were left without electricity, and work is underway to restore power as quickly as possible.
A border crossing point on the Romanian border was deliberately damaged, as was export infrastructure. Seven people were killed in Kyiv in a strike on a railway depot. Kherson, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts also came under attack.
Quote: "Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people's lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defence capabilities are insufficient. I am grateful to everyone helping Ukraine receive anti-ballistic capabilities through PURL and bilateral supplies, and it is very important that these deliveries increase this autumn. The number of victims of Russian terror directly hinges on every new package of assistance."
Background: On the night of 31 August-1 September, Russia attacked Ukraine with Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400 ballistic missiles, Zircon anti-ship missiles, Kalibr cruise missiles, Kh-31P anti-radiation missiles, Banderol missile drones and 218 UAVs of various types. Strikes were recorded at 28 locations. Ukrainian air defence downed 199 Russian aerial assets.

articles.title: Indian Citizen Among 12 Killed as Russia Pounds Kyiv and Ukraine With Ballistic Missiles, Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Indian Citizen Among 12 Killed as Russia Pounds Kyiv and Ukraine With Ballistic Missiles, Drones
An Indian citizen was among 12 people killed as Russia unleashed ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones across Ukraine overnight, striking homes, a Kyiv railway depot, businesses and critical infrastructure.
An Indian citizen was among 12 people killed in a massive Russian missile and drone barrage across Ukraine, with strikes hitting apartment buildings, a Kyiv railway depot, businesses and critical infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 1.
Dozens more were injured as Russia deployed large numbers of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles against Kyiv and several other regions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“In many cities and communities, work to address the aftermath of the Russian attack has been ongoing since last night—nearly 350 first responders are involved in Kyiv and the region alone. A significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack,” Zelenskyy said.
He added that residential buildings and civilian infrastructure were among the sites hit.
“Unfortunately, residential buildings and civilian infrastructure have been damaged,” the Ukrainian leader stated.
Boryspil, east of Kyiv, was among the hardest-hit cities. A five-story apartment building was damaged there, forcing emergency crews to evacuate 50 people. Businesses were also struck.
“In Boryspil, an ordinary five-story residential building was damaged. Fifty people were evacuated. All necessary services are on the ground. Businesses were also struck. Overall, 4 people were killed and 13 injured in the city. My condolences,” Zelenskyy said.
Kyiv itself suffered a deadly ballistic missile strike on railway infrastructure.
Russian forces deliberately targeted a railway depot and other railway facilities in the capital, according to Ukrzaliznytsia CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi.
Seven people were killed at the depot, six of them Ukrzaliznytsia employees. Another railway worker was hospitalized with injuries.
Dozens of employees survived because they had moved into shelters during the air raid alert.
The strike caused extensive destruction around the depot, including the complete destruction of a workshop, while emergency crews continued fighting several fires.
Rail traffic was temporarily suspended along two sections following the strike before service was restored.
“All of this is nothing compared with the terrible loss of our colleagues,” Pertsovskyi wrote, adding that the company was contacting the families of those killed and providing support.
Zelenskyy later confirmed the death toll at the railway facility.
“In Kyiv, a strike on a railway depot killed 7 people,” he said.
Russian strikes also continued against Odesa and the surrounding region, leaving thousands of households without electricity.
“Since last evening, guided aerial bomb and drone strikes have continued against Odesa and the region. Thousands of families were left without electricity, and work is ongoing to restore power to people as quickly as possible,” Zelenskyy stated.
Russia also damaged a border crossing with Romania and infrastructure used for Ukrainian exports.
“A border crossing with Romania was deliberately damaged, as was export infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said.
The Kherson, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Zhytomyr, Sumy and Dnipro regions also came under Russian strikes.
“Overall, 12 people were killed, among them an Indian citizen, and dozens more were injured in the attack. My condolences to everyone who has lost family and loved ones,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader said the casualty toll once again showed how strongly civilian survival depends on the availability of air defense systems.
“Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defense capabilities are insufficient,” Zelenskyy stated.
He called for increased deliveries of systems capable of intercepting ballistic missiles, particularly through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, or PURL, and bilateral assistance from Ukraine’s partners.
“I am grateful to everyone helping Ukraine receive anti-ballistic capabilities through PURL and bilateral supplies, and it is very important that these deliveries increase this fall,” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that additional air defense support has an immediate impact on civilian casualties.
“The number of victims of Russian terror directly hinges on every new package of assistance. I thank everyone who is helping make Ukraine more resilient,” Zelenskyy added.
Previously, a large-scale aerial attack struck the city and region of Odesa, with local authorities reporting multiple explosions across the area.
The assault involved high-speed airborne targets, standard and jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, missiles, and guided aerial bombs launched from both northern directions and the Black Sea.

articles.title: Japan to Arm Fighter Jets with AARGM-ER Missiles to Counter Chinese Air Defenses
articles.body:
Japan’s Ministry of Defense will begin the procurement process for AARGM-ER anti-radiation missiles in 2027 to counter Chinese air defense systems.
This is indicated in the Japanese Ministry of Defense’s budget document for fiscal year 2027.
Following the establishment of Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force, the missile will become the first weapon of this class to be operated by the Japanese Air Self-Defense Force.
The procurement of these missiles is intended to enable their use from U.S.-made combat platforms, including the F-35, which Japan plans to operate for decades to come.
This comes amid increased Chinese military activity around Japan and the modernization of Japan’s air-launched weapons, which long remained predominantly defensive. This approach significantly limited the strike capabilities of Japanese combat aircraft.
The AARGM-ER (AGM-88G Advanced Anti-Radiation Guided Missile – Extended Range) is a next-generation U.S. air-launched anti-radiation missile designed primarily to detect, suppress, and destroy enemy air defense systems.
The missile is designed to engage not only fixed radar sites but also mobile surface-to-air missile systems, command posts, and other elements of an integrated air defense system.
One key feature is its ability to continue the engagement even after the adversary’s radar station has been switched off.
The missile uses a multi-mode guidance system that lets it detect and track a target after it stops radiating radar emissions.
The AARGM-ER was initially developed for the U.S. Navy’s F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler. The program was subsequently expanded to the F-35 family, including the F-35A, F-35B, and F-35C versions.
Militarnyi previously reported that the Japan Air Self-Defense Force had begun testing the F-2 fighter with a new long-range air-launched cruise missile.
The exact specifications of the air-launched variant are currently unknown.
Meanwhile, given that the ground-launched variant’s range is estimated at 1,200–1,500 km, the air-launched version will likely have similar performance, or potentially an even greater range, because it launches from an aircraft.

articles.title: Russia strikes Kyiv and surrounding region, killing more than 10 people
articles.body:
Russia strikes Kyiv and surrounding region, killing more than 10 people
Russian forces attacked civilian infrastructure and residential buildings in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi, Holosiivskyi, and Solomianskyi districts overnight on September 1, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported.
The strikes killed eight people and injured five others, including three children, sparking fires and partially destroying a residential building.
Russian forces also struck railway infrastructure in Kyiv, including a depot, the state railway operator Ukrainian Railways reported. The strike killed seven people — six of them railway employees — and injured another company employee. Ukrainian media reported that the strike hit the city’s Darnytskyi district.
In the Kyiv region, a Russian strike using ballistic missiles and drones killed four people and injured 13, local authorities stated. The strike also damaged residential buildings, vehicles, and infrastructure, the State Emergency Service reported.
In Boryspil, the strike damaged a five-story residential building, two private houses, and a store, and hit an industrial building at another address in the city. Rescuers evacuated 48 people.
Russian drones attacked the Orlivka ferry crossing on the border between Ukraine’s Odesa region and Romania, Ukrainian border guards reported. The crossing has since suspended operations.
In the Odesa region, a massive Russian strike damaged residential buildings and sparked a fire at a sewing workshop, injuring one person, local authorities stated.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its forces struck military enterprises and energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region, as well as infrastructure in Odesa, the Odesa region, and the ports of Odesa and Chornomorsk.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1650: Ukraine isolates 2,500 Russian troops on port-controlling spit
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
800 jet drones in four days: Russia is now firing type Ukraine's interceptors cannot catch. Of more than 1,500 drones launched over four days, about 800 have been jet-powered.
"In intercepts, they're screaming": Russia occupied this spit to control Ukraine's ports. Military says it has now isolated 2,500-strong grouping and destroyed all its artillery. Drone strikes and remote mining have cut supply, the Ukrainian soldiers say.
Intelligence and technology
Ukrainian company builds single device that detects FPV drone, reads its video feed, and jams it. Brama has passed lab and combat testing and is now going through codification.
About $150 for airframe, about $875 for finished glider: Ukraine's BlueBird is selling its drone at every stage of assembly. Units pick the control system, camera, and electronics themselves; the bare airframe starts near $150.
International
Fired Ukrainian minister offers to help build America's drone army— for Patriot missiles in return. Mykhailo Fedorov is courting US investors for a fund that would build defense tech companies itself, not just back them.
The US built itself a Russo-Ukrainian drone-war drill—Poland is the first ally in. A Green Beret officer expects most of NATO's 32 members to want a look, as Ukraine's war experience reshapes how the alliance trains.
Russia's shadow war on Europe is widening—NATO still sees no attack coming. A Polish warning, a US spy chief's Moscow trip, and an explosive drone found beside a cargo plane at a German airport all preceded the alliance's assessment.
New developments
Someone placed funeral wreaths near defense companies in Lithuania and Czechia. The head of a Lithuanian defense company called it "ordinary intimidation" by Russians.
