articles.title: ‘Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation’: Zelensky tells airlines still flying into Moscow to get out, days after ordering 1,000 drone attacks a day
articles.body:
‘Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation’: Zelensky tells airlines still flying into Moscow to get out, days after ordering 1,000 drone attacks a day
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines that Russian airspace is becoming unsafe because “there will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account.”
“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelensky said in his evening video address.
Zelensky said that Ukraine “does not threaten civilian aviation as such,” but that Ukrainian drone attacks mean “Russian airspace will effectively be closing”:
We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over. It is important that this is heard by the ambassadors of countries represented here in Ukraine, as well as by ambassadors working in Moscow. Every one of them knows exactly what Russia’s war means for our country and our people, and they must convey this information to their capitals.
It is important that the airlines currently flying to airports primarily in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and other key destinations in Russia hear this as well. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine and our other institutions will provide international organizations with full information about the dangers in Russian airspace. Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation.
Volodymyr Zelensky said on August 28 that he had ordered Ukrainian troops to launch 1,000 drones a day at Russia. “Today I held a meeting of the Staff. The key thing is to maximize production of our weapons to defend against Russian strikes on Ukraine. […] The task is 1,000 drones for long-range sanctions a day against Russia,” he said.

articles.title: Former Ukrainian president has made offer to Zelenskyy amid Russia’s new type of war on Kyiv
articles.body:
Former Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko, leader of the opposition European Solidarity party, has offered to unite with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a new type of government. He has explained his initiative as necessary to save the country and adopt crisis-response measures amid a new phase of the war.
Russia's strike campaign has become a governance problem as much as a military one. Each attack on Kyiv costs the city about $12 million, and they now arrive almost twice a week. Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said on 28 August that, roughly speaking, 90% of retail chains' food logistics had been destroyed in the latest attacks, which included jet-powered drones that trigger an air alert in Kyiv every hour.
"We are the opposition, but we are ready to cooperate with the authorities in the legislative provision of all necessary decisions, up to the creation of a coalition and a government of national unity," he said.
Speaking in a video address on 31 August, he set out five issues to solve for the parliamentary session.
One: keep the capital running
The current barrage has forced Kyiv to a near-standstill, with alerts sounding through the working day. If they are permanent, Poroshenko argued, the rules for how the city runs must change, and the government, military, transport operators, and business must agree on a single published procedure. When the capital is shut down for hours, much of the economy stops with it, and the lost billions never reach the army, he added.
"Let us say honestly what Putin is doing. He wants to switch Kyiv off. To make people finally say: it is impossible to live here," Poroshenko said.
Two: give parents a school plan
The school year opens on 1 September under a rule allowing in-person classes only where a school has a shelter with room for everyone. Kyiv's administration told UNN that 94% of city schools have basic shelters, but capacity limits set the ceiling, forcing shifts or blended formats when a shelter cannot hold every child at once.
"Tomorrow is 1 September. Thousands of parents still do not understand how their children will study, especially where there are no proper shelters," Poroshenko said.
Three: return Kyiv's money
Kyiv has lost revenue to the central budget even as its defense costs climb, a dispute with the government that predates the barrage. Poroshenko demanded the return of about $180 million to the budget, along with the personal income tax paid by combat brigades.
"This week Kyiv is forced to carry out a budget sequester for the first time," he explained, cutting spending on doctors, teachers, and the socially vulnerable to fund the city's own defense.
Four: scale up war-risk insurance
Russia's strikes have hit businesses faster than any recovery system can answer, with warehouses and logistics hubs among the targets this month. Business needs war-risk insurance, money for rapid recovery after strikes, new logistics, and the ability to invest in its own protection, including private air defense, Poroshenko said.
Five: fund energy resilience now
Putin has named energy as his main target, the former president pointed out, and the coming winter is the pressure point. Kyiv's small, maneuverable generation, cogeneration, and backup power for hospitals, water utilities, and communications must be installed now, he added.

articles.title: China сomments on Finnish President’s statement on Russia’s nuclear weapons use
articles.body:
China сomments on Finnish President’s statement on Russia’s nuclear weapons use
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said this at a media briefing in response to a question about the Finnish leader’s statement, according to Ukrinform.
“Following the meeting between Foreign Minister Wang Yi and the President of Finland [on July 5 – Ed.], we issued a press release,” Guo said in response to Ukrinform’s request to comment on Stubb’s remarks about China’s non-public position regarding Russia’s nuclear weapons.
The Chinese diplomat did not deny Stubb’s claims, merely noting that Beijing’s position on the Russia-Ukraine conflict and nuclear weapons remains unchanged.
“China’s position on the ‘Ukraine crisis’ [the official term used by China for Russia’s war against Ukraine – Ed.] and on the use of nuclear weapons is consistent and clear. We continue to call for peace talks and a political settlement of the conflict,” the foreign ministry spokesperson said.
The Chinese authorities declare adherence to a defensive nuclear doctrine and a no-first-use policy, which means that China’s nuclear arsenal would be used exclusively in retaliation for a nuclear attack against China.
The official Chinese Foreign Ministry statement on Wang Yi’s meeting with Stubb on July 5 does not mention either Russia’s war or nuclear weapons.
“The current international landscape is marked by changes and turbulence, and the world risks returning to the law of the jungle. China will continue to be an important force for peace, stability and development in today’s world,” China’s top diplomat said to the Finnish president at the time.
See also: Kuchma explains why abandoning the Budapest Memorandum would not have saved Ukraine from war
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said that China had assured him in private talks that it would not allow Russia to use nuclear weapons.

articles.title: On the front line, 210 clashes took place over the past day, August 31 — General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
articles.body:
On the front line, 210 clashes took place over the past day, August 31 — General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Russian forces carried out 93 airstrikes and launched 210 attacks. Ukrainian forces eliminated 1,440 occupiers, 4 tanks, and 1,775 drones.
Over the course of the past day, August 31, there were 210 combat engagements at the front. The enemy launched 93 air strikes, during which it dropped 319 guided aerial bombs. This is reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Details
The invaders also deployed 10,947 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,872 shellings of populated areas and the positions of the Defense Forces.
In the Sumy region, the enemy shelled the populated areas of Mala Korchakivka, Yastrubshchyna, Pysarivka, Kucherivka, Ulanove, and Bachivsk. In addition, the area of the populated locality of Korenok came under an air strike.
Over the past day, the aviation, missile forces, and artillery of the Defense Forces struck three areas where enemy personnel were concentrated, one artillery system, three control posts for unmanned aerial vehicles, and one communications hub.
On the North Slobozhanskyi and Kursk axes, the enemy conducted no assault operations over the past day.
On the South Slobozhanskyi axis, Ukrainian units repelled 16 enemy attacks. The invaders attempted to advance near Starytsia and Vovchanski Khutory, as well as toward Chuhunivka, Khatnie, Mala Vovcha, Dovhenke, and Okhrimivka.
On the Kupiansk axis, the enemy attacked once toward Hlushkivka.
Attempts to breach the Ukrainian defense were repelled on the Lyman axis, where the occupiers attacked six times near Dibrova and Stavky, as well as toward Novoselivka and Drobysheve.

On the Kramatorsk axis, the enemy conducted no assault operations over the past day.

articles.title: What do Canada and Iran have in common? The US bullies both
articles.body:
What do Canada and Iran have in common? The US bullies both
Canada has very few similarities with Iran – to Canada’s own shame.
Let’s leave aside the basic differences, such as location, demographics, weather, and cuisine, and focus on the essentials: Historically, Iran is old and firmly based on an ancient civilization; Canada, like the US, is young and a little accidental, a leftover of the British Empire in its settler-colonial-ethnic-cleansing variant.
In terms of religion, Iran is shaped by pious Shia Islam; Canada displays the flaccid mix of an emasculated Christmas-and-jingle-bells-only Christianity and aggressive anything-goes consumerist secularism typical of the contemporary West.
Geopolitically, Iran is a proud and victorious opponent of the US and Israel; Canada is a fairly ordinary vassal in the American empire.
Accordingly, Canada is deeply and proudly involved in the West’s proxy war against Russia by way of using up Ukraine. Indeed, the Canadian contribution is particularly ironic because it also serves a frenetic and powerful nationalist Ukrainian lobby, rooted in deliberately privileged fascist World War Two runaways and Cold War conspirators. Iran, on the other side, has long helped Russia and, for its efforts, been directly attacked by Kiev’s Zelensky regime. In return, Western sources claim, Moscow has been helping Tehran with its ongoing defense against the US and Israel.
Most importantly, Iran is a country on the side of elementary decency, fundamental human ethics, and international law and therefore against the genocide committed by Israel, the US, UK, Germany, and various other Western accomplices against the Palestinian nation. Canada – Israeli murders of Canadian citizens and some cheap and, in effect, empty gestures from Ottawa notwithstanding – has been, at the very best, yet another camp follower of the Western genocide coalition.
And yet, strange as it may be, recent events have produced something that Iran and Canada have in common. Or to be precise, it’s Washington’s bizarre policies that have created this odd overlap: both Canada the long-standing vassal and Iran the steadfast antagonist are currently at the receiving end of both fresh attempts at coercion by economic warfare and escalating rhetoric from Washington.
Of course, there are orders-of-magnitude differences between the Trump administration’s ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ against Tehran and the latest round of tariff and trash-talk launched against Canada.
The ‘Operation’ targeting Iran, according to its mastermind and cheerleader Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, aims to combine a naval blockade, intelligence gathering, “mapp[ing] every node, every facilitator and every network that Iran” is using to trade abroad, and wide-ranging secondary sanctions to, in Bessent words, “asphyxiat[e]” Tehran. The declared end goal is to “collapse” Iran by inflicting an “Economic D-Day,” as President Donald Trump has put it.
There’s no such intention to wage total economic war in the case of Canada. Regarding Ottawa, Washington has merely initiated a pressure campaign within its empire. Its goal is not absolute destruction but the punishment and coercion of a wayward vassal.
In essence, the Canadian government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has rejected Washington’s offer of a crudely disadvantageous and interfering trade deal, featuring, according to the Financial Times, “ludicrous” American demands.
Faced with “clodhopping bullying” so extreme no leader could have submitted – except maybe, say, the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen or Germany’s Friedrich Merz – Carney had an excellent opportunity to make a stand. He declared that Canada is under US attack and, in effect, at war – all restricted to the economy, of course – and that his government will retaliate tit-for-tat, dollar-for-dollar.
Washington is striking at Ottawa with 50% tariffs on Canadian goods worth $20 billion, and, in return, Ottawa will give as good as it gets. That’s the plan at least. But while the Wall Street Journal reports that both sides are getting ready for a long fight, there also is still some time for last-minute off-ramps.
Things need to be kept in proportion: the new US tariffs would affect about 5% of Canadian exports to its overbearing southern neighbor. The Canadian retaliation would target about 6% of what the US sends north. Meanwhile, US rhetoric is surging. Trump has renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America and posted an extraordinarily odd AI-generated video about it, featuring (Canadian?) wild geese marching in lockstep under US flags and firing assault rifles. In Canada, for now at least, Carney’s hardline response is popular.
In short, what is really happening between Ottawa and Washington may well seem like a farce if compared to the state of things between Washington and Tehran. Unsurprisingly, the Iranian leadership has declared that it won’t budge. And why should it? It has already won two rounds of war against Washington. While its economy is certainly suffering, the American-Israeli aggression has, in effect, fully immunized Iranian society against any regime-change schemes.
Finally, Washington will not succeed in making key players submit to its secondary-sanctions blackmail. China, now the world’s great oil power, as The Economist concedes, and a crucial partner for Iran not merely in economic terms, has already made that much clear. Russia is very unlikely to be impressed either.
But take a step back and look at the picture as a whole. Here we are: the US is waging economic war – of different intensity – against both opponents and so-called allies. More importantly, it is meeting resistance in both cases. And most importantly, in both cases, there is no reason to assume that Washington will win. All of that is happening against a background of the US escalating its use of brute force: There is the fresh “deal” – really, steal – to siphon off 65 billion barrels of crude from the de facto US protectorate of post-Maduro Venezuela. Regarding the much-disturbed bond markets, meanwhile, Trump has openly threatened to use the US military to shape them to Washington’s advantage.
The idea is about as smart as trying to fix a microchip with a sledgehammer. But, with the US, that doesn’t mean it won’t be tried. For the red thread running through all of the above is a combination of slipping real power, escalating aggressiveness, and rising resistance from others. What makes this so dangerous is that Washington seems to have entirely lost the ability to realistically adjust its aims and demands to its declining capabilities. Think of it as a bully past his prime who is not only very violent but also not smart enough to see when being more flexible would be in his own best interest.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Von der Leyen and NATO secretary general will meet on 2 September to discuss rising hybrid threats from Russia
articles.body:
Von der Leyen and NATO secretary general will meet on 2 September to discuss rising hybrid threats from Russia
European Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said that the meeting between European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on 2 September will focus primarily on the growing hybrid threats posed by Russia to Europe and strengthening EU-NATO defence cooperation.
Source: European Pravda
Quote from Pinho: "Indeed, and it's frequently the case that meetings are added to the calendar of President von der Leyen also at short notice. Now, this meeting tomorrow between the president and Secretary General Rutte is to be seen in the context as we strengthen our defense cooperation within Europe and with NATO."
Details: The spokeswoman stressed that this is particularly important in light of the "increasing hybrid threats that we are seeing".
"So it's in this context that it's taking place. I cannot prejudge what will be discussed specifically," she added.
Asked whether Ukraine and its need for interceptor missiles would be discussed at the meeting, Paula Pinho noted that she does not "think that there can be such a discussion without referring to Ukraine, without referring to what is going on in Europe, which obviously has major consequences also for us in the EU".
Background:
- EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas announced the creation of a high-level group made up of former political and military leaders from European countries and Ukraine, who will work on issues related to the bloc's defence capabilities.
- On 28 July, the US Department of Defense officially began a six-month review of its military presence in Europe, which could pave the way for a reduction in US troops on the continent.
- The Pentagon's review of the deployment of US troops in Europe, which is expected to be completed by 6 November, will create at least four possible courses of action for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

articles.title: New US ‘precision’ missiles responsible for multiple civilian deaths in Iran – report
articles.body:
New US ‘precision’ missiles responsible for multiple civilian deaths in Iran – report
The US killed multiple civilians in southern Iran using new “precision” missiles with a wide damage radius, conflict monitoring group Airwars has found. Tehran has repeatedly accused Washington of war crimes since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran which has killed up to 3,000 civilians.
In an investigation published on Monday, the London-based watchdog examined three February 28 strikes in the city of Lamerd that killed at least 21 civilians, including seven children. It concluded that the weapons used were likely Lockheed Martin’s Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), which made their combat debut during the opening phase of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The PrSM is designed to explode above the ground, spraying tens of thousands of dense tungsten pellets in all directions rather than relying primarily on the blast itself.
Airwars found that civilians were killed at least 50 meters from the estimated detonation points, while damage extended as far as 150 meters. The three missiles exploded over two residential neighborhoods and a sports center.
Among those killed was a two-year-old girl struck while playing outside her home around 50 meters from one blast. Another strike over a sports hall killed seven civilians, most of them children.
No military personnel were reported killed, and Airwars found no evidence that military infrastructure had been hit. A nearby Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps compound appeared undamaged.
The Associated Press separately reviewed the evidence and consulted six weapons experts, including two former military officials, who also assessed that PrSMs were responsible for the strikes.
“You would be hard-pressed to find a reason to use the PrSM in a densely populated area,” former US Army adviser Michael Meier told AP.
US Central Command has acknowledged deploying PrSMs against Iran, describing their use as a “historic first,” but has denied firing any weapons at Lamerd. It has instead suggested that an Iranian cruise missile was to blame, although weapons experts cited by AP and Airwars disputed that assessment.
The PrSM had only recently completed its prototype phase and had not completed operational testing before its combat debut in Iran. A US Army official later said a deployed unit exhausted its entire stock of the missiles early in the war. Washington has since committed billions of dollars to expanding production.
Tehran has repeatedly accused Washington of war crimes over strikes on civilian areas. The Lamerd attack came on the same day as the US bombing of an elementary school in Minab, which killed 175 people, most of them children.
The Airwars findings come as direct US-Iran hostilities resumed over the weekend after a month-long lull. Washington struck Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday, prompting Tehran to launch missiles and drones at US military facilities in Jordan.
US President Donald Trump has since threatened another round of attacks, saying Washington would “hit Iran hard.”

articles.title: Japan Modifies ASM-3 Anti-Ship Missile to Destroy Air Targets
articles.body:
Japan is likely to modify the ASM-3 supersonic anti-ship missile into an ultra-long-range air-to-air missile for intercepting aerial targets.
The Japanese Ministry of Defense announced its plans to procure air-to-air missiles for 2027 in a budget document.
Converting the anti-ship missile into an air-to-air interceptor is intended to create a means of countering long-range enemy aircraft — such as long-range radar detection aircraft, aerial refueling tankers, and strategic bombers.
Thanks to its ramjet engine, the upgraded air-to-air version of the missile will be capable of reaching an estimated range of 400-600 km.
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries began developing the basic ASM-3 anti-ship missile in 2003 to replace the obsolete ASM-1 and ASM-2.
The development program lasted more than a decade, and in 2017, test launches from the decommissioned destroyer Shirane confirmed the new weapon’s performance characteristics.
However, the initial version of the missile, with a range of 200 km, never entered serial production because the Japanese Ministry of Defense deemed this range insufficient to penetrate modern naval air defense systems and demanded upgrades.
As a result, an improved version, the ASM-3A, was developed; by reducing weight and optimizing fuel consumption, its range was increased to 400 km or more.
In its basic anti-ship version, the ASM-3 is 6 meters long, has a body diameter of 350 mm, and a total launch weight of approximately 940 kg.
The missile is equipped with a penetrating high-explosive warhead weighing about 150 kg, designed to engage medium- and large-displacement surface ships.
The primary platform for the ASM-3 family of missiles is the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s F-2 fighter jets.
It should be noted that, starting in 2027, the Japanese Ministry of Defense will begin the procurement process for AARGM-ER anti-radar missiles to counter Chinese air defense systems.

articles.title: Germany blames Moscow for Leipzig drone attack, closes consulate and cultural center among sweeping diplomatic measures
articles.body:
An explosives-laden drone aimed at a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport was part of a Russian state operation, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on 1 September.
Germany has moved from suspecting foreign sabotage to formally blaming Russia for the Leipzig attack. The finding has prompted diplomatic and security measures against Moscow while the criminal investigation continues.
Police investigations, the attack pattern, and intelligence findings established Russian responsibility, Dobrindt said. The drones' configuration, components, explosives, and detonation systems resembled those used in other Russian hybrid operations—covert sabotage and disruption below the threshold of open war—and in Russia's war against Ukraine, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said.
The first drone, carrying explosives, was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft on the evening of 4 August and defused. Investigators believe a DHL freighter may have collided with a second drone while aborting its landing after the airport closed; that drone was never recovered. A third drone was found on 14 August in a field at Kabelsketal, where investigators subsequently discovered roughly 50 grams of suspected military explosive.
Leipzig/Halle is an international freight hub used by Ukrainian Antonov aircraft and NATO's strategic airlift program, through which allies charter heavy transport aircraft to move oversized military cargo.
Berlin will close the Bonn consulate on 18 September, end the operating agreement for the Russian House, a Moscow-backed cultural center, tighten entry controls for Russian nationals, seek to add more targets to EU sanctions lists, and pressure Russia's shadow fleet—opaquely owned tankers used to move Russian oil outside Western restrictions. Wadephul also summoned the Russian ambassador. Russia's Berlin embassy will remain open.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Interfax that Moscow would respond to Germany's “anti-Russian action,” without specifying how.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance stood in full solidarity with Germany, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described Berlin's measures as a strong response.
Dobrindt said Germany expects further Russian hybrid attacks. The Leipzig incident follows a widening campaign of suspected Russian sabotage across Europe, including a 2024 incendiary-device attack at the same airport that Western security officials suspected Russian intelligence organized.
How the Leipzig attack unfolded
Euromaidan Press reported on 12 August, citing Die Zeit, that footage showed an explosives-laden quadcopter striking the wing of a parked Ukrainian Antonov An-124 before falling without detonating. The article also noted that a US Defense Department official told CNN that Washington assessed the drone belonged to Russian intelligence.
On 25 August, EP reported, citing Tagesschau’s NDR/WDR/SZ investigation, that investigators had expanded the case to three drones and found the third with suspected military explosive nearby in Kabelsketal, 10 days after the original attempt.

articles.title: Germany blames Russia for Leipzig plane sabotage attempt, expels diplomats, and restricts visas
articles.body:
Germany blames Russia for Leipzig plane sabotage attempt, expels diplomats, and restricts visas
The German government has officially blamed Russia for an attempted act of sabotage against a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane at the Leipzig airport. Berlin’s position was presented at a news conference by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.
Dobrindt said the findings of the police investigation, the “characteristic features” of the incident, and intelligence reporting “clearly point to Russia’s involvement in hybrid operations that were planned, that were carried out, and that were also thwarted.”
Wadephul laid out the retaliatory measures: Germany will close Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. Russia’s ambassador will be summoned to the German Foreign Ministry. German authorities will also tighten controls on the entry of Russian citizens into the country. Exactly how has not yet been specified.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, for her part, said that the EU “stands in full solidarity with Germany in the face of this attack by Russia.” She said she would take the matter up with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, and she said the foreign ministers of EU countries would begin preparing additional sanctions.
Rutte himself said that “the evidence is clear.” “I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response,” he said. Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Latvia’s Foreign Ministry, and officials from other EU countries also expressed solidarity with Berlin’s actions and a readiness to continue supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova criticized the German government’s moves. “They made up a pretext. And Berlin itself is thoroughly tainted both by inflaming the Ukrainian conflict and by taking part in terrorist attacks against civilians,” she said. Zakharova also said the Russian House had “long been a thorn in the side” of the German authorities, and she said Russia would “respond” to the decision to close it.
Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Germany was “moving further down the path of escalation.” “It’s hard to comment on this, because if accusations this serious are being made, they have to be backed up by something. If I’m not mistaken, no supporting argument was presented,” Peskov told reporters.
A drone with explosives attached to it was found at the Leipzig airport overnight on August 5. The drone was next to a Ukrainian An-124 transport plane that was carrying ammunition. It later emerged that there were several drones — another was found 10 days later, west of the airport, and a third, according to media reports, may have struck the cargo plane, though no trace of that drone was ever found.

articles.title: “Russian airspace will effectively be closing”: Zelenskyy warns airlines Russian skies are no longer safe
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines, insurers, and other aviation stakeholders on 1 September that Russian airspace is becoming increasingly dangerous as Ukrainian drones operate deeper inside the country.
The warning comes as Ukraine has increasingly carried out long-range drone strikes deep inside Russia, targeting military, energy, industrial, and other infrastructure. Russian authorities have repeatedly reported temporary airport closures and flight disruptions during drone attacks as part of air defense measures.
“We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelenskyy said.
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine does not intend to threaten civilian aviation or civilian aircraft, but warned that the growing presence of drones over Russia means airlines must account for the risks.
“We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” he said.
Zelenskyy accused Russian authorities of failing to properly inform airlines about the risks, saying they have not adequately communicated the growing danger posed by drones in Russian airspace.
“Although the Russian authorities are not properly informing people about this, Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” Zelenskyy said, arguing that Russia’s war against Ukraine is making its own airspace unsafe.
Zelenskyy warned that the growing scale of Ukrainian drone operations over Russia will have to be factored into aviation risks. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said.
He called on foreign ambassadors in Ukraine and Russia to relay the warning to their governments, and said Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry and other institutions would provide international organizations with information about the risks to Russian airspace.
“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine closed its skies in 2022. Russia has kept flying
The warning highlights a stark difference between the two countries. Ukraine has kept its airspace closed to civilian aviation since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The risk is familiar to Ukraine. Russian forces have repeatedly attacked Ukrainian airports and aviation infrastructure during the full-scale invasion, making the continued operation of civilian aviation impossible.
Russia is also responsible for the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over occupied eastern Ukraine, which killed all 298 people aboard, showing the danger Russia’s military activities can pose to civilian aviation.
Russia, meanwhile, has continued operating major airports and regular passenger flights despite Ukrainian drones increasingly reaching deep into its territory. EASA has warned that Russian air defenses responding to Ukrainian drone and missile attacks could pose risks to civilian aircraft, including through misidentification, particularly around major airports.
Russian airports increasingly disrupted by Ukrainian drones
Russian authorities have repeatedly restricted or suspended flights at Moscow and other airports during Ukrainian drone attacks. The disruptions have generally come as Russia activates air defenses against drones targeting military, energy, industrial, and logistics infrastructure.
Russia has also moved toward broader restrictions on civilian aviation. In June, Russia imposed new restrictions on light aircraft around Moscow and neighboring regions, while regular passenger and charter flights remained exempt.
The result is a growing disruption to Russian aviation even as Moscow continues to keep its main passenger airspace open: Ukrainian drones are not being used to target civilian aircraft, but their increasing presence is making normal aviation operations more difficult and forcing Russia to restrict or suspend flights during attacks.

articles.title: Meet Sean Parnell, Pentagon's Chief Spokesperson and a Contender to Succeed Army Secretary Driscoll
articles.body:
Prior to Army Secretary Dan Driscoll submitting his resignation Monday, Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had been suggested by some close to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as a potential replacement for the Senate-confirmed position.
The Hill reported last week that Parnell’s name was being floated, citing two unnamed sources familiar with the matter.
Asked about the reports, a senior Administration official told TIME: “Sean Parnell is 100% focused on the job he was appointed to by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth.”
News of Driscoll’s departure from the role he held for around 18 months came after months of reported tensions with Hegseth and turmoil within the department.
A person familiar with Driscoll’s resignation is quoted as telling media that for Army Secretary had recently “brought up concerns with the Administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible.”
White House spokesperson Anna Kelly did not address the tensions and fallout when approached by TIME, but instead emphasized that the United States Army is “more powerful than ever thanks to [Driscoll’s] work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War.”
Driscoll’s resignation is the latest in a series of high-profile departures within the Pentagon, following the April ouster of the Army’s top uniformed leader, Gen. Randy George, and the June departure of the lead commander in Europe and Africa, Gen. Christopher Donahue.
The firing of George was reportedly a source of contention between Driscoll and Hegseth.
Driscoll openly praised George, referring to him as “an amazing, transformational leader” whom he loved and respected during an April House Appropriations Committee Hearing. Driscoll told lawmakers that after George was fired, his family drove to the former general's house and gave him a hug.
Alongside the reported tensions, Hegseth has also come under serious scrutiny for the duration and mounting cost of the Iran war, which surpassed the six-month mark last week.
“I don’t have any confidence in him anymore. I think he’s all over the place—he’s accelerating the retirement or forcing out some of the most distinguished leaders in the DOD that we have,” Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina said in July.
Meanwhile, under Parnell, the Department of Defense has imposed various restrictions limiting journalists’ access in the Pentagon.
In an unprecedented move in June, the department designated its press office a classified area.
“The Pentagon Press Office has been redesignated as a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility due to speechwriters from the Office of the Secretary of War sharing the facility,” said deputy Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez. “As a result, journalists will no longer be permitted to enter the office space. There’s nothing controversial about that.”
Now, with talk turning to who may replace Driscoll in the pivotal role of Army Secretary, Parnell's name continues to be floated. Notably, whoever is selected would need to be confirmed for the position by the Senate.
Here’s what to know about Parnell's military record, his past controversies, and more.
Parnell is an Afghanistan veteran who penned a memoir on his experience
Parnell arrived in Afghanistan in 2006 and during his 16-month deployment was awarded two Bronze stars and the Purple Heart. He was deployed alongside his platoon, nicknamed the Outlaws.
He returned home with shrapnel in his leg and a brain injury that had left him with vision problems.
Following retirement on medical grounds, he penned a 2012 war story memoir titled Outlaw Platoon, in partnership with author John R. Bruning, detailing his experiences in the region.
Parnell went on to become a senior advisor for the Concerned Veterans of America and is credited with playing a key role in the passage of the Mission Act in 2018 under President Donald Trump, with the goal of delivering care and support for U.S. veterans.
Parnell previously criticized Trump before becoming a staunch supporter
Parnell backed now-Secretary of State Marco Rubio for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination where he faced off against Trump, who went on to win both the nomination and presidency.
According to Parnell, his support for Rubio, who at the time was a Senator in Florida, was cemented by his vocal backing of matters related to Veterans Affairs (VA).
“There are lots of strong options. But if fixing the VA, rebuilding our military, and doing right by our veterans is a top priority for you, then Senator Rubio should be your first and only choice,” Parnell said in a campaign press release.
In a separate interview, he described Rubio as a "unifying voice” who the country “desperately needs” and labeled him “my guy.”
By contrast, Parnell had called out Trump in 2015, referring to his criticism of the late Republican Sen. John McCain, a prisoner of war, as “the height of arrogance,” arguing that Trump had “no clue what our Vietnam POWs endured.”
However, Parnell had a change of heart once Trump took office, stating in a 2019 interview that the President had earned his respect “because he forces us to talk about issues. Political correctness doesn’t allow us to talk about them.”
At the 2020 Republican National Convention, Parnell further praised Trump, insisting he had “unleashed the economic might of this nation like no other President in our history.”
Parnell suspended his campaign for Senate amid abuse allegations
Parnell, after running unsuccessfully for the House in 2020, went on to launch a bid as the GOP Senate candidate in Pennsylvania. He suspended his Trump-backed campaign in November 2021, after losing a fight for custody of his children to his then-estranged wife, who had accused him in court of abuse.
Laurie Snell had alleged that Parnell choked her and injured their children. Parnell vehemently denied the claims.
Snell also testified in court that Parnell had been unfaithful.
Following Trump’s announcement in February 2025 that Parnell was tapped to become chief spokesperson for the Pentagon, some media coverage saw the abuse allegations revisited.
If Parnell were put forward for a Senate-confirmed position in the future, the historical allegations could be brought up in his confirmation hearing.

articles.title: Petraeus urges UK to lead NATO military overhaul
articles.body:
Britain should become the first major Western country to reorganise its defence institutions around lessons emerging from the war in Ukraine and use that experience to help drive a wider transformation of NATO, General David Petraeus has told the House of Lords.
Delivering the Lord Speaker’s Lecture on 1 September, the retired four-star US Army general argued that the nature of warfare is changing quickly enough to require more than conventional modernisation programmes. Petraeus said Britain’s early recognition of the threat posed by Russia and its sustained support for Ukraine had demonstrated what he described as strategic clarity, giving the UK an opportunity to take a leading role in reshaping how Western militaries organise, train and equip themselves.
Petraeus said: “Britain now has an opportunity to demonstrate that same quality once again. Just as it helped lead the Alliance in recognizing the strategic implications of Russia’s aggression, it can now help lead the Alliance in recognizing the revolutionary implications that Ukraine holds for the future of warfare itself.”
He described Ukraine as “the defining military laboratory of the twenty-first century”, arguing that its importance lies not simply in individual technologies but in the way sensors, software, unmanned systems, electronic warfare, precision weapons and industrial adaptation are being combined. Petraeus said information is being collected, analysed and acted upon at unprecedented speed, while commercial innovation is moving directly onto the battlefield and software, hardware and operational methods are being adapted while fighting is underway.
He told peers: “Much of the discussion has understandably focused on individual technologies—unmanned systems, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare, cyber capabilities, precision strike, battle management systems, and others. Each matters. But the principal lesson is larger: the very concept of warfare is changing.”
Petraeus said Britain’s Strategic Defence Review and Defence Investment Plan showed an appreciation of the changes taking place, pointing to their focus on unmanned and autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare, industrial resilience, procurement reform and accelerated innovation. He cautioned, however, that those measures should be regarded as the beginning of a larger transformation rather than its completion.
He said: “The most consequential military transformations seldom begin with new equipment. They begin with new ideas. Additional resources will clearly be required in important areas, but the greatest obstacle to transformation is rarely money alone. More often, it is the difficulty of questioning long-established assumptions and overcoming institutional inertia.”
Petraeus continued: “And I believe the United Kingdom is unusually well positioned to do precisely that. Not because Britain is free of serious economic, fiscal, or political constraints—it plainly is not—but because, as we have seen in Ukraine, Britain has demonstrated the capacity to recognize strategic reality early and act decisively.”
He added: “That now presents Britain with another opportunity: to become the first major Western nation to organize its defence institutions around the new concept of warfare that Ukraine has been pioneering—and, in doing so, to help lead the transformation of NATO itself.”
Petraeus said NATO itself would also have to change, including the operational headquarters responsible for commanding Alliance forces. He argued that NATO needs a common understanding of the emerging concept of warfare before individual nations can reorganise their forces effectively around it.
He said: “NATO must now summon that spirit again, with far greater urgency, by developing a common understanding of the new concept of warfare and the institutional transformation that must follow.” Referring to NATO’s operational headquarters, he added: “Those headquarters will have to think, organize, and operate differently if they are to lead this transformation successfully.”
Petraeus said the process could not be limited to another incremental modernisation programme, calling instead for changes to force structure, professional military education, training, procurement, personnel policy, industrial engagement and the way battlefield lessons are identified and incorporated.
He said: “The question is not whether this transformation will occur. It is already underway—most visibly in Ukraine, but also in Russia, the Middle East, and elsewhere. The question is whether we will lead it—or be forced to catch up to those who do.”

articles.title: NATO and EU press Spain and Greece to transfer interceptors for Patriot systems to Ukraine, Bloomberg says
articles.body:
NATO and EU press Spain and Greece to transfer interceptors for Patriot systems to Ukraine, Bloomberg says
NATO and the European Union are pressuring Spain and Greece, which hold some of the largest stocks of missiles for Patriot air defence systems, to sell interceptors to Norway so that Norway can transfer them to Ukraine.
Source: Bloomberg, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The requests to Spain and Greece were made this summer and include the possibility of Norway purchasing the missiles and then transferring them to Ukraine, according to Bloomberg sources.
The issue is also expected to be discussed at today's meeting of EU defence and foreign ministers in Ireland, which will also be attended by representatives of Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway, Iceland and Switzerland.
Among Ukraine's partners, Spain and Greece hold some of the largest stocks of missiles for Patriots, some of which are also approaching the end of their shelf life.
Greece was one of the first countries to send ammunition to Ukraine after Russia's full-scale invasion. However, it has refused to provide Patriot missiles, citing the need to retain them for its own defence amid its long-standing rivalry with Türkiye.
Earlier this year, Spain said it would provide Ukraine with €1 billion in military aid in 2026.
Some air defence systems are still expected to reach Ukraine in the coming months under the PURL programme, which allows NATO allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv.
However, the EU is considering whether to allow Ukraine to purchase more Patriot missiles using a €90 billion loan for Kyiv. Countries such as France and Italy want the funds to be directed towards the SAMP/T system, while others fear this could create unnecessary difficulties for Kyiv.
EU member states will vote on the issue on 7 September.
Background:
- On 1 September, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said EU member states should provide Ukraine with the interceptor missiles it needs, including those whose shelf life is about to expire.
- UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said European leaders are considering holding another meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in the United States, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in September, to discuss supplying Ukraine with Patriot interceptor missiles.
- Earlier, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said the Netherlands, which operates Patriot air defence systems and their interceptor missiles, had given Ukraine everything it could from its stocks.

articles.title: G20 backs final statement despite Russia tensions, China dissent
articles.body:
G20 backs final statement despite Russia tensions, China dissent
G20 finance leaders wrapped up two days of talks in Ashville, North Carolina, on Tuesday with broad backing for a final statement, despite tensions over Russia’s participation and divisions with China. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Moscow’s presence had not disrupted discussions, as ministers also grappled with the war in the Middle East, tariffs, global trade imbalances and continued support for Ukraine.
G20 finance leaders closed their two-day gathering on Tuesday with a statement that all but China backed in full, as Washington insisted that the presence of a Russian minister had no effect on talks.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the fact that nearly all participants agreed to the chair's final statement suggested "there has been no impact" from Russia's attendance.
Ukraine's European allies had expressed frustration after Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov was welcomed at the US-hosted meetings in Asheville, North Carolina.
The broiling Middle East war and President Donald Trump's tariffs also loomed over the gathering.
Read moreWhat to know about Trump's Canada tariffs and the escalating trade war
The chair's statement called for "free, safe, and predictable navigation through the Strait of Hormuz," though China dissented from that section.
The key waterway has been largely blocked by Tehran since the war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
A traditional "family photo" of G20 participants was taken Monday without Siluanov, following European officials' protests.
An EU spokesperson said representatives were only given short notice of Siluanov's attendance.
"It created discomfort, no doubt about that," Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne told AFP on Tuesday when asked if Siluanov's appearance had a bearing on discussions.
EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis told reporters that it was not the time to "normalize" Russia's presence at such events.
He said Moscow's inclusion entails discussing sensitive economic matters with representatives of a government that is "waging an aggressive war" and "killing civilians on a daily basis" in its conflict in Ukraine.
But Bessent countered at a press conference: "I know that some Europeans had a sour taste, but I think it's very important to engage."
"And I will point out that the finance minister who I met with is unsanctioned," he added of Siluanov.
The tension also comes as Germany blamed Russia on Tuesday for an attempted "hybrid attack" involving a drone at a strategic German airport last month, and unveiled diplomatic counter-measures.
Read moreUS Treasury bars certain journalists from G20 meeting in North Carolina
The United States holds the rotating G20 presidency, and Washington was also pushing this week to rally support from partners on Iran sanctions and reducing trade imbalances.
Asked if he also pressured Russia to cut its support for Iran, Bessent earlier told reporters that "many conversations are best done privately."
'Persistent imbalances'
Another topic China took issue with was a declaration that "excessive and persistent imbalances pose risks and can generate economic distortions."
This echoes criticism of excess industrial capacity in the world's second biggest economy, which critics say create unfair competition and drive prices lower.
"We need to discuss and look at collective action, because global imbalances as they are today are not sustainable," Champagne said. "Everyone has to be at that table."
The G20 comprises 19 nations plus the EU and the African Union, and was established in the wake of the 1997-1998 Asian financial crisis to boost global economic and financial stability.
The G20 finance talks also set the stage for a leaders' summit that Trump will convene in December in Miami.
Another issue that came up was support for Ukraine, which was discussed as well on the sidelines of the meeting by the narrower Group of Seven advanced economies.
Moscow has intensified its strikes on Kyiv this summer. US-brokered talks remain frozen while the Kremlin has maintained its maximalist demands to end the war.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said Tuesday that there has been an "increase in brutal rocket attacks on the civilian population."
"This all has to come to an end," he added.
Klingbeil said that he and other European ministers "made our position on Ukraine absolutely clear." As G7 leaders met late Monday, he said Ukraine's finance minister joined remotely for talks on support for Kyiv.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Northrop gets $86M for security systems at nuclear missile bases
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force awarded Northrop Grumman an $86.1 million sole-source task order to maintain its Remote Visual Assessment missile silo monitoring system.
- Work covers four bases, Hill, F.E. Warren, Malmstrom and Minot, and is expected to run through September 2031.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Northrop Grumman an $86.1 million task order to maintain the security cameras and sensors that watch over America’s nuclear missile silos.
The task order covers program management, maintenance, sustaining engineering and support services for the Remote Visual Assessment program, a ground-based camera and sensor network that monitors Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missile silos. The award falls under a broader ground subsystem support contract Northrop Grumman has held since 2021. The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center at Hill Air Force Base, Utah, is the contracting activity.
Work under this task order will take place at Hill Air Force Base, along with F.E. Warren Air Force Base in Wyoming, Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, and Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota, the three installations that oversee the Air Force’s dispersed fields of Minuteman III silos across the northern United States. The contract is expected to run through September 2031.
The Remote Visual Assessment system lets Air Force personnel confirm what’s happening at a missile silo without physically traveling to the site, an important capability given how far apart individual silos sit across the missile fields. When a security sensor detects unusual activity at a silo, cameras tied into the RVA system let a missile alert facility crew visually verify the alert before dispatching a security response team, cutting down on unnecessary trips to remote locations.
The award was made as a sole-source acquisition, meaning the Air Force did not open the work to competitive bidding. Of the task order’s total value, $15.2 million in fiscal 2026 procurement funds was obligated at the time of award, with the remainder expected to be funded as the work progresses.

articles.title: Germany blames Russia for drone incursion, announces retaliatory measures
articles.body:
Alexander Dobrindt arrives for the first day of a two-day retreat of the federal government coalition cabinet at Schloss Neuhardenberg on Aug. 25, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
BERLIN — Berlin squarely placed the blame for an incursion of explosive-laden drones last month on the Kremlin and announced a raft of retaliatory diplomatic measures.
The incident and Germany’s response mark a new chapter in Europe’s fraught relationship with Russia, with EU leaders lining up to support Berlin.
“Russia’s leadership is treating our country with open hostility,” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said in Berlin on Tuesday. “With the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership has, in fact, deliberately chosen to further and significantly damage our already severely strained bilateral relationship.”
Standing alongside Wadephul, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the German government determined Russia is responsible even as investigations remain ongoing.
“The attack involved tools such as the drone configuration, various components, explosives and cyber technology that we recognize from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine,” Dobrindt said.
Wadephul announced a series of domestic countermeasures, including the closure of Russia’s Bonn consulate on September 18, stricter entry controls for Russian nationals and the termination of the agreement governing the Russian House in central Berlin — a cultural institution suspected of serving as a hub for espionage operations and whose Russian operator is under EU sanctions.
Germany will also propose new EU sanctions targeting Russian individuals connected to hybrid attacks, while pushing to increase measures targeting Russia’s shadow fleet, Wadephul said. A senior German government official also said Berlin would advocate that the EU reduce the number of 90-day tourist visas issued to Russian citizens and restrict the freedom of movement of Russian diplomats.
The announcement comes as EU foreign ministers are set to meet in Ireland on Tuesday night and Wednesday. “The matter, including additional sanctions, will be prepared by Foreign Ministers at their upcoming meeting,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media after the German announcement.
Advertisement
Given the significance of the announcement, it was not immediately clear why German Chancellor Friedrich Merz didn’t make it himself. But the ratcheting up of tensions with Moscow comes at a sensitive political moment ahead of a state election on Sunday in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) is far ahead in polls.
Dobrindt said the attack was carried out by low-level agents, adding that the technology found at the scene indicated “a high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort in the planning and execution of the attack.”
He also suggested German officials expect more such attacks to follow.
“We assume that Germany is the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia. It can also be assumed that there is a willingness to cause even greater damage through hybrid attacks,” he said. “Thankfully, in Leipzig, this did not happen as had apparently been planned.”
European leaders on Tuesday expressed support for Germany’s retaliatory measures.
Advertisement
“If the gravity of the events is confirmed”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told reporters earlier on Tuesday morning, “there will inevitably be consequences, particularly regarding the sanctions that might be imposed on Russia.”
“NATO stands in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig,” the alliance’s secretary-general Mark Rutte said on X. “I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response,” he added.
This article has been updated. Hans von der Burchard contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘No negotiations with terrorists’ – Putin on Zelensky’s threat to civil aviation (VIDEO)
articles.body:
‘No negotiations with terrorists’ – Putin on Zelensky’s threat to civil aviation (VIDEO)
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said there can be no “negotiations with terrorists,” responding to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s threat against civilian aviation over Russia.
Zelensky warned foreign airlines, insurers and governments on Tuesday that Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign would increasingly endanger civilian flights over the country.
“The safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelensky said.
Putin was asked to respond to the remarks at a press conference on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan on Tuesday.
“If this was said out loud, then it is simply a move toward state terrorism,” Putin said. 
“I would also draw attention to the fact that they are asking us to resume negotiations; they are asking for face-to-face meetings,” he added.
There are no negotiations with terrorists.
Putin added that Moscow would find a way to respond if Kiev’s threats resulted in any tragedies.
“Let no one doubt that,” he said.
Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone strikes on Russia in recent months, repeatedly grounding flights and forcing prolonged disruptions at airports as air defenses respond to incoming threats.
Kiev’s campaign has also systematically targeted civilian infrastructure, including Russian e-commerce warehouses, prompting Moscow to retaliate with drone and missile strikes on Ukraine’s military-linked infrastructure and shipping facilities. The strikes have effectively crippled Ukraine’s main export route through its Black Sea ports.
In July, Putin warned that Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory would be met with a far stronger response.
“We will respond in kind – only several times more powerfully,” he said.

articles.title: Russian oligarch Yevtushenkov and relatives of high-profile officials profit from construction in occupied territories of Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian authorities have created extremely favorable conditions for developers in the occupied territories of Ukraine, offering tax breaks, nearly free land leases, and loans at 3% annual interest. By August 2026, more than 1.3 million square meters of mortgage-financed housing had been under construction in the Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine’s Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
Among those profiting from this construction are entities linked to oligarch Vladimir Yevtushenkov, the family of State Duma deputy Sergei Kolunov, major regional businessmen, and a company connected to the brother of a Presidential Executive Office staffer. These individuals and entities are featured in an investigation by the independent outlet Vot Tak, which examined developers’ project declarations and financial statements.
Yevtushenkov’s AFK Sistema holds the controlling stake in construction company Etalon Group, which in turn is closely tied to the Republican Construction Company (RSK). According to Vot Tak’s calculations, Russian state-controlled VTB bank has already allocated RSK more than 26.5 billion rubles ($305.5 million) for construction in occupied Mariupol, Luhansk, and Henichesk, meaning that entities linked to Yevtushenkov are among the largest recipients of mortgage construction loans in the regions seized by Russia. In addition, employees of Yevtushenko’s AFK Sistema can buy RSK apartments through a special program offering a discount and interest-free installment plan.
RSK and Etalon tend to downplay the ties between them. In June 2025, the Russian-appointed head of the so-called “Luhansk People’s Republic,” Leonid Pasechnik, announced the signing of an agreement with RSK, describing the company as part of the Etalon group. Eight minutes later, the mention of Etalon disappeared from the post, and Russian state media later removed the reference as well.
Vot Tak interprets this caution as part of an effort to shield Yevtushenko from Western sanctions. In May 2025, the businessman filed a lawsuit with the EU court seeking to have the restrictions on his business activities lifted — and publicly available information linking his entities to construction in Russian-occupied Ukraine would seriously hinder his chances for success.
Another major developer in Mariupol is the Sadovoye Koltso group, founded by Sergei Kolunov, a State Duma deputy from the ruling United Russia party. Before being elected to parliament, Kolunov transferred his stake in the firm to his wife, and then to his son, Ilya, who now heads the company.
Sadovoye Koltso entered Mariupol in October 2025 and is now building more than 80,000 square meters of housing there — more than any other company. VTB has offered the group a credit line of over 12 billion rubles ($138 million). Its projects include the Dom u Morya residential complex on the Sea of Azov coast and Sadovye Kvartaly near the site of the destroyed Azovstal plant.
Kolunov, meanwhile, serves as deputy chairman of the State Duma Committee on Construction, Housing, and Utilities. As Vot Tak notes, the member of parliament must have been apprised of numerous complaints from Mariupol residents who found themselves unable to obtain equivalent housing after their previous apartment buildings were rendered uninhabitable by the Russian military. Anti-corruption expert Ilya Shumanov called the situation a potential conflict of interest: Kolunov takes part in shaping policy for an industry in which his family’s business operates.
The largest recipient of loans specifically in Mariupol is SU-2007, a company owned by Viktor Budarin, a banker from Russia’s southern Kuban region. According to the investigation, his company received roughly 19 billion rubles ($219 million) for the construction of more than 170,000 square meters of housing.
YugStroyInvest, owned by Rostov developer Yuri Ivanov, ranks second with about 18.4 billion rubles ($212 million) in loans and nearly 150,000 square meters of housing under construction. In the summer of 2026, Ivanov signed an agreement to build housing and infrastructure in occupied Donetsk and Makiivka, with a stated investment volume of more than 100 billion rubles ($1.15 billion).
The top recipients of loans in Mariupol also include the Yevtushenkov-linked RSK and Voronezh-based Proekt Invest, owned by Nikolai Stupin. Other major players include Maxim Radchenko’s Antares, Tatyana Antipova’s Transyuzhstroy, Artem and Natalya Martynov’s Evolyutsiya, Andrei Slashchuk’s Vertikal Yug, and Mirastroy, linked to one of Moscow’s biggest developers, Pavel Te.
In total, according to Vot Tak’s calculations, Russian state banks have allocated at least 61.4 billion rubles ($707.8 million) for the construction of apartments in Mariupol. The outlet estimates developers’ potential combined profit from these projects at more than 18 billion rubles ($207.5 million).
Even more housing is currently being built in the occupied part of Luhansk Region — almost 600,000 square meters. The largest recipient of loans there is Vyacheslav Semenkov’s Zhilstroyinvest, which has been allocated around 18.9 billion rubles ($217.9 million) for building 205,000 square meters of housing in Luhansk. Ukrainian journalists have previously reported on Semenkov’s possible ties to Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) and to Leonid Pasechnik’s inner circle.
Next on the Luhansk list is RSK, with loans of about 17 billion rubles ($195.9 million), and another 15.7 billion rubles ($181 million) was allocated to the Moscow-based company Everest by PSB, the key bank for Russia’s Defense Ministry, in order to build a residential complex of about 136,000 square meters in Luhansk. Before the war, Everest had not built any major residential complexes independently, limiting its activities to capital repairs and installation work.
The company was founded by Begali Nurgushiev, former head of the investigative department of Kalmykia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs, who had previously received a suspended sentence for abuse of power. Everest is now headed by his son, Bulat Nurgushiev.
Bulat’s younger brother, Azamat Nurgushiev, works for the Presidential Executive Office. According to Vot Tak, in 2020 he was an assistant to the deputy head of the Foreign Policy Directorate, and he now holds the position of referent in the secretariat of the head of the Presidential Executive Office. His former boss, Denis Agafonov, heads the Expert Directorate, which prepares analytical materials for Vladimir Putin.
Construction in the occupied territories is not only profitable in itself but is also underpinned by state support, which includes a “free economic zone” regulatory regime that is set to remain in effect until 2050, exempting market participants from property tax and from the federal portion of profit tax for ten years. Developers can obtain project financing at around 3% annual interest and lease land almost for free, without tenders.
According to Vot Tak’s calculations, the profit margin of individual residential construction projects in Mariupol can exceed 30%, compared to the nationwide average of 7–15%, as estimated by experts surveyed by the outlet.
Reconstruction of the seized territories is being overseen by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin, who also chairs the supervisory board of the Territorial Development Fund responsible for granting companies free economic zone participant status.
Khusnullin is known for distributing these benefits to his long-time acquaintances, including Pavel Te, whose affiliated entities received more than 1 billion rubles ($11.5 million) for construction in central Mariupol. The Insider previously found that during Khusnullin’s tenure at the Moscow mayor’s office, he and Te made repeated trips to France together on a private jet. Yevtushenkov, who is neighbors with Khusnullin in the upscale suburban Moscow district of Serebryany Bor, received lucrative Moscow city government contracts for years.
The construction boom has coincided with a massive redistribution of property in Mariupol. Homes damaged or destroyed during Russia’s assault on the city have been torn down, and the land has been handed over for commercial residential complexes. Former owners are being offered compensation of up to 70,000 rubles per square meter, while the median price of new housing reaches 170,000 rubles per square meter.
In addition, Russian authorities declare apartments “unclaimed” if their owners have failed to register them with the national Rosreestr property registry. According to the BBC Russian Service, by August 2026 Russian officials in the occupied territories had confiscated or placed on lists for seizure more than 34,000 properties belonging to Ukrainian nationals, including 14,000 in Mariupol.

articles.title: Russia launches massive overnight attack on Ukraine – 12 killed
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight killed 12 people, including one foreign national, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
“A total of 12 people were killed, including an Indian citizen, while dozens of others were injured in the attack. My deepest condolences go to everyone who has lost loved ones,” Zelenskyy said on Telegram.
“A significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack. Unfortunately, residential and civilian infrastructure was damaged,” the president said.
Eight people were killed and seven others injured in Kyiv and the Kyiv region as a result of the massive Russian attack, the Prosecutor General’s Office said.
Read also: Quotas, raids and deportations: Latvia plans stricter rules for third-country nationals

articles.title: Gaza's roadmap to nowhere: Why Israel won't give up control
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Gaza's roadmap to nowhere: Why Israel won't give up control
Israel was caught by surprise when Hamas agreed at the end of July to decommission its weapons in Gaza in lockstep with the Israeli army’s withdrawal from the enclave.
Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has even referred to the acceptance of the Board of Peace’s roadmap by Palestinian factions as a “diplomatic 7 October”.
For months, Israel has made disarmament in Gaza its sole pretext for its continued genocide in the enclave and systematic violations of the October 2025 ceasefire.
“If only Hamas were to lay down its arms, all of this would be over” has been Israel’s standard talking point to justify killing over 1,200 Palestinians in the past 320 days of supposed calm, as well as restricting aid and movement, banning reconstruction, and advancing the “Yellow line” of ethnically cleansed areas.
Yet, as soon as Hamas and seven other Palestinian factions agreed to Tel Aviv’s demand, the Israeli government went into panic mode. Netanyahu rushed to formally reject the roadmap while his ministers called it “dangerous for Israel” and vowed to continue daily killings and ethnic cleansing.
The Israeli army, meanwhile, has escalated its bombing campaign in Gaza.
Even after the Board of Peace tried to provide ample assurances to Israel that it could continue to bomb Gaza, occupy 70% of Gaza’s territory, and only withdraw after Hamas’s total disarmament, Netanyahu has continued to reject the deal.
“Hamas accepted [the roadmap] to call Netanyahu’s bluff,” a senior Arab mediator told The New Arab. “They knew he would not comply.”
Israel's grip on Gaza
Despite the Board of Peace rewriting the terms of the roadmap to Israel’s satisfaction, Netanyahu’s reluctance to accept it stems from the fact that any progress in Gaza would threaten the far-right coalition that keeps him in power.
The Israeli Prime Minister promised his base ethnic cleansing in the Palestinian territory. Half of his coalition ministers and Knesset members recently marched for rebuilding Jewish-only settlements in Gaza, while Israel’s Defence Minister is campaigning on how he wiped out entire Palestinian cities.
Even if Hamas disarms without any Israeli withdrawal or suspension of airstrikes, the roadmap remains a nonstarter for Israel because it would constrain its ability to control Gaza.
For instance, under the roadmap, Israel would have to allow the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) to enter the enclave along with an International Stabilisation Force (ISF) to collect weapons.
The Israeli government views this as a nightmare scenario, because the presence of international forces on the ground would make it difficult for Israel to retain military operational freedom in Gaza.
That is why Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich warned that a multinational force in Gaza would be “dangerous for Israel” because it “will monitor us, separate us from Hamas and restrict [Israeli military] activity in the Strip”.
Likewise, the roadmap would oblige Israel to fulfil its obligations under Phase One of the Trump 20-point ceasefire plan before or alongside Hamas’s disarmament.
Those obligations include allowing a minimum of 600 trucks of humanitarian aid to cross into Gaza daily as well as 60,000 temporary housing units and 200,000 tents, while allowing the repair of basic infrastructure such as electricity, water, sewage, roads, hospitals, and bakeries.
But this would negate Israel’s policy to keep Gaza "destroyed for generations to come," as put by former Israeli General Giora Eiland.
Even minimal humanitarian measures that would make Gaza less uninhabitable are viewed by Israel as an existential threat. Its war, which has cost more than $140 billion, was explicitly aimed at transforming the enclave into an apocalyptic wasteland, leaving Palestinians with no option but to leave.
The status quo suits Israel
A former senior Israeli official, who had until 2024 worked closely with Netanyahu, told The New Arab that the Israeli premier prefers the current stalemate over making any “big changes.”
“We have all the leverage, we have the upper hand, what’s the incentive for us to engage?” he said.
The former official explained that Israel is comfortable with the current status quo in Gaza because it allows it to retain control of a depopulated 70% of the enclave, while avoiding the cost of feeding and sheltering its displaced population.
Similarly, the façade of the ceasefire means Hamas cannot attack Israeli troops behind the ‘Yellow Line’, so Israel doesn’t need to station a significant number of troops to defend the area.
Two senior officials from mediating Arab countries told The New Arab that the current status quo is ideal for Israel, with no changes in Gaza expected at least until after the October elections.
One official said that their expectation for the Trump plan has from the start been to “reduce the killing, get more food in, and prevent ethnic cleansing”.
The other official told The New Arab that the only way to move forward with the roadmap is to “drag Israel kicking and screaming”, but Trump’s Board of Peace has so far exerted no meaningful pressure on Netanyahu.
Israel's opposition isn't any better
The former Israeli official cautioned against any optimism over the likelihood of Israeli opposition parties winning in the upcoming elections.
“The opposition is attacking Netanyahu from the right, not the left. They are saying he’s about to squander the achievements in Gaza and bow down to Trump,” he told The New Arab. “They are promising to be tougher.”
The veteran Israeli politician Haim Ramon even warned that “people who choose [Naftali] Bennett are actually choosing another Netanyahu - only more extreme”.
He added that Israeli opposition leaders such as Bennett or Avigdor Lieberman “may be trying to present themselves as centre or ‘moderate’ right-wing, but in reality, they are political hawks, advocates of the complete Land of Israel, whose extremist views are identical to those of Ben-Gvir and Smotrich”.
Bennett, for reference, once infamously bragged: “I already killed lots of Arabs in my life, and there is absolutely no problem with that.”
A senior Arab official from a mediating country told The New Arab that if the opposition wins, it could complicate the situation in Gaza even further.
“If [Gadi] Eisenkot becomes prime minister, the international pressure on Israel would disappear, and we’d get told we need to give him time and space to consolidate his regime to prevent Netanyahu from returning to power.”
Muhammad Shehada is a Palestinian writer and analyst from Gaza and the EU Affairs Manager at Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor
Follow him on Twitter: @muhammadshehad2
Edited by Charlie Hoyle
