articles.title: At least 12 people killed in Russian overnight attacks on Ukraine – Europe live
articles.body:
Germany directly blames Russia for attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
Dobrindt says specifically that “the means used to carry out the act” of sabotage in Leipzig - and he lists the drone’s configuration, various components used and explosives - “are known to us from other hybrid operations conducted by Russia and its war against Ukraine.”
He says “the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport on 4 August fits the established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe.”
He concludes directly that “the German government therefore concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig on 4 August.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
The German government has blamed Russia for the drone attack on Leipzig airport last month, calling it “dangerous behaviour” and part of a systematic and concerted effort by Moscow to “cause great damage” through hybrid attacks in Europe (17:41).
German foreign and interior ministers said the attempted attack fitted a broader pattern of Russian behaviour across Europe (17:38), warning Germany is “not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare” (17:43).
Berlin ordered Russia to close its remaining consulate in Bonn and its Russian House of Science and Culture in Berlin as part of a package of retaliatory measures (17:46, 19:19).
The ministers also insisted Germany will continue its support for Ukraine (17:49).
In a coordinated show of support, Nato, EU and national leaders rallied behind Germany, joining in condemning Moscow’s hybrid attacks in Europe (17:50, 17:53, 18:00, 18:01, 18:09, 18:32, 18:37, 18:52, 18:54, 19:24, 19:25).
Russia’s foreign ministry said it would respond to “all anti-Russian actions” in due course (18:14).
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen will hold talks with Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte on Wednesday to discuss this issue, among others (12:17), while EU ministers are set to hold talks in Ireland.
Elsewhere,
Several devices – believed to be in “double digits” – were found near a power substation in the eastern region of Brandenburg in what investigators believe was an attempt to cause a power outage in the region (14:38, 16:57, 17:15, 17:26).
At least 12 people were killed in Russian overnight attacks on Ukraine with “dozens” more injured (9:52, 10:34).
Separately,
King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance before Norway’s parliament in the first major stage in the passing of the crown since the death of his father after 35 years on the throne (12:39, 12:59, 13:01, 13:09, 13:13, 13:15, 13:20, 13:32).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
'Russia considers itself at war with Europe, even if Europe does not see itself at war with Russia,' Ukraine's FM warns
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha warned that “Russia’s hybrid attack at the Leipzig airport is part of its aggressive strategy toward Germany and the rest of Europe.”
“Acts of sabotage, disinformation, election meddling, espionage, attack on critical infrastructure and industrial facilities. These are not incidents, but part of Russia’s deliberate strategy. And they cannot go unpunished, because this will only fuel the aggressor’s appetite. We express solidarity with Germany and call for strong responses to Russia’s brazen actions, including additional sanctions.”
He added that “Europe needs a decisive strategy to counter Russian threats, especially ahead of next year’s elections throughout Europe.”
“Ukraine stands ready to share its vast experience and protect Euro-Atlantic stability. The reality is that Russia considers itself at war with Europe. Even if Europe does not see itself at war with Russia. Supporting Ukraine and increasing pressure on Russia are the best responses to Leipzig and other similar incidents.”
The Bonn consulate – which will now have to close by 18 September – is Russia’s last remaining consular post in Germany, aside from its embassy in Berlin.
It’s the latest escalation in diplomatic relations between the two countries.
In 2023, the German foreign ministry revoked the licences for four other Russian consulates in Frankfurt, Hamburg, Munich and Leipzig, after Moscow moved to cap the number of German officials allowed in Russia and Germany had to shut its own consulates in Kaliningrad, Ekaterinburg, and Novosibirsk.
At the moment, Germany still has two diplomatic outposts in Russia: its main embassy in Moscow and its last remaining consulate in St Petersburg. It also has three honorary consults in Kazan, Saratov and Vladivostok, its website shows.
Following today’s decision, it’s probably not entirely unreasonable to suspect Russia may target that St Petersburg post as part of its response.
'The security of our allies is the security of us all,' Meloni says as she backs Germany's measures against Russia
Italy’s prime minister Giorgia Meloni also throws her support behind Germany’s actions.
“Italy stands in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig.
The security of our Allies is the security of us all. Attempts to intimidate us or to drive a wedge between Allies will not succeed: hybrid actions against any one of us are a matter of concern for all of us, and will be met with a united response.
At times like this, it is essential to remain steadfast, to keep working closely together, and to maintain a credible posture of deterrence in defence of our citizens’ security.”
'Russia must stop its war ... instead of escalating,' EU's Costa says
European Council president António Costa is the latest European leader to offer solidarity with Germany and condemn Russia’s actions.
In a statement, he said:
“We condemn in the strongest possible terms Russia’s attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport. Russia must stop its war of aggression against Ukraine, instead of escalating.
The EU stands in full solidarity with Germany.
The EU remains strong and united and Russia will not prevail. Our support to Ukraine is unwavering. We will work with Germany and other Member States to ramp up the pressure on Russia until it shows a willingness to change course.”
Hungary 'deeply concerned by growing number and intensity of Russian hybrid activities,' minister says
Hungarian deputy prime minister and foreign minister Anita Orbán said that Budapest is “deeply concerned by the growing number and intensity of Russian hybrid activities on European soil.”
“Recent incidents in Germany demonstrate an increasingly dangerous and reckless pattern of behaviour that poses a serious threat to European security and resilience.
Hungary stands in full solidarity with Germany and is ready to support our partner in countering hybrid threats.
In the face of these challenges, strengthening the resilience, unity and collective preparedness of the European Union and Nato is more important than ever.”
'Russia will not win this war,' Poland's Tusk says
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk is the latest leader to comment on Germany’s move to name Russia as responsible for the Leipzig attack.
In a post on X, he said:
“Poland, the Baltic states, Romania, and now Germany. Russia is escalating tension across the whole region. We’ll not be intimidated and our response will be our continued support for Ukraine and full coordination of NATO states against the aggressor. Russia will not win this war.”
Moscow to 'respond to all anti-Russian actions,' foreign ministry says
Russian foreign ministry told Interfax news agency that Russia “will respond to all anti-Russian actions” after Germany’s move to publicly blame Moscow for last month’s Leipzig drone attack.
Several other EU leaders have issued their versions of the statement, which in many parts are almost exactly the same.
Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson says he will chair a meeting of the National Security Council tomorrow to discuss Stockholm’s response to the incident.
“We are united, and we will continue to stand up for our ally and neighbour,” he says.
Lithuania’s president Gitanas Nausėda also says he assured chancellor Merz of Vilnius’s “full solidarity.”
“The strong measures taken by the German government show: Hybrid action against any one of us will be met with a clear response. Anyone who attacks us will pay a price,” he says.
“Finland stands in full solidarity with its ally Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig.
We know the Russian playbook. It attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine in its defense against Russia’s invasion. It will not succeed.
We will stand united and deter anyone from attacking our freedom and security.
As the strong measures announced by the German government show, any action against any one of us will be met with a clear response.
Our commitment to supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russia’s aggression is unwavering.
I continue to be in close touch with Chancellor Merz and other Allies.”
EU ministers to discuss next steps tonight and tomorrow, Poland's Sikorski says
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski also backs Germany’s statement and says EU foreign ministers will discuss the next steps during their meeting in Ireland tonight and tomorrow.
He says:
“Poland stands foursquare behind every ally attacked by Russia’s hybrid war. In this case, full solidarity with Germany. Looking forward to discussing collective countermeasures at the Gymnich meeting in Ireland tonight and tomorrow.”
Sikorski has a history with closing down Russian consulates in response to what Poland said were Russian-inspired acts of sabotage in Poland.

articles.title: Jordan says air defenses intercepted 10 of 13 ballistic missiles entering airspace: Reports
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gökmen
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
Jordanian air defenses intercepted 10 of 13 ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom’s airspace, while three fell in remote areas, the Jordan News Agency reported Wednesday.
The report came amid heightened tensions in the region and a second Iranian missile attack directed toward Jordan in less than 48 hours.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said earlier that it had targeted a US Marine base in Jordan, known as “Camp Titin,” with ballistic missiles in retaliation for a US strike on a residence hosting a wedding ceremony in Sirik County, in Iran’s Hormozgan province.
The IRGC claimed that numerous US soldiers were killed in the attack, while the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said Tuesday that it had launched strikes against IRGC targets inside Iran. Iranian officials said an initial assessment showed at least four people were killed and 50 injured after a US strike hit a residence and wedding ceremony in Kuhestek.

articles.title: Thai resort prepares to host USS Abraham Lincoln sailors after more than 270 days at sea
articles.body:
Authorities in the Thai resort city of Pattaya have stepped up security as they prepare to welcome thousands of sailors and marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln who have spent more than 270 consecutive days at sea.
“About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” the provincial governor, Narit Niramaiwong, told AFP.
The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier sailed past Singapore over the weekend on its way back to the US after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East as part of the US war against Iran.
It left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before the US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.
Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health onboard, including attempted suicides, have made headlines in the US and provoked criticism of Donald Trump’s war against Iran.
Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the carrier would dock just after midnight on Wednesday (about 5pm GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port. About 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups before the carrier departs on Sunday.
After meeting US officials on Monday, Poramase said service members would be banned from certain recreational activities such as parasailing and cannabis use. Medical cannabis was legalised in Thailand in 2022 and dispensaries have become common in Thai cities.
Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam war in the 1960s, when US soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation.
The city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.
Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied this was linked to the US arrivals.
Government officials are warning local businesses not to overcharge US sailors, and Poramase said there would be a greater police presence in popular areas along Pattaya beach and Walking Street.
The city’s police chief, Anek Srathongyoo, said law enforcements agencies had been ordered to step up security measures to prevent undesirable situations. He said that if any US service members broke Thai law, they would be prosecuted accordingly.
Local business owners feeling the tourism slump from the Iran war are eager for the new arrivals. A banner hung over a local bar near a beach read: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.”
Bualuang Ponok, a bar employee, said she had seen US service members during past visits but she did not expect many from this crew. “They said 5,000 people will come here but how many will reach us?” she said.
Earlier in August, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington relieved the long-deployed Lincoln in the Middle East. The Lincoln, one of the US navy’s largest warships, was part of American efforts in the Iran war, which flared back up over the weekend for the first time in a month.
The deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 270 days. Trump downplayed concerns over conditions onboard and said the deployment was “not nearly long enough”.
Thai officials have said the Lincoln will return to the US after its port call in Thailand.
Associated Press and Agence France-Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Kallas: Tough summer for Putin, EU to further increase support for Ukraine
articles.body:
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said Russia had suffered significant economic and personnel losses over the summer, while EU member states were preparing tougher sanctions against Moscow and planned to further increase support for Ukraine.
Kallas made the remarks in Wicklow, Ireland, on Tuesday following an informal meeting of EU defence ministers, which was also attended by Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara.
She said the EU would increase support for Ukraine while continuing to invest in its own defence, describing this as the most effective way to stop Russian President Vladimir Putin. Kallas added that the EU was also preparing its most far-reaching sanctions against Russia.
According to her, Ukraine was increasing military pressure on Russia, with Ukrainian drones disrupting Russian logistics and striking oil refineries deep inside the country, contributing to what she described as Russia's worst fuel crisis in a decade. She also said Russia was losing more than 30,000 troops a month and concluded that the summer had been difficult for Putin.
Kallas said Khmara had stressed during the meeting that air defence remained Ukraine's top priority. She noted, however, that interceptor missiles were in short supply across Europe. She thanked EU member states for reviewing their stockpiles again and said Patriot missiles nearing the end of their service life should, in particular, be transferred or sold to Ukraine.
She added that member states were also considering reallocating existing orders and approaching partners for additional supplies. Kallas stressed that every interceptor provided to Ukraine reduced the risk of a Russian missile hitting a Ukrainian school, home or hospital, while every form of assistance to Ukraine also strengthened European security.
Turning to financial support, Kallas said bilateral assistance to Ukraine needed to continue. She noted that, in addition to equipment, Ukraine required modernised training facilities. Kallas recalled that earlier in the year she had proposed funding the modernisation of training grounds in Ukraine and thanked member states, including Ireland, for providing additional funding for this purpose.
She also said ministers had discussed the future of the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM), including the creation of a coordination group in Kyiv aimed at better incorporating battlefield experience and strengthening military education.
Kallas further noted that cooperation between Ukraine and the EU in the defence industry was expanding. She said there were now more than 120 industrial partnerships between Ukrainian and European companies and described Ukraine as a global leader in battlefield innovation. According to her, deeper integration between Ukrainian and European defence companies was in the mutual interest of both sides.

articles.title: ‘Germany and Russia are at war,’ says top defense exec
articles.body:
German defense entrepreneur Stefan Thumann argued sabotage operations carried out by Moscow against his country are an “act of war … controlled and coordinated here by the Russian armed forces.”
Speaking exclusively with Paul Ronzheimer of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network in a podcast episode released Tuesday, Thumann rejected the “hybrid war” label used by EU leaders to describe the Kremlin’s campaign in Europe.
“Germany and Russia are at war,” he insisted.
Advertisement
The warning lands as Berlin hardens its stance on suspected Russian sabotage. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is preparing to blame Moscow for an attempted drone attack in Leipzig and unveil “extensive” sanctions, officials told POLITICO and WELT AM SONNTAG.
Thumann’s company, Donaustahl, supplies combat drones to Ukraine, according to the executive. He says he has been forced to live under round-the-clock protection after authorities uncovered an alleged Russian intelligence plan to poison him in 2025.
Authorities warned him shortly before Christmas that he could be in danger. “Yes, it comes from Russia. And yes, it is very serious — your life is at risk,” he said they told him. Within days, a suspected low-level operative had been detained.
Thumann said he had turned official addresses into surveillance-heavy “honeypots” — locations deliberately designed to lure hostile actors into a trap. “The low-level operatives were only there to find out where I was,” he added. “Then an assassination using poison was supposed to be carried out.”
The threat has upended his life. Thumann said he now lives at undisclosed locations with bodyguards, has not seen his family for months, and has prepared a will and advance health care directive in case he is killed.
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network is a multi-publication initiative publishing scoops, investigations, interviews, op-eds and analysis that reverberate across the world. It connects journalists from Axel Springer brands—including POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, and Onet— on major stories for an international audience. Their ambitious reporting stretches across Axel Springer platforms: online, print, TV, and audio. Together, the outlets reach hundreds of millions of people worldwide.

articles.title: What 248 books reveal about Kaja Kallas
articles.body:
While actively running the EU’s foreign policy on the world’s most demanding issues, Kaja Kallas still finds time outside work to read about … more foreign policy.
The top EU diplomat and former Estonian prime minister frequently talks about her love of reading, citing her favorite authors in speeches and meeting with them privately to discuss their work. Since taking up her most recent post in December 2024, she has read at least 52 books she has shared publicly — all of which she has posted on her Instagram — most of them related to international affairs. In total, she has shared more than 200 titles since 2017.
“You know, my reading list is quite long,” said Kallas, who officially serves as the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, at a press conference in January. “By the end, when I finish this job, I will be very smart,” she joked.
Advertisement
The collection closely tracks the subjects Kallas is most involved with in her role, evolving alongside her professional remit: 24 books on Russia and Ukraine, nine on China, and seven on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Further-flung regions pop up only rarely, with just three books on the rest of East Asia and none on South American politics beyond Venezuela.
“Reading books is a valuable advantage, especially as it is not so common nowadays,” an official from Kallas’ team told POLITICO. “The Middle East wars, Russia’s aggression and China’s growing influence are major geopolitical issues, so naturally they feature on the High Representative’s reading list.” Noting that she meets with ministers, officials, staff and experts daily and receives countless briefing papers, memos and other sources of information, “books are a nice addition on long-distance flights,” the official added.
The reading lists alone have not shaped the full contours of Kallas’ foreign policy, of course. But they provide a view into which political subjects Europe’s chief diplomat is interested in learning more about and where she goes looking for answers.
So, what does Kallas’ bookshelf reveal about the person shaping Europe’s diplomacy? To find out, POLITICO reviewed the 248 titles she has included on public reading lists since 2017 and spoke to 24 of the authors.
Noted bookworm
Kallas is not the only avid reader in Brussels, but few politicians talk about their love of literature quite as often. Since 2023, she has released reading lists twice a year on Instagram, and before that, she blogged about her latest reads monthly.
“I read a lot, but you’re always influenced by the books you’ve read most recently,” Kallas told POLITICO in 2025.
Political scientist Ivan Krastev, who co-authored 2019’s “The Light That Failed: A Reckoning” on why liberalism failed to spread in Eastern Europe, said Kallas had reached out to him after reading his book. She was trying to find a publisher to translate it into her native Estonian, he told POLITICO. The translation was eventually released in 2022.
Advertisement
While Kallas was prime minister, her government had similarly pushed for the translation of political scientist Mark Leonard’s “The Age of Unpeace: How Connectivity Causes Conflict,” which she said she would “often cite.”
“It’s interesting, particularly when a politician in a high position reads a book,” said Krastev. “They’re trying to make sense of their own experience” and “trying to answer some of the questions that [they] are struggling with.”
Indeed, Kallas’ book choices appear to closely reflect her scheduled diplomatic trips. Visiting Montenegro for the EU-Western Balkans Summit in June this year, the top diplomat had read the memoirs of Richard Holbrooke, architect of the 1995 Dayton Accords in Bosnia, and Martti Ahtisaari, the former Finnish president and mediator of the 1999 Kumanovo Agreement forcing Serbia’s withdrawal from Kosovo.
“A lot to learn also today, and actually a lot of parallels,” said Kallas of Holbrooke’s book in July.
Ahead of her trip to Sarajevo a month later, she then contacted former Swedish Prime Minister and High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina Carl Bildt about his 1998 book “Peace Journey: The Struggle for Peace in Bosnia,” a memoir about his work in the region.
“She sent me a text and said, ‘I’m reading your book, and I like it very much.’ And I said, ‘How on earth did you get hold of that one?'” Bildt told POLITICO, joking that the book was published nearly three decades ago. “She wanted to go down into the weeds of the history … and that could be useful.”
Advertisement
Earlier in the year, after the U.S. forcibly captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, Kallas picked up two books about the South American country, too: “Comandante: Hugo Chávez’s Venezuela” and “Things Are Never So Bad That They Can’t Get Worse: Inside the Collapse of Venezuela.”
“She is one of the best-read people I know,” said Marietje Schaake, a friend and former liberal MEP who served with Kallas in the European Parliament. “That depth has shaped her thinking and her career.”
What’s in the library?
Six of the authors who spoke to POLITICO for this article specifically cited Kallas’ hawkish stance on Moscow as echoing the messages in their books — perhaps unsurprising given Kallas warned of Russia’s threat to Europe back in 2021, during her first term as prime minister.
“What is happening in Ukraine right now is what I was reading about in our own history books,” she told Vogue Greece in 2023.
Sylvie Kauffmann, author of 2023’s “Blindsided” (Les aveuglés) — which argues that Germany and France failed to recognize the Russian threat — told POLITICO her book “confirms everything that Kallas thinks” about how others downplayed Moscow’s aggression.
Advertisement
Speaking to POLITICO about his 2018 book “Identity,” famed political philosopher of liberal democracy Francis Fukuyama said the work contained “a kind of ideological roadmap to be able to better explain what it is that … we’re fighting for.” Noting that Ukraine’s fight against Russia was one of the reasons he wrote it, Fukuyama then praised the chief diplomat’s support for the country.
Kallas has also read extensively on Israel-Palestine, a conflict on which her stance has attracted both attention and controversy in Brussels.
Far more critical of Israel than her peers in the European Commission, Kallas reportedly compared the situation on the ground to South Africa under apartheid during a closed-door meeting in June, causing Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar to sever contact.
Two of the authors on the subject who feature on Kallas’ reading lists told POLITICO her reported comparison mirrored the arguments made in their books, with 2024 Pulitzer Prize winner Nathan Thrall saying his “aim in writing [“A Day in the Life of Abed Salama: Anatomy of a Jerusalem Tragedy”] was to influence people like her.”
“The fact that she has come to the conclusion that Israel is practicing apartheid is most welcome as far as I’m concerned,” he said.
“I explain the aspects of apartheid, and I hope she’d see that her judgment is well founded,” echoed Michael Scott-Baumann, author of “Palestinians and Israelis: A Short History of Conflict.”
Advertisement
But not every author on Kallas’ lists approves of her foreign policy decisions when it comes to their topics of specialization.
Kim Ghattas, who wrote her book “Black Wave” on the Middle East, for example, said Kallas has been too passive on the Israeli-U.S. war with Iran. “That is not good policymaking. I would hope that reading books like mine can help prepare policymakers like her, specifically for moments like the one that we find ourselves in right now.”
Former U.S. National Security Adviser John Bolton, who has long advocated for regime change in Iran, said he, too, wished Kallas had become more involved — though in support of President Donald Trump’s military operation.
He also noted that Kallas’ blunt style risked further alienating the U.S. from the EU, with her comments advocating for the bloc’s sovereignty “giving [Trump] the excuse to do what he probably wants to do anyway.”
Criticism extended beyond the Middle East as well. Robert D. Kaplan, author of 1993’s “Balkan Ghosts” — which heavily influenced former U.S. President Bill Clinton’s initial reluctance to militarily intervene in the region, according to his biographers — told POLITICO that Kallas’ impolitic moments “may be things that she’ll come to partially regret over time.”
“When you get far quick, you tend to make mistakes. Because you’re confident, you’re even arrogant,” said Kaplan.
Booking ahead
It’s not all about world affairs and global diplomacy, though — some of Kallas’ more recent political predicaments lie a little closer to home.
Recent months have seen the top diplomat losing a turf war with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over the bloc’s foreign policy, while her diplomatic service, the European External Action Service, has struggled to build consensus across a divided Europe.
So with the rentrée almost upon us in Brussels, there may be no better time for Kallas to get through a few more books — a strategy she has turned to previously.
Advertisement
While serving as prime minister, during a 2023 podcast, Kallas recalled how she once considered foreign policy to be her greatest political weakness — until she turned to books.
“It’s not my weakness anymore because I’ve read so much about this,” she said.
Perhaps this time it will be Brussels that sends her back to the stacks.

articles.title: Armenia drops Russia’s ‘strategic partner’ label, but foreign minister says alliance remains
articles.body:
Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said in an interview aired on 31 August that Russia remains "more than a strategic partner" because existing treaties make the two countries allies, adding that the change in the government program's wording should not be interpreted as an end to that relationship.
Mirzoyan was responding to Armenia's new 2026–2031 government program, which replaces the "strategic ally" and "strategic partnership" language used in the previous five-year plan with a commitment to "transform and deepen" relations with Russia. The previous program referred to an "Armenian-Russian strategic alliance" and pledged to strengthen "allied relations and strategic partnership" with Moscow.
Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan explained on 27 August that keeping the strategic-partnership language would raise questions about why Russia and the Russia-led Collective Security Treaty Organization had failed to fulfill their security obligations to Armenia in 2022.
Armenia has removed the language of alliance from its government program without ending the treaties, CSTO membership, or energy ties that still bind it to Moscow.
Azerbaijan attacked Armenian territory near Jermuk in September 2022, striking positions inside sovereign Armenia rather than the disputed Nagorno-Karabakh region. Yerevan invoked Article 4 of the Collective Security Treaty, the clause treating an attack on one member as an attack on all, and requested assistance. The alliance sent a fact-finding mission but no troops. requested military assistance. Armenia froze its participation in the CSTO at all levels in 2024, stopped financing it, and has boycotted its summits and military exercises.
Why the alliance frayed
Armenian trust in Moscow had deteriorated further by September 2023, when Azerbaijan retook Nagorno-Karabakh after a brief offensive and Russian peacekeepers deployed to the region did not intervene. Armenian officials accused them of failing to protect the enclave's population.
Yerevan has since moved closer to the European Union. In March 2025, Armenia's parliament passed a law to launch the accession process, though Pashinyan has said any actual membership would require a referendum, and Armenia has not applied to join.
What still ties Armenia to Russia
Even so, Armenia remains heavily dependent on Russia for energy. Russia supplied the bulk of Armenia's natural gas in 2021, and Armenia imports all of its nuclear fuel from Russia, leaving it effectively reliant on imported fuel for nearly 70% of its electricity, according to the International Energy Agency. The country remains a member of the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union.
Mirzoyan acknowledged that strains had emerged in recent years, citing statements by Russian officials, coverage in Russian media, and Moscow's restrictions on imports of Armenian goods. He called for relations to be made "healthier" and returned to a course of "mutual respect," and said Yerevan did not want a "war of words" with Moscow. Pashinyan said on 1 September that he expected to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin later that day in Bishkek.

articles.title: Polish Fighter Jets Intercept Russian Il-20 Reconnaissance Aircraft for Seventh Time in 2026
articles.body:
Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 ELINT surveillance-reconnaissance aircraft near the Polish coast.
Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Polish Minister of National Defense, announced this.
Approximately 30 km north of Łeba, the fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft flying over the Baltic Sea.
According to the Polish military, the Russian aircraft did not violate Polish airspace. Polish fighter jets intercepted and escorted it in accordance with established procedures.
The Polish Armed Forces noted that Russia was once again testing the readiness of Poland’s deterrence and air defense systems.
Since the beginning of 2026, Polish fighter jets have intercepted Russian military aircraft over the Baltic Sea at least nine times.
The first recorded incident occurred on March 13, when Polish MiG-29s intercepted and escorted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft.
The number of such incidents increased in April. On April 8, Polish F-16s intercepted a Russian Il-20. The following day, April 9, Polish fighter jets intercepted another Russian Il-20.
On April 24, Polish F-16s intercepted two Russian Su-30 fighter jets over the Baltic Sea.
The next such incident was recorded on May 13, when Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over international waters in the Baltic Sea.
July was particularly active. On July 14, Polish fighter jets intercepted an Il-20 approximately 30 km off the coast of Ustka. On July 15, they intercepted two Russian Su-30SM2 fighter jets that had arrived from the Kaliningrad region.
On July 16, Polish aircraft were scrambled twice to intercept Russian aircraft. First, the fighter jets intercepted two Su-30s, and later that same day, an Il-20.
Thus, in 2026, Polish fighter jets have conducted nine separate interception operations involving Russian military aircraft.
In addition to Poland, multinational forces under NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission also protect the airspace of the Baltic states.
In June 2026, French Rafale fighter jets conducting NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission intercepted six Russian military aircraft in the Baltic region.

articles.title: From Bill Gates to Bernie Sanders, most agree the AI arms race is disastrous. Only Europe can make it stop | Alexander Hurst
articles.body:
At this point, it should be clear that AI is a choose-your-own-adventure book where every option ends in disaster. Exploding carbon emissions and ecological collapse? Turn to page 37. Other outcomes include some or all of: the bubble bursting and an ensuing financial crisis; mass unemployment via automation; the end of democracy and the rise of authoritarian surveillance states; raving cults who believe the pattern-matching algorithm is a consciousness; terrorists who create devastating bioweapons; nation states that deploy autonomous weapons systems that act on non-human timeframes; nation states or terrorists that hack all the myriad systems we depend on; or an AI that, conscious or not, pursues directives that are at odds with human wellbeing.
Imagining that people such as Elon Musk, the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, Palantir’s Peter Thiel and the Trump administration tech adviser Marc Andreessen will lead us to a utopian future of flourishing environmentalism, social harmony and endless leisure requires hallucination and sycophancy so great that that choose-your-own-adventure scenario could only have been written by ChatGPT.
There is a growing, if wildly delayed, realisation that we are heading for calamity, with accompanying calls to slow down, regulate or even put all of this on pause while we wrap our minds around it. These calls are coming not only from activists, but from a collection of politicians, experts and big-tech insiders too ecumenical to dismiss, from Bernie Sanders to Bill Gates, who wrote recently that “if someone had a credible plan for slowing down AI advances globally, I would likely support it”. He is merely the latest insider to acknowledge the reality that AI company Anthropic did earlier this summer, when it called for a “brake pedal”. Industry self-restraint will not work. A pause, if there is to be one, must be imposed from the outside.
Despite this, an international agreement is sadly unlikely. AI is analogous to nuclear weaponry, and follows the same logic: each individual actor is incentivised to run this foolish race, with the sole justification that it does not want to be at the mercy of whoever wins. The best chance of inducing a slowdown, it seems, would be for a single actor to control a choke-point, and have an incentive to close it. Curiously, the EU holds such a card – and even has an incentive to play it, should it dare.
The Dutch tech company ASML is Europe’s most valuable company, thanks to its production of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. These underlie the most advanced chip-making in the world, and as such are one of few possible choke-points on the entire AI industry. ASML has mastered the technology and intricate supply chain to make the $400m per unit machines needed to etch patterns on to silicon, where light is focused to a 13.5 nanometre wavelength (about 1/10,000th of the width of a human hair). Without its machines, there are no chips; without the chips, there are no more datacentres. That means everything from Taiwanese chip-maker TSMC’s $265bn investment in future fabrication facilities (known as “fabs”), to the $7tn-worth of datacentres that the industry is expected to build globally (though primarily in the US) by 2030. Without more datacentres using these current and next-generation chips, AI’s progression along an exponential growth (and risk) curve would come to a halt.
This is why the US government imposes extraterritorial export controls on ASML, blocking exports of its most advanced EUV machines to China in an effort to slow down its advanced chip-fabrication abilities. In imposing those restrictions on ASML, the US has revealed its own vulnerability to this choke-point: as much as Europe is dependent on (ultimately replicable) financial and software services from the US, the future of all chip-based technology is wholly dependent on ASML. A straight ban on exports of ASML’s machines would force the global AI industry to in effect tread water, to jog in place.
The resulting chip shortage and slowdown in the development of AI would give regulators time to catch up with the technology, give lawmakers time to update everything from copyright law to tax law, and give societies time to have real debates about what role we want AI to play in our lives.
Why would the EU do such a thing? Not merely for humanist reasons, but for self-interested ones. In the best case, a flat export ban would result in a reorganisation of the supply chain, and bring more crucial decisions under EU jurisdiction – where it would be subject to the regulatory oversight of the only player that has shown it will regulate AI extensively. Of course, the best case is a far-fetched one: it is more likely that the US would retaliate by blocking ASML’s access to US-based suppliers. But even if this happened, it would still be in the EU’s interests to provoke such a showdown, based on the narrow logic of pure economic and geopolitical self-interest, in that the EU would cease to fall behind in relative terms in AI models and the datacentre “compute” (processing power) needed to run them.
Europe’s own AI-boosters agree – even though what concerns them is the EU’s relative disadvantage, rather than AI’s vast panoply of risks. The Europe 2031 project is a techno-political forecast – compiled by a group of industry experts – of what might happen to the EU in a scenario in which AI radically transforms the economy, and the EU lags far behind the US. They argue that Europe must throw hundreds of billions into the AI arms race before both frontier models and “compute” become what TSMC and ASML are today: beneficiaries of a gap too large for any competitor to close.
In their scenario, sometime in the near future the EU will be forced to put access to ASML on the table in order to secure access to the US-controlled models and compute that its economy and security will come to depend on – only to find that ASML’s supremacy has weakened over time. (The more EUV machines that get exported, the more fabs get built elsewhere, and the more time China and the US have to replicate ASML’s technology.)
Nuclear-weapons theorists worry that, if the unspeakable were to happen, states would be pushed towards launching because of a “use it or lose it” calculation. The exact same calculation applies to the one thing that can halt the breakneck development of the AI industry: the EU can use the leverage that ASML gives it at present or risk losing the chance entirely. It’s rare that disparate groups all arrive at a similar conclusion: there is one single European card to play, and that it must be played. Instead of racing towards folly, let’s just halt the race. Right now, and for everyone.
- 
  Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoir Generation Desperation is out now

articles.title: Putin says Zelensky’s warning to civilian airlines operating in Russian airspace ‘amounts to state terrorism’
articles.body:
Putin says Zelensky’s warning to civilian airlines operating in Russian airspace ‘amounts to state terrorism’
Russian President Vladimir Putin called Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s remarks about threats to the safety of Russia’s skies “amounts to state terrorism.” “And I’d point out that they’re the ones asking us to resume talks, asking for face-to-face meetings. You don’t negotiate with terrorists,” Putin said.
He also said that “if tragedies like this do happen, we’ll find a way to answer.”
In his evening address, Zelensky warned airlines that Russia’s skies are “becoming completely unsafe,” declaring that “the safe days in Russia’s skies are over.”
The Russian Armed Forces have been given orders to prepare and carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities, Putin said at a press conference in Bishkek following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit.
“They’re striking ours — they’ll get an answer,” he also said.

articles.title: Why did Modi urge Putin to end Ukraine war - and will he listen?
articles.body:
Why did Modi urge Putin to end Ukraine war - and will he listen?
- Published
Russian President Vladimir Putin has been urged by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a close ally, to end Moscow's war against Ukraine.
"Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said on Monday.
Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
BBC correspondents in Delhi and Moscow look at what lies behind Modi's renewed appeal for peace, and Putin's response.
Modi's comments on ending the war in Ukraine are not surprising and don't suggest any tactical change in India's foreign policy.
In fact, speaking on the sidelines of a regional summit in 2022 - less than a year into the conflict - Modi told Putin publicly that "now is not the time for war".
But it would be an oversimplification to suggest that Modi's current or past statements on the war can be seen as a rebuff to Putin or Russia's strategy.
Western countries have pushed Modi hard to take a clear stand on the war - but Delhi has largely stayed neutral, urging dialogue to end the war instead.
The stand hasn't made many Western capitals happy but they have continued to court Modi and India - it's just too big and too fast-growing an economy to be ignored.
In this context, Modi's current statement cannot be seen as an attempt to please a third country.
If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly?
The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses.
Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades.
Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries.
But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association.
Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs.
So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats.
As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war.
This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine.
Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table.
He didn't. And he hasn't.
There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations.
To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied:
"Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path."
Polite, but vague. And non-committal.
After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long.
And "moving forward" at what pace?
And, crucially, on which path?
All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success.
Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on.
Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory.
And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country.
In recent days Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine.
"After [Russia] intensified its strikes on Ukraine's military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure," wrote the Kommersant newspaper this morning, "the Russian side is convinced that in the military confrontation time is working against Kyiv."
While Putin believes that, he'll be reluctant to pause his so-called "special military operation".
  - Published14 hours ago

articles.title: Iran’s top military cmdr. urges stronger defense preparedness
articles.body:
In a message to the commander of Iran’s Air Defense Force on the occasion of Air Defense Day, Major General Abdollahi congratulated the force’s personnel and highlighted the key expectations outlined in the appointment decree of martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei.
He described those expectations as a clear roadmap for the transformation and advancement of the strategic force, particularly amid the current critical circumstances facing Iran.
The top general said Iran is currently facing the “third imposed American-Zionist war,” adding that the country’s defense strategy should focus on offensive defense capabilities and the creation of an integrated, active, dynamic and preemptive air defense network.
Major General Abdollahi also stressed the need to connect all reconnaissance, radar and missile layers through an intelligent and resilient network capable of intercepting and neutralizing potential threats at the greatest possible distance.
He further called for the localization and smartification of defense systems through the development of advanced technologies and the deployment of systems designed specifically for electronic and cyber warfare.
“Reliance on domestic capabilities and elite young people” is essential to enhancing the Air Defense Force’s electronic and cyber warfare capabilities, the commander said.
MNA

articles.title: NATO jets scramble after drones enter Baltic airspace
articles.body:
NATO fighter aircraft were scrambled after drones entered the airspace of Estonia and Latvia during the early hours of 1 September, with Estonian authorities issuing an air-threat warning as one aircraft approached the country’s border with Russia, according to the Estonian Defence Forces.
The Estonian Defence Forces said the warning was issued after drones involved in a Ukrainian strike against targets in Russia flew close to the border and briefly entered Estonian airspace. Residents in affected areas were alerted as the situation developed.
Estonian Air Force Commander Brigadier General Riivo Valge said an air-threat alert was issued at around 3am local time after a drone approached Estonian airspace near Narva, the northern border city immediately adjacent to Russia. According to Valge, the drone subsequently changed course and returned towards Russian territory.
The incident formed part of a wider overnight airspace alert involving both Estonia and Latvia, with NATO fighter aircraft scrambled after drones entered the airspace of the two Alliance members. The information released so far does not identify the NATO aircraft involved in the response, their operating bases or how long the incursions lasted.
Estonia’s warning system was activated while the drone was approaching the country’s eastern border, allowing authorities to notify residents while military personnel monitored its movement. Narva sits directly on the Estonian-Russian frontier, separated from the Russian city of Ivangorod by the Narva River. The area is one of NATO’s easternmost borders and lies immediately alongside Russian territory.
The 1 September alert differed from routine interceptions in that the aircraft involved were drones associated with a strike against targets inside Russia rather than conventional crewed military aircraft.
The Estonian Defence Forces said the drones had been used in a Ukrainian attack against targets in Russia before flying close to the border, with at least one briefly entering Estonian airspace.
NATO aircraft were subsequently scrambled in response to the incursions affecting Estonia and Latvia, while Estonian authorities issued warnings to residents in the areas considered potentially affected.

articles.title: Iran launched 13 missiles at Jordan, most of which were intercepted by air defenses
articles.body:
Iran launched 13 missiles at Jordan, most of which were intercepted by air defenses
Kyiv • UNN
Iran launched a missile strike against Jordan. Jordanian air defenses intercepted 10 of the 13 ballistic missiles; three fell in remote areas.
Iran launched missile strikes against Jordan on Tuesday evening, September 1. At the same time, most of the Iranian missiles were shot down by air defense systems. This was reported by The Times of Israel, according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that at approximately 11:00 p.m., messages warning of possible danger were sent to the mobile phones of residents of Jordan. Shortly beforehand, information emerged that Iran had launched missiles toward the country. A few minutes later, an air raid alert was declared in the country.
Jordanian air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 13 ballistic missiles that entered the Kingdom's airspace, successfully intercepting and destroying 10 of them.
They clarified that three missiles fell in remote areas far from populated areas.
We remind you
The day before, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of Iran stated that it had carried out strikes on U.S. military facilities in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates in response to the U.S. attack on Larak Island.
Iran attacked a US base in Jordan29.07.26, 05:33 • 17019 views

articles.title: IDF conducts strikes across Gaza Strip amid reports of attempted kidnapping of Hamas official
articles.body:
The IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) on Tuesday night confirmed in a statement that they had captured Hamas’s head of internal security in the Gaza Strip in the first high-level capture operation deep in Gaza in a long time.
The official statement did not make any direct mention of Gaza gangs being central to the operation, though there was a hint with a reference to Shin Bet’s “special forces.”
However, The Jerusalem Post and other media have received clear indications, along with confirmations in foreign reports, that anti-Hamas Gaza gangs were at the heart of the operation, even while supported by the IDF and the Shin Bet.
Another mystery that was solved over the course of the day was the importance of the Hamas official who has been arrested.
Earlier in the day, an Israeli official told the Post that the captured terrorist is Mu’in al-Arabid, head of Hamas’s internal security apparatus, which would have made him one of the top security officials in the Strip.
Katz, Netanyahu play up al-Arabid's importance to Hamas
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz both sought to emphasize Arabid’s importance, with the prime minister saying he played a major role in managing the hiding of the over 250 Israeli hostages after October 7, 2023.
However, a Palestinian source in Gaza told the Post that the man captured was in charge of Hamas’s internal security department in the area of Gaza City only, which would have made him more of a mid-level official.
The source added that members of an anti-Hamas group played a role in the operation and that the terror organization is trying to “downplay the incident” and “its internal security forces are actively pursuing militias supported by Israel.”
The final statement by the IDF and the Shin Bet seemed to settle on the official being more important than Hamas claimed but less important than Netanyahu and Katz contended.
While multiple Hamas chiefs of internal security and of Hamas’s entirely military have been killed, the terror group, while severely weakened, remains in control of the Palestinian population in the Strip.
“A short time ago, a senior Hamas terrorist was arrested, and this is our policy: We do not wait for threats. Instead, we pursue Hamas terrorists, thwart them, and destroy their terrorist infrastructure. We have built a strong and unprecedented security zone in Gaza to protect residents and IDF soldiers,” Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday afternoon.
Strangely, Katz added, “Any attempt to bypass the security zone through aerial launches will be met with a harsh response,” though Hamas has not attacked Israel from the air. The balloons Hamas sent into Israel last week had already resulted in an increase in Israeli assassinations of Hamas officials.
Netanyahu congratulated the Shin Bet and IDF for their “bold action in arresting the head of Hamas’s general security apparatus from his home,” in a statement released on Tuesday evening.
He called the terrorist “one of the most senior Hamas leaders,” adding that he was “responsible for hiding and transporting our hostages, hiding Hamas senior figures, and building the terror force, including attempting to restore the terror group’s capabilities.”
The prime minister added, “Recently, he was involved in attempts to restore Hamas’s governance in Gaza, deception on the issue of demilitarizing the strip, and assisting in carrying out terrorist acts against the IDF and Israeli civilians.”
It was unclear what strategic change could be achieved in the standoff with Hamas by means of this operation. Yet its daring, coupled with the entrance of Israeli-aligned forces deeper into a Hamas enclave, has grabbed media and public attention in the lead-up to the election more than regular airstrikes – which barely register in the press most days.
What has the IDF done in Gaza recently?
Later Tuesday night, the IDF announced yet another of its nearly daily assassination airstrikes against a Hamas official.
Following a series of heavier-than-usual airstrikes, which it appears were carried out to support the Gaza gangs, the IDF stated that there had been no Israeli casualties.
Initially, Al Hadath reported that the IDF had coordinated with Gazan militias to attempt to “kidnap a figure near the Red Cross headquarters in Gaza.”
According to Al Hadath, the strikes occurred after the operation was exposed.
IDF sources would not deny foreign reports that Israel worked alongside Gazan militias to arrest the senior Hamas official.
Ten explosions were heard in the Gaza City area as a result of the strikes, Palestinian sources reported earlier on Tuesday.
Al Jazeera reported that Israeli military aircraft were flying at low altitude over the area, while Al Hadath reported that drones continued to drop a large number of bombs in the area.
Additionally, reports claimed that IDF special forces had entered the area of the American Hospital in the al-Katiba area of western Gaza City.
Palestinian reports described exchanges of fire and shooting involving special forces in western Gaza City. There were also reports of a large number of casualties among Gazans as a result of the strikes.
Separately, there were reports of smoke shells being fired in the Shati refugee camp in western Gaza City, along the coast.
Local gangs contribute, but they are not the primary drivers in toppling Hamas.
Political leaks suggesting that Gaza’s local gangs have any chance of taking over the Strip from Hamas in the near or medium term are referred to by most defense establishment figures as being divorced from reality.
Most defense officials acknowledge that each of these groups can only survive with clear IDF protection and can only confront Hamas in small and limited operations.
Even if their numbers range between the dozens and a couple of hundred, Hamas still has thousands or more foot soldiers.
In other words, these local gangs might contribute over the long term to Hamas’s fall, but most defense officials say they will not be a central component of it.
Rather, most experts agree that either some arm of the Palestinian Authority or a hybrid of the PA, Egypt, the ISF, and some outside IDF support would be needed to overcome Hamas in the long term.
James Genn and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title: US launches new strikes against Iran
articles.body:
US launches new strikes against Iran
TEHRAN — The United States has launched a fresh wave of military aggression against Iranian territory. Four projectiles struck the counties of Chabahar and Konarak in Sistan and Baluchestan, confirmed by provincial security officials and General Ali Khalil Abadi.
Concurrently, reports indicate that American forces also hit targets in Hormozgan Province. Tasnim news agency said Iran launched retaliatory strikes against US bases on Tuesday night.
The latest American strikes follow an earlier hostile US strike on Larak Island on Sunday. In immediate response, the Iranian Armed Forces retaliated against US military bases in Jordan and the UAE.
Iran has reiterated that any US aggression will be met with a crushing, decisive blow. Iranian political and defense officials have long warned that Washington’s attempts to challenge the Islamic Republic’s sovereign presence along this vital waterway only expose the enemy’s strategic bankruptcy.
